text: [founder-process] Before acting on feedback that includes a screenshot, crop the same region from your own render at 2x or more, state in one line what is actually wrong there (measured), then change only that.
why: Kestrel round 3: the words said "too rounded", the crop showed misaligned heights; acting on the words broke the loved radii.
check: the reply names the measured cause (heights, radius, offset) before the fix.

text: [founder-process] After any tweak to an accepted design, rebuild the accepted commit and diff computed styles (radius, size, colour, spacing) element by element against the new build; anything not asked for must be identical.
why: Kestrel round 3 silently sharpened every radius by about 4px when classes were "normalised"; the founder caught it immediately.
check: a diff script output with only the requested properties changed.

text: [founder-process] Record every founder message as rules in the same turn: one rule per point, verbatim quote in
why: The engine only gets better from verdicts it keeps.
check: `git log` shows a founder-taste.md change in the commit that applies the feedback.

text: [founder-process] Deliver each round as: the image (2x, plus 4K when asked), a live localhost URL, and a short list of what changed mapped to what the founder said; end with one question asking for the verdict.
why: The founder reviews visually and on the live page; mapping changes to their words lets them verify fast.
check: reply contains image, URL, change list.

text: [founder] Never hand-draw icons or logos in SVG paths; use a professional icon set (Phosphor or Lucide) or supplied/traced artwork.
why: Founder: hand-made icons look amateur ("it's ass").
check: icons come from an installed icon package or a supplied/traced file.

text: [founder] A logo is a mark plus wordmark with no rounded-rectangle container behind the mark; wordmark at 20px+ in the nav (not 17px).
why: Founder rejected icon-in-a-box logos and asked for the wordmark "a few pixels bigger".
check: nav wordmark font-size >= 20px; logo has no filled container.

text: [founder] Hero headlines use Title Case (every word capitalised) and run two lines maximum at desktop.
why: Founder asked for "title has all first letters capitalized" and two lines max.
check: h1 renders <= 2 lines at 1440px; each word starts uppercase.

text: [founder] The hero subtitle runs two lines maximum at desktop (about 100-120 characters at 18px in a ~520px measure).
why: Founder: "title and subtitle two lines max".
check: hero p renders <= 2 lines at 1440px.

text: [founder] Nav is divided: a white pill holding logo, a hairline divider and the links on the left, and the actions (Log in, primary) on the right; both aligned to the content edges, with generous spacing (40px link targets, 14px link padding, 20px around the divider).
why: Founder preferred the divided nav over a single full-width bar, but wanted it "spaced out better" and aligned with the content.
check: nav pill left edge == content left edge; actions right edge == content right edge.

text: [founder] Everything in the hero shares one left edge (nav, chip, headline, body, buttons, product card) on the content gutter inside the rail.
why: Founder asked for the nav "to be aligned with the other stuff".
check: left x of nav, chip, h1, p, actions and first card are equal within 1px.

text: [founder] Rails/dividers must be continuous and deliberate: a rail that meets artwork dissolves before it instead of being cut off or crossing it.
why: Founder: "fix the borders also like dividers".
check: visual: no rail ends abruptly mid-section or crosses the hero visual.

text: [founder] Place the hero visual deliberately on the grid: in the right column, pushed right and down so it bleeds off the frame edge, top roughly level with the headline, never floating mid-page.
why: Founder found the globe "a bit out of place", then asked to move it right and down.
check: visual: the visual's mass sits right and low and bleeds off the frame.

text: [founder] Keep the hero product card simple: title + status badge, one context line, one large figure, one progress element, three small stats. Do not add icon tiles, avatar stacks or extra rows.
why: Founder: the richer card was "too complicated, the original one was better".
check: card has <= 5 visual rows.

text: [founder] Buttons follow Kaching's spec: 14px radius, 18px label at -0.54px tracking, solid ink primary with #303030 hover and no lift, press scale 0.98, secondary white with 1px border and an optional 5px-inset image or icon tile.
why: Founder pointed to Kaching's buttons as the standard.
check: computed radius 14px, font-size 18px, letter-spacing -0.54px on hero CTAs.

text: [founder] Every hero needs a creative signature visual field (live dither, halftone, shader, real-data map), not a flat or empty background.
why: Founder asked for "a more creative bg"; the halftone globe was called "cool".
check: visual: a signature visual occupies at least 30% of the fold.

text: [founder] Desktop first when the deliverable is an image; do not spend effort on mobile unless asked.
why: Founder: "no mobile just desktop focus right now to get me an image".
check: n/a.

text: [founder] Floating cards use quiet depth: a 1px hairline ring plus a faint lift (about 0 8px 20px -12px at 12% ink). Never a large, blurry, high-opacity drop shadow.
why: Founder: "why so massive shadow and unprofessional stuff"; Deel/Rippling references use whisper-level shadows.
check: box-shadow blur <= 24px and alpha <= 0.16 on cards.

text: [founder] Side rails/dividers run the full height of the hero and pass BEHIND artwork (the artwork's empty space is transparent so the rail shows through between its marks); never fade a rail out early and never draw it on top of the visual.
why: Founder: the right border "fading off too soon" looked broken, then asked for the border "to be below the globe".
check: both rails span the full hero height; the rail's z-index is below the hero visual.

text: [founder] A large hero visual that touches the frame edge dissolves softly into the page (mask fade) instead of being hard-cropped mid-shape; make it big enough to feel intentional.
why: Founder: the globe needed to be "bigger or blurred out at sides where it touches".
check: visual: no hard crop line on the visual at the frame edge.

text: [founder] Data callouts on a visual all follow one placement rule (same side of their point, short leader line), never cover their own line or another route, and are curated to the clearest three rather than five.
why: Founder: the travelling points "are a bit off and need to be placed better".
check: visual: no callout overlaps any arc or another callout.

text: [founder] Money amounts in hero product UI are bold sans (Geist semibold, tight tracking, tabular) with the decimals muted; mono is for meta (times, IDs), not headline figures.
why: Founder asked for the money card to be styled better; Deel's payroll card is the reference.
check: large currency figures use the sans family.

text: [founder] Look at several strong real references for the same product category before redesigning a weak area (for payroll: Deel, Remote, Rippling in knowledge/references/payroll/).
why: Founder: "search for more examples or what would look better and cleaner".
check: DIRECTION.md cites the references opened.

text: [founder] Default nav (when the brand has no nav system of its own) uses Kaching's exact spec: one pill 43px tall (padding 5/5/5/16, radius 14, white 80% + 8px blur), 16px between brand and links, 2px between links, links 6/11 padding at 15px/21px and -0.45px, chevron 5px from its label with 14px left padding on that link, actions 9/16 at radius 12 on the right. Compact, never airy.
why: Founder: "the first original one was best", the respaced version was "too spaced out", with no gap after the Product chevron.
check: nav pill height 43px; link padding 6px 11px; gap after chevron >= 5px. A new brand may define its own nav at the same polish (compact, aligned, no stray gaps) and should, so pages do not all look like one kit.
source: founder, Tideline round 5 and Vigil round 1; knowledge/larpo-shipped Kaching hero.css

text: [founder] Hero headlines have no full stop at the end.
why: Founder: "no dot at the end of title text please".
check: h1 text does not end with ".".

text: [founder] Break the two-line subtitle by hand so the lines are balanced (first line not much longer than the second); do not leave a long top line and a short bottom line.
why: Founder asked to cut the subtitle "after every" so the top line is not so long.
check: visual: line lengths within ~20% of each other.

text: [founder] The "New" announcement badge keeps white text; deepen the badge colour until white passes contrast instead of switching the text to black.
why: Founder: "why randomly the text there is black when it should have been white".
check: badge text is white; colour bright, not burnt (Tideline uses #ea580c, ~3.6:1: the founder judged #c2410c 'a bit too dark', so brightness wins over AA on this decorative badge).

text: [founder] The hero product card anchors to the bottom of the hero (bottom-left on the content edge), not floating mid-column under the buttons.
why: Founder: "the ticket box should be on the bottom".
check: card bottom within ~40px of the hero bottom.

text: [founder] One depth and shape language across every floating surface: shared shadow tokens (ring for pills/secondary buttons, card shadow for cards and chips), radius 18 for cards, 14 for chips and hero buttons, 12 for nav controls and dark labels.
why: Founder: "match consistency everywhere".
check: floating surfaces use the shared shadow variables.

text: [founder] Data routes and connecting lines flow: a gradient stroke that fades in from the origin and a soft moving highlight (comet) along the line, rather than flat static strokes with a dot.
why: Founder asked for "nicer strokes flowing".
check: visual + motion: routes have a gradient and a looping highlight; reduced motion shows static gradients.

text: [founder] Give the hero copy block air at the top: roughly 80-90px between the nav and the announcement chip at 1440x900.
why: Founder: the title "and everything should be a little bit more down".
check: chip top - nav bottom ~= 80-90px.

text: [founder] Founder rules set the polish floor, not the style. Each new brand must explore its own effects, button style, type voice and graphics from the engine library (art-direction moves, Heckel shader recipes, Comeau button/depth recipes, Rauno/Emil craft details) instead of reusing the last project's kit; the diversity gate checks the fingerprint, and the designer must also check the components (nav, buttons, chips, cards) for sameness.
why: Founder on Vigil v1: "too alike the project we just did, explore better effects, buttons, styles, shaders, graphics... use the engine".
check: DIRECTION.md names the moves and recipes used, and at least nav, primary button and product card differ in construction from the previous accepted project.

text: [founder] The default SaaS hero is centred and product-led: a two-line headline (no chip above it), a one-line subtitle and the CTA centred at the top, then a full, rich product dashboard in a window frame filling the lower half of the fold and running off the bottom edge (AlignUI Pro, Commslayer). The dashboard is the visual.
why: Founder on Vigil v2 (dark mono split hero with a lens shader): "this looks ass... I need something clean centre layout and like SaaS with full dashboard visual, clean smooth and aesthetic with cool and clean visuals like Commslayer... the AlignUI aesthetic I love most".
applies: SaaS and AI-SaaS landing heroes, unless the brief asks for something else.
check: h1 centred; the dashboard frame is >= 1000px wide, starts in the top 65% of the fold and is cut by the bottom edge; the dashboard shows a believable workflow (sidebar, KPIs, chart, table or list, an AI panel).

text: [founder] The founder's favourite aesthetic is AlignUI: light, clean and smooth. Soft grey canvas, white surfaces, hairline strokes, soft layered shadows, Inter-class type at 500-550 weight with tight tracking, one confident accent, precise small UI. Effects (shaders, glows, beams, rulers) support the product and stay quiet; a dark, moody, conceptual or "techy poster" hero with an abstract effect as the main visual is a reject.
why: Founder rejected Vigil v2 (dark field, glass-lens shader, mono poster headline, 3D push button): "this looks ass", "clean smooth and aesthetic".
check: light canvas by default; the largest visual element is product UI, not an effect; no more than one effect layer at low contrast.

text: [founder] "Explore the engine" means fresh components and details inside the clean SaaS look (new nav construction, button grammar, frame, accents, icon set, motion), not a jump to an experimental art direction. Novelty lives in the details; the overall read stays clean, premium SaaS.
why: Vigil round 1 was "too alike"; Vigil round 2 overcorrected into an art-piece and was rejected as "ass".
check: DIRECTION.md lists the component-level differences from the last accepted project and confirms the hero class is product proof.

text: [founder] No announcement chip or small text above the hero headline by default; the headline opens the hero and sits ~80-90px under the nav.
why: Founder on Kestrel round 1: "I'd put no little text above the title and move the title up".
check: nothing between the nav and the h1.

text: [founder] Nav controls are never cramped: link items at least 36px tall with ~14px side padding inside a 44px track, sign-in and primary buttons 40px tall with ~16px side padding.
why: Founder on Kestrel round 1: "the nav bar would be taller like buttons, they're a bit cramped now".
check: nav links >= 36px tall, nav buttons >= 40px.

text: [founder] Background texture (a fine dot grid, Commslayer-style) lives only inside the rails, behind the copy and the product; outside the rails the canvas stays plain. Fade it softly behind the headline so type stays clean.
why: Founder on Kestrel round 1: "dotted bg texture in the inner stuff, behind the product, but not outside the borders (same as Commslayer)".
check: the texture element's box equals the rail-to-rail area.

text: [founder] Hero buttons share the product's roundness: when the product UI is soft (cards 12-16, frame 22), the CTAs are 44px tall at ~14px radius and nav buttons ~12px; never square-ish 10px buttons next to a soft product.
why: Founder on Kestrel round 1: "if the product is that rounded why the Start for free or other buttons are so stiff".
check: CTA radius >= 0.3 x height; within ~4px of the product card radius.

text: [founder] Inside a hero dashboard, keep small controls tight (sidebar items, search and switcher at ~6px radius) and do not mark a "selected" card with an accent outline ring; selection is shown by the story (chart, AI panel), not a blue border.
why: Founder on Kestrel round 1: the sidebar was "a bit too rounded", and "the 3 cards, the blue outline I don't like".
check: no accent-coloured ring on KPI cards; sidebar item radius <= 6px.

text: [founder] When the founder supplies a logo image, trace it to SVG (node potrace from the root node_modules), crop to a square viewBox, fill with currentColor and use it unchanged, ink on light; reuse the mark inside the product (AI assistant tile) for brand continuity.
why: Founder on Kestrel round 1 supplied the flower mark: "the logo to be same as the Kestrel logo which I found online, you could recreate".
check: the logo path comes from `work/<name>/brand/*-mark.svg`, not an icon-set glyph.

text: [founder] Product UI inside a hero uses one soft radius ladder, measured as rendered (Kestrel round 2, loved): sidebar items, workspace switcher, search, badges, inner segments and tooltips 8; 32px header and panel controls (segmented track, icon buttons, small buttons, inputs) 12; cards, chat bubbles and the app surface 16; outer frame 22. Do not tighten it: 4/6/10 and 6/8/12 both read stiff (founder Kestrel rounds 3-4: "too little rounding", "where is the product roundness smooth as it was").
why: Founder on Kestrel round 2: "the dashboard has components too rounded, not consistent and not spaced centre" (the 7d/30d/90d control vs the share button).
check: distinct radii inside the product <= 5 and each maps to the ladder; adjacent controls have equal heights; segment widths equal.

text: [founder] Secondary hero buttons are text-only; no decorative play or arrow icon in front of the label.
why: Founder on Kestrel round 2: "except the see it answer icon, please remove that".
check: the secondary CTA has no leading icon.

text: [founder] Every hero loads in as one orchestrated Framer Motion timeline on Kaching's motion tokens (`ease.reveal [.26,.32,.14,1]` 1.2s travel + 0.9s fade, 70ms stagger, 6px blur on text only, stage lifts from 97%, controls 220ms `outQuint`): frame lines draw, then nav (it animates too), then headline word by word, subtitle, CTAs, then the product stage, then its contents in reading order, then decorative tiles and routes. Nothing is visible before its moment: connection dots appear only when their route lands, and only then do pulses and comets start. Hover states slide (shared `layoutId` pills in nav, segmented controls, sidebars). Reduced motion shows everything in place.
why: Founder on Kestrel round 5: "the blue dots that connect, why are they always visible, no animation, plus nav bar too? make everything smooth using framer motion", "make the entire load-in smoother with stagger... check how we have Kaching".
check: a frame at ~0.4s shows only the frame; no element with a looping animation is visible before its entrance; all delays come from one timeline object; tokens live in one `motion.ts`. Also check the nav and tiles are clickable (no transparent layer above them).

text: [founder] Looping accents (pulse rings, pings, comets) must be invisible until their moment: start every looping keyframe array at opacity 0 (`opacity: [0, 0.4, 0]`, `times: [0, 0.05, 1]`) or wrap the loop in a group that enters at that moment. Framer Motion paints the first keyframe during the delay, so `opacity: [0.4, 0]` shows a static dot from page load. Order effects as cause then effect: the note lands, its connector draws, the target line lights up and the dot lands as the connector arrives, then the pulse starts.
why: Founder on Margin build 1: "the red bubble doesn't fade in, it just stays there when loading in, very distracting".
check: filmstrip at 300ms steps: no looping element visible before its entrance; grep `animate={{ .*opacity: \[0\.[1-9]` for loops starting visible.

text: [founder] Range is mandatory: no two consecutive builds may share the same page family and skeleton. Rotate between image-led heroes (engraving, painting, photo, generative scenes behind crisp product), framed pages (site as a sheet on a backdrop), left-aligned editorial heroes, mono/sharp operator styles, AI-composer heroes and the centred product-over-canvas default. Polish rules (spacing, nav comfort, radii consistency, motion discipline) carry across; the aesthetic does not.
why: Founder after Kestrel and Margin: "now I see the patterns, you're a bit repetitive and we need a lot of different styles and aesthetics", with references from @1Aakib and @uisabor (knowledge/web/style-refs-x-2026-10.md).
check: DIRECTION.md states the family of this build and of the last two; they differ.

text: [founder] Leave real air between the hero CTAs and the product frame: at least 64px from the bottom of the buttons to the top of the frame (Strata had 44px and read cramped). Measure it; do not eyeball it.
why: Founder on Strata: "not bad, just the product is too close to the buttons".
check: frame.top - cta.bottom >= 64px at 1440x900.

text: [founder] Generative, one-of-a-kind backgrounds are welcome when they are crafted (Strata's live engraving: "interesting style choice, really unique"); keep exploring bespoke shaders and illustrations per brand instead of stock gradients.
why: Founder on Strata's engraved landscape.
check: DIRECTION.md names the bespoke visual and why it fits the product.

text: [founder] Do not ship the generic "everything loads in" parade (every word, block and row rising out of blur in sequence). Choreograph the load-in around the brand's idea with ONE conceptual reveal (dawn light sweeping across a dark product, ink developing on paper, a flow drawing itself), and keep the rest either present at first paint or arriving in at most 2-3 quick groups within ~1.2s. Word-by-word headline reveals are a deliberate choice for one brand, not the default. Vary the motion vocabulary per brand exactly like layout and type.
why: Founder on Nocturne: "not up to our quality levels... everything is just loading in and it's a bit noobish". Kestrel's load-in was praised once; repeating the same kit stagger on Margin, Strata and Nocturne turned it into a template. Research agrees: 8 of 15 top heroes show the headline in the first frame and the median hero settles in ~1.5s (knowledge/web/product-motion-patterns.md).
check: filmstrip at 0/300/800/1500ms: the composed hero (headline + CTA) is readable by 300ms unless the concept needs otherwise; entrance groups <= 3; DIRECTION.md names the conceptual reveal and how it differs from the last build's.

text: [founder] Every product visual on one site speaks ONE visual language: one edge treatment for white boxes (a 1px hairline OR a faint 6% ring, never both, never a borderless box with a muddy shadow), one radius ladder by element height (nested radius = outer minus inset), one grey shadow scale of at most 3 levels, type roles at 500/600 only, one accent rule (accent only for the selected/primary thing, tints at ~8%). Benchmark is Commslayer/Attio product UI. Audit computed values across ALL visuals before shipping, not one at a time.
why: Founder on the Kaching app visuals (2026-10-09): "the animations are in 3 completely different styles of colours, effects, roundness... what the hell", "random box components without borders and bad shadows or double pixel stroke"; client: "I saw 3-4 different styles of borders and how things look and move". Root cause found in code: three competing box-shadow recipes in one style file.
applies: every animated product visual / bento scene / card.
check: across all visuals: distinct box-shadow strings <= 3, no element with both a border and a 0 0 0 1px ring, distinct radii map to the ladder, font weights in {500, 600}.

text: [founder] Sibling pages built from one template keep an identical bento: same box sizes, positions and padding at every breakpoint; only the content differs. Never mirror or resize the grid for one page.
why: Client on Kaching app pages: "the Bundles section size and how things work is not the same as Subscriptions".
check: bento box rects match across all sibling pages at 1440/768/375.

text: [founder] Each product visual has its own signature build-in (rows assemble, a cursor acts, a dithered product photo develops, a number counts, a connector draws) on shared timing tokens; never the same generic "panel fades/rises in like a card" for every visual.
why: Founder: "each visual is like a card, it loads in just like a card, couldn't it do something of its own?"
applies: bento scenes, hero visuals, step visuals.
check: filmstrip of two visuals side by side: their first 800ms differ in choreography, not just content.

text: [founder] Product photos inside an app/section visual are tinted from that section's own palette (or neutral grey); a red tee glowing on the green Cart card is wrong. Palettes stay clean: gold is a clean amber, never olive or muddy.
why: Client: "why does the red T-shirt glow on the green card instead of being green", "the yellow is too dirty compared to the new one".
applies: dithered/duotone product art and app colour fields.
check: each product-art ramp's hue sits within ~25deg of its section accent or is neutral.

text: [founder] Dither (and gradient) fields should end in a slow, uneven, drifting wave, not one straight horizontal line, and the wave stays modest: depth about a quarter of the fade band, capped near 85px, wavelength ~640px. 0.36 of the band / 120px cap read "good but a bit too big".
why: Client: "make some waves so it's not all one straight horizontal line, it looks basic"; founder after the first pass: "they're good but just a bit too big".
check: the fade boundary varies along its length; peak depth <= ~86px at 1440.

text: [founder] Never reproduce a friend brand's signature section identically (Kaching's founders' letter mirrored Commslayer's structure and was rejected); take the idea, then make it unmistakably ours (Kaching: a torn notebook page with 2px dither fibres along the tear).
why: Client: "it's not similar, it's identical to Commslayer, I'll be ashamed to look their founder in the eye".
check: structure, material and copy rhythm all differ from the reference.

text: [founder] Hero title sizes are one scale across a site's secondary pages; no page gets a one-off giant h1 (Kaching About was "huge and out of place").
check: h1 font-size is identical across secondary pages at each breakpoint.

text: [founder] Auto-advancing tabs show progress as a small circular ring beside the active label (or a fill inside a full-width segmented track), never a 1px line under a pill.
why: Client: "that 1px line at the bottom of the pill doesn't look good, try a small circular progress next to the name".
check: no progress hairline under pills; the indicator is driven by the same clock as the advance.

text: [founder] Product dashboards default to the compact, calm grammar measured from Rico's and Kargul's real screens (knowledge/web/heyrico-recreation-lessons.md, kargul-source-study.md), not to a "spacious AlignUI template" reading: one size smaller than instinct everywhere (sidebar ~260px, rows 28-30px on a 30-32px pitch, controls 28-30px, icons 14px stroke at text size, labels 13-14px, KPI numbers ~18px semibold-tabular, card padding 16px, page gutters 24px); hierarchy from two text greys, not from size or weight; group labels small and sentence case, never uppercase; active nav row = grey fill + darker text only (no accent bar or chevron); canvas and sidebar share one neutral, cards are white with a 1px border and no shadow (one shadow per screen at most); the accent appears only in data (bars, lines, meters, progress); tight inside, generous between (2px between rows, 20px between cards). Build one primary view to full detail with real-looking data and working interactions, and put secondary content in overlays (sheets, popovers, dialogs) instead of stacking six blocks.
why: Founder rejected Acquisity v1 (boxed, colourful, cramped) and v2 (an "AlignUI template" reading with uppercase labels, 24px numbers, 32px padding): "it copied it mostly and just changed surface level stuff... nothing like Marcel Kargul's style nor Rico... too noobish... nothing like Attio". Recreating Rico 1:1 and auditing Kargul's code showed the engine's product UI is one notch too big, too many sizes (7 type sizes vs 3, 5 control heights vs 1, 8 radii vs 4) and too boxy.
check: distinct font sizes in the main view <= 4; one control height for actions; icon size = adjacent text size; shadows <= 1 per screen; no uppercase group labels; overlay side-by-side with a Rico/Kargul reference via tools/compare.mjs.
source: founder verdicts on Acquisity v1/v2; Rico recreation and Kargul source study, 2026-10-09

text: [founder] A content reference (an existing screen, a kit, a brief) is content only: redesign structure, sizes and hierarchy from scratch in our own system, and add what the product is missing (sections, states, live elements) instead of re-skinning the original layout box for box.
why: Founder: "that example I gave you was just like the content, you should design the stuff in your own size and way or even add stuff there isn't and just do it consistently".
check: DIRECTION.md lists what was restructured and what was added, not only what was restyled.

text: [founder] The product-UI bar is Marcel Kargul's, Rico's (@_heyrico) and Attio's shipped product work, not "AlignUI-flavoured". Before building product UI, study and recreate reference screens at 1:1 (overlay your render on the reference and close the gaps), build from a measured product kit, and judge every screen side by side with a reference at the same zoom. A redesign that keeps the source layout and changes surface styling is a reject.
why: Founder on Acquisity v1/v2: "it seems to have copied it mostly and just changed surface level stuff", "nothing like Marcel Kargul's style nor Rico... too noobish... nothing like Attio... spend more time perfecting product craft".
applies: all SaaS app UI and dashboards.
check: DIRECTION.md names the reference screens used, includes a side-by-side at equal zoom, and lists the structural changes (not only restyling).

text: [founder] Bento visuals (Commslayer-measured): no grey stage boxes; each visual starts exactly on its copy's left edge, one fixed gap under the copy, top-aligned (never centred in a tall box), filling the cell's width; only the lead cell carries the brand dither, across the whole lower cell edge to edge; the longest visual goes in the tall lead cell and the widest in the wide cell; on tablet and phone every cell has the same height. Never replace an accepted bento layout with a "systemised" fixed grid without diffing it against the accepted one.
why: Founder on Kaching round 2: "not in a rectangular grey box", "this bento was clean, neat, consistent when scaling down, on mobile all the same heights, and now you messed it up everywhere", "we had the long visual, so put it first and the calendar as the long one".
check: visual.left == copy.left per cell; gap copy->visual identical across cells; no stage background; tablet/phone cell heights equal.

text: [founder] Visuals inside dark sections are dark visuals (dark panels with a faint white ring, light text, accent only on the selected/primary element). Never drop a bright white UI window onto a black band.
why: Founder on the Kaching migration section: "dark sections should have dark visuals, what's going on?"
applies: any product visual on a dark surface.
check: in dark sections, no visual panel has a background lighter than ~#2A2A2A.

text: [founder] When a founder-approved visual already exists (a motion artist's scene, a shipped section), revise it app by app: keep its composition, polish styling and motion, check it side by side against the original, and only then move to the next. Never regenerate a whole set in parallel from a new system; it drifts ("what you replaced is a bit shit", "let's go one by one").
check: each revised visual has a side-by-side with its original in the report.

text: [founder] An app sidebar follows Attio: one refined outline icon family (Phosphor regular, 16px, grey #7c7f85; the active row's icon goes fill), record types as 16px solid colour tiles (radius 4.5) with a white filled glyph, and enough real pages to feel like a product (workspace pages, Favorites, Records, Lists, Agents), grouped under small sentence-case headers. The whole nav fits a 1440x900 viewport without a clipped group; secondary actions (invite, help, settings) collapse into icon buttons in the user footer. White buttons get a crisp 1px ring plus a soft 1-2px lift (`.btn-white`), never a blurred halo.
why: Founder on Acquisity v3 (renamed Ferry): "not bad actually, you're getting better... I'd just improve the sidebar and the white buttons a tiny bit.. the sidebar icons look trash... overall sidebar itself should look more like attio and have more pages".
applies: SaaS app UI and hero dashboards.
check: one icon library in the sidebar; record tiles solid with white glyphs; no group cut at 900px tall; white button shadow = 0 0 0 1px ring + <= 2px blur lift.

text: [founder] The last 5% to Marcel/Rico level is tiny effects plus consistency, so finish every product screen with this pass: one icon family across sidebar and canvas (state = fill weight, never a second library); one card-header grammar everywhere (16px solid tile + white glyph, 14/600 title, soft meta, actions right, same 48px band); micro-visuals that carry data (KPI micro-bar sparks with the latest period in the accent, segmented meters for rates, dotted underline on metric labels); charts compare against something (previous period dotted grey under a 1.5px accent line, monotone smoothing that never overshoots a real value, dashed gridlines, a hover crosshair + tooltip, an end-point dot); only one attribute per row is a filled chip, other statuses are icon + text; table edge cells share the card's 16px inset; dense cells use compact values ("12m", "1d") so nothing clips.
why: Founder on Ferry: "we're so close but not marcel or rico quality by a tiny bit, which comes down to tiny effects and consistencies"; while studying Rico's analytics, Attio's charts and Kargul's CRM: "you're looking at fire examples tho".
check: icon libraries imported in the product = 1; every card header renders through one component; each chart has a comparison series and a hover state; filled chips per table row <= 1; no clipped cell text at 1440 wide.

text: [founder] A split product hero stays clean: plain canvas behind the copy (Lightfield, Attio), the copy block vertically centred and the product doing the visual work. The copy side still needs quiet substance (founder round 3: "titles subtitle and buttons and that's all??? ... too empty"): one row of three stats under the CTAs (big display number + one-line soft label, hairline dividers, product specs not invented results) and a minimal texture such as the fine dot grid, cleared behind the type and stopping before the product stage. If the hero needs art, confine it to one stage panel directly behind the product (Folk's grain gradient, Cursor's painting, Granola's collage); never a full-page pattern, contour field or scattered decorative numbers, and never a "how it works" step list in the hero.
why: Founder on the Ferry hero: kept "the title subtitle buttons nav bar the product nice", rejected the live sea-chart contour background and the three lit-up steps: "BG WITH THOSE LIKE THREE STEPS LIKE WTF IS SO STUPID... find better cleaner examples of this and do it better".
check: no busy pattern (contours, scattered numbers, step lists) anywhere; copy side = headline, subtitle, CTAs, one stats row, optional dot grid faded behind the type; at most one floating surface over the product.
source: founder, Ferry hero round 1, 2026-10-09; knowledge/benchmarks/split-heroes/lightfield-1440.png, folk-1440.png, attio-1440.png, product-heroes/cursor-1440.png

text: [founder] A product hero must feel alive and show enough of the product: render the dashboard at hero scale (about 0.8 zoom, ~11-12px text) so sidebar, KPIs and a full table read at once, and let the story play inside the product (rows arrive, AI states change, a cursor acts inline, numbers tick) with at most one narrating chip above the window (Lightfield's agent pill). No pop-up cards floating over the copy side; a static 1:1 crop of one table reads "empty... too simple". A soft blue stage panel behind the product was "not bad".
why: Founder on Ferry hero round 2: "the bluish not bad just idk about second card like popping up nor the size of the dashboard... it's just empty and no stuff going on, it's not good... too simple".
check: something in the product changes at least every ~1-1.5s for the first ~10s; visible product shows the sidebar, KPIs and >= 8 table rows; no floating card overlaps the copy column.

text: [founder] Hero products build in fully and in order, and numbers roll: after the frame lands, every part of the product enters on a top-to-bottom stagger (sidebar items, header, tabs, KPI cards, table rows), and every number rolls up digit by digit in its own slot (kit `RollingNumber`), never a plain fade or a whole-number count. The live story starts only after the build completes.
why: Founder on Ferry hero round 4: "product should like load in with stagger and fully load in plus like the numbers to count up professionally by sliding up each number... more professional".
applies: product heroes and product visuals in sections.
check: filmstrip at 0.3/0.7/1.0/1.4s shows frame, then staggered contents; KPI digits roll; nothing in the product is static from frame 1.

text: [founder] Dark heroes must be premium dark (Linear, Vercel, Raycast grade), never "dev-tool template" dark: no neo-brutalist hard offset-block buttons, no muddy coloured glow on graphite, no flat dark product slab that sinks into the canvas, no random pastel data colours, no heavy 700 headline with crushed tracking. The product window in dark needs light: a defined edge (1px top highlight + hairline ring), a surface step above the canvas, and one controlled key light; data colours come from one tuned ramp. The split band layout (headline left, subtitle + CTAs right on the headline baseline, full-width product below) is good and reusable.
why: Founder on Tracewell (V1 dark hero #1): "straight up dogshit"; "the app and the buttons and everything else about it (except layout, I know that layout is good to use)... those buttons... looking ass and in general the dark design of the SaaS ass as well".
applies: every dark hero and dark product UI.
check: side-by-side with knowledge/benchmarks/dark/linear and vercel folds via tools/compare.mjs before delivery; product window luminance step >= 4% above canvas with a visible top edge; buttons from knowledge/web/button-grammars.md dark recipes, not offset blocks.

text: [founder] Florian Hoeller (@flohoeller; affectui.com, adfects.com) is the top quality bar for product UI, components and light SaaS heroes, alongside Kargul, Rico and Attio. Study his work before building those: calm Inter 500 headlines at modest size (46-52px, about -0.03em), muted #666-#737373 copy, a dark pill built from two stacked gradients with a 1px ring plus a 4% grey ghost twin, card-in-card showcase frames (r24 outer, r18 grey inner stage), believable content in every pixel (real-feeling names, numbers, sources), product states that move (thinking timers, steps landing one by one, morphs into success), and his depth-of-field collage hero (tilted UI fragments at different blur depths around a clean centre).
why: Founder: "STUDY THIS GUY FULLY I WANT HIS QUALITY EVERYTHING LIKE HIM... HE'S THE BEST".
applies: components, product UI, light SaaS heroes.
check: compare against knowledge/benchmarks/flohoeller/*.png with tools/compare.mjs; read knowledge/web/flohoeller-craft.md.

text: [T13] Use as few font sizes as possible in a form; differentiate size only between sections (labels/placeholders at one small size) and actions (the button label larger). The good mock uses 12 for both label and placeholder and 32 for the button label; the bad mock mixes 16 (label), 12 (placeholder), 32 (button).
why: Every extra size is another thing to decode, so the form takes longer to process.
check: count distinct computed `font-size` values inside one `form`; label and input/placeholder sizes should match.

text: [T31] Use one typeface across a card/page. The bad mock sets heading and body in a serif next to a sans eyebrow; the good mock sets everything in one sans.
why: Mixing faces creates confusion and hurts readability; a single face lets users learn the pattern.
check: set of distinct `font-family` primary families on page (expect 1, at most 2 with a clear role split) `[engine note on the "at most 2"]`.

text: [T35] Limit line width by characters per line, not by pixel width; wide full-width text lines bore users and hurt readability. Good mock: text column narrower with larger side padding than the card edge.
why: Long measures lose the reader's eye at line return.
check: measure chars per line of paragraphs (`ch`-based `max-width`); see T94 for the numeric range.

text: [T94] Keep paragraph line length in check: stick to 45-75 characters per line "if you want to play it safe". The good example is labelled 55-65 characters per line; the bad example is labelled ~120 characters per line.
why: Too-long lines make text harder to read.
check: `ch` count of rendered lines on `p`: 45-75, target 55-65.

text: [T86] Body text must be no smaller than 14pt. The page shows 12pt as the bad body and 16pt as the good body (the 16pt example also has visibly more leading than the 12pt one).
why: Small text is hard to read clearly.
check: computed `font-size` of body copy >= 14 (pt as the book uses it; read as px-equivalent 14+ in CSS) `[engine note: book says pt, web sizes are px; treat 14 as floor, 16 as default]`.

text: [T87] Do not set continuous running text in all caps; use sentence case and keep caps for moderate, short uses (the book's good mock sets a paragraph in normal case; bad sets the whole paragraph in caps).
why: All-caps blocks are difficult to read.
check: `text-transform: uppercase` should not be on paragraphs/long strings; flag uppercase runs > a short label.

text: [T17] Align description text to the title text, not to the icon. Good: icon sits in its own column, title and description share one left edge. Bad: description starts under the icon, so title and body have different left edges.
why: Unaligned text makes content hard to scan; aligning cleans up the design.
check: `getBoundingClientRect().left` of title and its description are equal.

text: [T95] Right-align numbers in tables so the decimal point is always in the same place; numeric column headers are right-aligned over their numbers too (good mock), text column (ticker symbols) stays left-aligned.
why: Aligned decimals let you compare values at a glance; ragged decimals look cluttered.
check: numeric `td`/`th` have `text-align: right` (`font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` is an `[engine note]` addition).

text: [T6] Break dense text into headed, scannable items: small letter-spaced uppercase grey eyebrow ("PROPERTY FEATURES"), then per feature an icon, a bold descriptive heading, and a short grey description of two lines. Do not show important features as one paragraph.
why: People scan; headings plus icons let them find a feature without reading the block.
check: no paragraph > ~3 sentences that contains multiple distinct features; visual.

text: [T1] Use human language that ties labels to values: "Only 7 left in stock!" instead of "In stock: 7"; "Add to Cart" instead of "Cart" on the button.
why: Robotic label/value pairs confuse; natural phrasing explains what the number and the button mean.
check: visual / copy review; button labels on commerce actions are verb phrases.

text: [T8] In confirmation dialogs make the options descriptive and consistent with the question. Bad: "Are you sure you want to cancel your upload?" answered by "OK" (grey) and "Cancel" (primary): ambiguous. Good: "Yes, Cancel" (grey) and "Don't Cancel" (primary).
why: "OK/Cancel" next to a "cancel?" question forces the user to decode which one does what.
check: dialog buttons are not generic "OK"/"Cancel" when the question itself contains "cancel".

text: [T29] Drop the verb from a navigation/menu label when the noun is already clear: "My address", "Order history", "Discounts", "Payment methods" instead of "Edit my address", "View order history", "View discounts", "Edit payment methods".
why: Verbs make labels long and over-detailed in a list that is already an action menu.
check: list-row labels are short noun phrases; visual.

text: [T47] Write opt-in button copy that makes users excited to join: "Join the Club!" instead of "Submit" on a subscribe form.
why: Generic words make people less interested in the program.
check: primary button label on sign-up/subscribe is not "Submit".

text: [T57] Button labels must state what will happen: "Create account", never "OK" or "Next" for the final form action.
why: Vague actions leave users unsure about the outcome.
check: submit button text is not in {OK, Next, Submit, Continue} without context.

text: [T42] Do not repeat the logo on the same page. When the hero shows the brand in the header and again as the hero headline, replace the hero text with a headline that conveys style and what you do (good: "MODERN STYLE"; bad: "LOOHOO FASHION" repeating the header logo).
why: Repetition wastes the most prominent text slot; a headline sells the offer.
check: brand name occurs in nav only, not also as the `h1`.

text: [T2] On dark UI limit saturation: keep brand colours at tone levels 200-500 (a Tailwind-style 50-950 scale); do not use fully saturated colours on dark cards. Good mock: title and button are a desaturated lavender; bad: vivid saturated blue title and button on the same dark card.
why: Highly saturated elements damage contrast and vibrate on dark surfaces.
check: HSL/OKLCH chroma of accents in `.dark` is lower than in light; accent lightness in the 200-500 band.

text: [T3] Build two colour palettes, one per theme: dark mode uses light pastel tones of each hue; light mode uses darker, deeper shades of the same hues. Do not reuse identical colours in both modes. (Good mock: lavender/mint/sky/salmon bars in dark; indigo/emerald/blue/coral-red darker versions in light.) The book adds "most people prefer light theme" (opinion).
why: The same swatch has different contrast on dark vs light backgrounds.
check: accent tokens differ between `:root` and `.dark`.

text: [T15] Avoid pure black (#000000) and pure white for surfaces; use a dark grey such as #333335.
why: Pure black/white can cause uneasiness in the eyes.
check: `background-color` or `color` not exactly `#000`/`#fff` on large surfaces and body text.

text: [T54] Build the colour scheme from one family: pick a few tones of the same hue (good: four steps from dark navy to pale periwinkle) rather than unrelated hues (bad: black, orange-red, mustard, magenta).
why: Too many inconsistent colours looks terrible.
check: palette hue spread: all brand/neutral tokens within a narrow hue range (excluding semantic colours).

text: [T55] Use the primary colour only on the most crucial components. In the good mock the header becomes light neutral, the tab bar becomes white with the primary colour only on the active icon, buttons and card titles carry primary; photos have no colour overlay. The bad mock floods header, tab bar, card backgrounds and image tints with primary.
why: Too much primary colour does not look nice and kills its signalling power.
check: share of page area filled with the primary colour is small (`[engine note]` rule of thumb under ~10% of viewport area); primary reserved for CTA, active, key accents.

text: [T19] Keep the colours used for navigation/state to two, one of which denotes the selection: good mock keeps active icon in blue and the others grey; bad mock gives every icon its own colour (blue, orange, green, purple).
why: Multiple colours in navigation add to the cognitive load.
check: distinct non-neutral colours among sibling icons <= 1 (the selected one).

text: [T92] Emphasise by de-emphasising: give inactive nav items a softer (lighter grey) colour so the active item (indigo/darker) pops. Bad mock: all links dark, active barely different.
why: The active item only stands out relative to the background of its siblings.
check: contrast/lightness delta between active and inactive nav link; inactive lighter but still readable `[engine note: still meet 4.5:1 for text]`.

text: [T88] Use accent colours to help users categorise sections: in the pricing mock, a 3-4px coloured top rule (violet on "Start", mint-green on "Pro") differentiates two otherwise identical cards.
why: Identical sections look the same and cannot be told apart at a glance.
check: sibling cards carry distinct accent token (rule/dot/icon); visual.

text: [T75] Add colour-based distinction to highlight significant classifications: status rendered as small uppercase coloured pills (SHORTLISTED violet, REJECTED red, IN-PROCESS green) with alternating row tint, not plain grey text.
why: Plain text statuses create no visual distinction between rows, so scanning is slow.
check: status cell uses a coloured badge, not default text colour.

text: [T12] Use red for destructive actions: the "Yes, Delete" button is red (bad: blue), the neutral Cancel is light grey.
why: Red alerts the user and acts as a warning sign; blue looks normal.
check: destructive buttons use the destructive/red token.

text: [T25] When text sits on a photo that is not dark enough, add a contrast overlay: good mock adds a darkening gradient behind the white "Hello, welcome to our academy" text; bad mock leaves white text on bright pink umbrellas, partly unreadable.
why: Without contrast the text does not appear clearly on a bright image.
check: contrast ratio of text vs the image pixels beneath >= 4.5:1 (`[engine note]` threshold).

text: [T26] Make gradients smooth by placing the gradient handle's start and end farther away from the object (outside its bounds); handles at the corners give a direct, sharp-looking gradient.
why: Close end points compress the transition and look harsh.
check: visual; the gradient's colour stops should not both be fully reached inside the element box.

text: [T21] Keep a second layer (e.g. dropdown) at least two shades or tints different from the layer behind it. Good: white dropdown over a grey page; bad: grey dropdown on grey page.
why: Similar shades for different layers are uneasy to the eyes and the layers blend.
check: luminance delta between popover bg and its backdrop element.

text: [T77] On dark themes communicate elevation with shades of grey (nearer/higher card is lighter, deeper ones darker), not shadows alone. Bad mock: stacked cards all the same mid grey with only blurred shadows.
why: Shadows are barely visible on dark surfaces and do not separate layers.
check: elevated surface tokens get lighter with elevation in `.dark`.

text: [T61] All shadows come from a single light source: same direction on every element. Bad mock: one button's shadow falls right, the next one's falls left.
why: Random shadow directions look odd and complicate the experience.
check: `box-shadow` x/y offset sign identical across components.

text: [T84] Never keep default shadows from design tools. Bad: X 0, Y 2px, blur 4px, #000000 at 50%. Good: X 0, Y 8px, blur 24px, #000000 at 15% (lower opacity, larger blur).
why: Default shadows look hard and dirty.
check: shadow blur >= ~3x Y offset and alpha <= ~20%; no `rgba(0,0,0,.5)` small-blur shadows.

text: [T43] Do not give inner elements the same corner radius as the container. Example: card 30pt outer, image inside 15pt (bad: 30 and 30).
why: Same radius for outer and inner looks uneven.
check: inner radius < outer radius (see section 5 for the 30 vs 15 vs "slightly" tension).

text: [T56] Avoid too many borders. Good mock: only the search input keeps a border; list rows have no row borders; the action footer is separated by a light grey fill. Bad mock: filled search band plus a bordered box around every row.
why: Too many borders complicate the experience and look cluttered.
check: count of elements with visible `border` per screen; list rows without `border-bottom` where tone/space can separate.

text: [T89] Create contrast between items with colour and space instead of divider borders: good mock alternates a light grey row tint with white rows and generous row padding; bad uses hairline borders between rows.
why: Borders for differentiation feel outdated.
check: list items without `border-top/bottom`; zebra or tonal fill used.

text: [T22] Use more padding and margin. Good mock: card content has larger insets, smaller hero image, clear room around title and photo; bad: title and image almost touch edges.
why: Too little margin/padding destroys visual hierarchy and looks cluttered.
check: card inner padding >= content-to-edge distance used elsewhere; visual.

text: [T20] Separate sections with spacing, not extra divider lines. Menu mock: "Options" group and "Settings" group split by an extra gap (good) rather than a hairline rule (bad).
why: Adding a new element (a line) just to create a division is not ideal.
check: group gap > intra-group gap; no `hr` between groups.

text: [T41] Leave space from edges and group related elements: card text inset visibly from the card edge, title/body spacing consistent, tag-title-description grouped. Bad: text hugging the left edge and title lines packed tight.
why: Less or inconsistent spacing hurts readability and grouping.
check: padding between content and card edge consistent on all sides; heading line-height not tight.

text: [T93] Avoid ambiguous spacing in forms: space between groups larger than between a label and its own input. Annotated: bad = 16px above label and 16px label-to-input; good = 16px above the label and 8px label-to-input.
why: Equal gaps make it unclear which label belongs to which input.
check: (gap between previous input and next label) > (gap between label and its input); good ratio 2:1 (16 vs 8).

text: [T67] Use consistent gaps in grids: same horizontal and vertical gap between tiles (bad mock: vertical gap noticeably larger than horizontal).
why: Uneven gaps give a bad experience and a sloppy grid.
check: `row-gap == column-gap` (or a deliberate token pair) across the grid.

text: [T58] Build on a grid and test it at different screen sizes; the layout must keep the same set of items and consistent columns across breakpoints. Bad mock: 3 columns on desktop, a 2x2 on narrow with one empty (crossed) placeholder tile. Good mock: 4 columns on desktop, 2x2 filled on narrow.
why: Irresponsive design has a negative impact on user experience.
check: screenshot at 375/768/1280/1440: no overflow, no empty slots, items preserved. (see section 7: image is ambiguous)

text: [T72] When several images share a screen, make some lead: good mock = one full-width hero tile, two half tiles, one full-width tile; bad = a uniform 2x3 grid of equal tiles.
why: With all images equal users cannot recognise the lead images.
check: tile area ratio between largest and smallest > 1 in a gallery.

text: [T73] Add dynamism to image layouts with multiple columns and tile sizes (mosaic: one big 2/3-width tile + two small stacked, then a narrow + a wide tile). Bad: a uniform 3x4 grid of equal tiles.
why: A uniform grid detracts from the appeal of the images and is boring to scroll.
check: more than one tile size; visual.

text: [T50] Prompt users to scroll by showing a glimpse of the next section at the fold. Bad: hero with big empty space below, so it looks finished; good: top edge of the next section peeks at the viewport bottom.
why: Too much spacing between sections makes users less likely to scroll.
check: next section's top within the first viewport at common heights (e.g. 1440x900, 375x812).

text: [T79] Overlap elements to add depth and clarity: good profile card has the avatar overlapping the cover image edge (half on photo, half on card) with the name below; bad has the avatar inline next to the name fully inside the white area.
why: Keeping all elements separate gives a basic look.
check: visual.

text: [T96] Scale hero images to fill the container so the visual content is visible across all display sizes. Bad: image scaled so its floating elements spill up onto the headline ("bills" collides with a coin); good: image is contained within its rounded frame, nothing overlaps the heading.
why: Scaling the image to the full screen feels different on different screen sizes.
check: hero image bounding box does not intersect heading; `object-fit` set; test at 375/768/1280. (see section 7)

text: [T49] Place the CTA at the end of the Z-shaped reading path (Gutenberg): 1 top-left logo, 2 top-right nav CTA, 3 diagonal to image/left-centre, 4 bottom-right CTA. Good mock mirrors the hero so image sits left and text + CTA sit bottom-right.
why: Eyes travel a Z from top-left to bottom-right, so the last stop gets the action.
check: primary hero CTA position in lower-right quadrant of hero; visual.

text: [T23] Maintain pattern repetition: all selectors of a kind share one shape and style. Good mock: footwear type, size and quantity controls are all pills with the same selected style (dark fill); bad: type = rounded pills, size = square boxes, quantity = pill.
why: Strange differences between visual elements make users re-learn controls for each task.
check: `border-radius` equal across same-role controls.

text: [T11] Keep the main CTA big and close to the thumb (Fitts' law): good mock puts a full-width tall button at the bottom of the card; bad has a small button at top right.
why: A small, distant target takes more time to hit.
check: primary action height >= 44px `[engine note]`; sits in bottom third on mobile.

text: [T28] Fill the CTA with the primary colour (white label) so it stands out: pricing card "Get Pro" filled primary, not a pale grey button with coloured text.
why: A dull CTA gets less attention and is harder to find.
check: primary button bg is the brand token, not neutral.

text: [T30] Use button hierarchy on a screen with two actions: "Log In" = filled primary; "Sign Up" = text-only primary-coloured link below. Bad: two identical filled buttons.
why: No hierarchy makes decisions hard.
check: at most one filled primary per view region; secondary uses outline/ghost/text.

text: [T51] Button padding: side padding = 2x the top/bottom padding (annotated x, 2x). Bad: label touches the left and right edges with ~no side padding.
why: Buttons with small padding do not look good.
check: `padding-inline / padding-block` ~ 2.

text: [T82] Never wrap a button label; keep it on one line and let the button grow ("Submit Form", not "Submit / Your Form" on two lines).
why: Wrapped button text is not good practice and looks cramped.
check: `white-space: nowrap`; button height == single-line height.

text: [T83] Differentiate button weight: neutral and negative buttons become outlined (grey border/text, red border/text), the positive action stays solid filled. Bad: neutral solid grey, negative solid red, positive solid blue, all competing.
why: Buttons with similar contrast compete for attention; the positive action should read as the clear one. (The book's caption says "lighter contrast"; see section 7.)
check: only one solid-fill button per button group.

text: [T98] On mobile make buttons full width within the system margins (good: Retry and Exit span the card minus margins; bad: ~60%-width centred buttons).
why: Small-sized buttons give an incomplete feeling.
check: button width == container inner width on viewport < ~480.

text: [T33] Make tappable cards look clickable by adding an actionable button that describes the action (good: small dark "Apply >" pill on each row; bad: bare rows).
why: Plain cards fail to indicate that they are clickable.
check: interactive card has a visible control or chevron/affordance.

text: [T48] Enhance the clickable area so it includes label plus icon plus padding: good mock shows the hit box around "Click Me ->" including text, around the radio including its label "I'm an option", and around the hamburger with padding; bad mock hit boxes are only the arrow, only the radio dot and a tight box on the icon.
why: Small hit areas make clicking buttons and elements difficult.
check: `<label for>`/wrapping `<label>` on radios; icon buttons >= 44x44 hit area `[engine note on 44]`.

text: [T65] Make text actions look clickable with colour or a button: "Read more" as a blue underlined link (bad: body-coloured plain text).
why: Users cannot identify clickable elements when they look like body text.
check: `a` elements differ from surrounding text by colour and/or underline.

text: [T4] Align forms vertically: labels left-aligned above fields, fields one edge, submit button on the same left edge. Bad: labels right-aligned beside fields at ragged offsets and the button centred, producing a zig-zag eye path.
why: Consistent alignment orients the user faster; inconsistent looks unprofessional.
check: labels, inputs and button share the same `left` coordinate.

text: [T14] Use a single column on small forms (group related fields otherwise). Bad: two columns of narrow fields.
why: Multiple columns disrupt vertical momentum.
check: inputs stacked, one per row, full width of the form.

text: [T16] Put social login first, then "or log in with" separator, then username/password and button, with "Don't have an account? Create here" at the bottom. Bad: registration form first, social option after.
why: Users see the one-tap option first and can log in without filling the form.
check: social buttons precede credential fields in DOM/visual order.

text: [T18] Checkboxes for multiple selections, radio buttons for a single choice (good mock: skills list uses squares with Design and Marketing checked; single-choice list uses circles with one selected).
why: The control shape tells the user whether one or many may be picked.
check: `input[type=checkbox]` for multi, `radio` for exactly-one groups.

text: [T24] Search fields need descriptive placeholder text that hints what can be searched: "Ebooks, audiobooks, and videos" vs bare "Search".
why: Without it the user is clueless about what kinds of things can be looked up.
check: search `placeholder` is more specific than "Search".

text: [T36] Fewer options for faster decisions (Hick's law): 8 radio options (bad) reduced to 3 plus "Others" which reveals a "Type Here" text field (good).
why: More options create complexity and delay choice.
check: radio group size <= ~5 with an Other/free-text escape `[engine note on 5]`.

text: [T38] Use input masks for phone numbers and dates: placeholders like (___) ____-____ and DD/MM/YYYY instead of generic "Number" and "Date".
why: Without a mask users are unsure about the format.
check: phone/date inputs have mask or format hint placeholder / `inputmode`.

text: [T39] When the user picks from 2-4 values, display all options side by side (radio rows), not in a dropdown. Bad: a "Light" dropdown for Light/Dark.
why: It is not ideal to hide 2-3 values inside a dropdown.
check: `select` with <= 4 options is a smell.

text: [T40] Avoid free typing when a control works better: price range with a dual-handle slider (value labels $47 and $150 above handles, green fill between) instead of From/To text inputs.
why: A slider makes the process fast and understandable; fields everywhere are not ideal.
check: range inputs use slider (see section 5 for precision caveat).

text: [T59] Keep forms short and clear: fewer fields (merge First/Last Name into "Name"; 4 fields became 3).
why: Every additional field lowers conversion and loses leads.
check: count of required inputs; flag unnecessary ones.

text: [T64] Use boxed fields: rectangles with visible borders and rounded corners, not underline-only fields.
why: It takes time for underline fields to be recognised as a form.
check: `input` has visible border on all four sides.

text: [T74] Do not use placeholder text as the label. Good mock: small grey labels above each filled field (Name, Surname, Address) with the entered value inside; bad: only "Name", "Email", "Address:" inside the empty fields.
why: Placeholder-as-label causes many usability issues (label disappears when typing).
check: each input has a visible `<label>`; placeholder is not the only identifier.

text: [T80] For selecting from a large multi-option list use toggle tokens (pills in a 2-column grid; selected = primary fill with white text, unselected = grey fill and grey text) instead of a long checklist.
why: A long list of checkboxes can make users abandon the form.
check: multi-select with > ~6 options uses chips/tokens.

text: [T90] Group form fields with section titles: bold "Personal Information" over First/Last Name, bold "Contact Information" over Address/City, with an extra gap between groups; do not leave one undivided list.
why: Ungrouped forms lack clarity; title plus grouping separates regions.
check: forms > ~4 fields have `fieldset/legend` or heading per group.

text: [T91] Differentiate the focused field: good mock shows a dark indigo thicker border on the active input (cursor in "Last Name"); bad shows the same grey border while the cursor blinks.
why: An obvious current-field state makes the form feel interactive.
check: `:focus` style differs in border colour from default.

text: [T99] Do not explain obvious fields (no "?" tooltip "Username is your user name"); when explanation is needed, put it directly below the field.
why: Stating the obvious in tooltips is noise.
check: helper text rendered inline below the field; no tooltip for self-evident labels.

text: [T100] Checkboxes must be squares ("boxes"), not circles. Bad: round checkbox with check looks like a radio.
why: Round checkboxes look too similar to radio buttons.
check: checkbox `border-radius` small (square/slightly rounded), radio fully round.

text: [T5] Use icon + label in menus for complex or abstract functions: each item (New Tab, New Incognito, Recent Tabs, Downloads, History, Bookmark) gets a leading outline icon plus its text; bad = label only.
why: Icon plus label gives rational and emotional impact.
check: menu items carry leading icon; visual.

text: [T37] Put the most important pages at the corners of the tab bar (serial position effect): good order Home, Search, Chat, Cart, Profile (Home first, Profile last); bad order Search, Home, Cart, Profile, Chat.
why: People remember the first and last items in a series.
check: primary destinations are first/last in tab bar.

text: [T81] The book recommends a hamburger menu instead of visible navigation links on the page shown ("visible navigation decreases conversion rate; hamburger increases it"). (opinion, no evidence on the page; see section 5)
why: Fewer competing links keep attention on the form/CTA.
check: visual.

text: [T9] Show a progress bar for multi-step flows: 3 steps with step 1 a green check, current step 2 a green numbered node, step 3 grey, solid green connector for done and dashed for remaining, step names below.
why: Without it users cannot track where they are in the flow.
check: stepper present in flows > 2 steps.

text: [T32] In mobile onboarding let users skip at any time and put "Skip" within thumb reach: centred at the bottom under the pagination dots, over a dark gradient scrim. Bad: tiny "Skip" in the top-right corner.
why: Top corners are hard to reach.
check: skip link in bottom half; present on every onboarding step.

text: [T34] Highlight the best plan: filled primary gradient card with white text and an inverted white button, next to a plain white card. Bad: both plans styled identically.
why: Same colour on both makes the most-used plan of no importance.
check: exactly one pricing card has the highlighted treatment.

text: [T44] Limit card content: truncate description with an ellipsis and add an "Explore More"/"See more" button; never make a card's text scroll internally (bad shows an inner scrollbar).
why: Scrolling within a card creates confusion.
check: no `overflow: auto/scroll` on card body; `line-clamp` used.

text: [T45] Use swipe actions on list rows (swipe reveals a red trash and a green star circle button) instead of a "..." menu button on every row.
why: Option buttons slow the process; swipe is fast and minimal.
check: visual.

text: [T53] For homogeneous content use a list (one container, hairline separators) instead of a stack of separate cards.
why: Cards do not give a sense of similarity; lists speed up scanning.
check: repeated identical items share one container.

text: [T85] Limit links in a card: one link or a limited set of actions. Good: plain body text, a filled "Primary Action" and an underlined "Secondary Action"; bad: also two inline blue underlined links in the paragraph.
why: Too many inline links look awful and give a negative impression.
check: inline `a` in card body = 0-1.

text: [T76] Avoid the super-minimal look in list rows: add detail ("Episode #1" instead of "#1", a progress bar with "42%" and a cancel x, rather than a bare bar).
why: Too little detail fails to describe the element and the process.
check: rows show secondary descriptor and progress value; visual.

text: [T68] Add a stroke (white ring) to avatars placed over photos or busy backgrounds.
why: Avatars without stroke blend with the background.
check: avatar over image has `border`/`ring` in surface colour.

text: [T7] Use one consistent icon set: the page's good example shows three coherent sets in rows (A filled circle, B outline ring, C plain line) while the bad mixes filled circle plus, outline trash and outline cart.
why: Inconsistent icons risk confusion and hurt brand credibility.
check: icons from one library, same fill style and size grid.

text: [T46] Use simple flat icons for UI (thin dark outlines), not glossy gradient "fancy" icons.
why: Fancy icons look unprofessional.
check: icons are single-colour line/solid glyphs.

text: [T70] Keep icons front-facing, not in perspective (good: flat-on image icon; bad: tilted glossy 3D icon).
why: Perspective views look complicated.
check: visual.

text: [T71] Use the same stroke weight throughout an icon set (bad pen icon mixes thick and thin strokes).
why: Inconsistent stroke weight is bad practice.
check: all SVG icons share one `stroke-width`.

text: [T66] Keep illustrations consistent: lock the figures' clothing colours to the brand palette (violet, charcoal, navy) rather than random red, yellow, green, blue.
why: Illustrations become part of the brand; inconsistent ones fail to define it.
check: illustration colours within brand palette hues.

text: [T69] Use high-resolution images, particularly where text goes over them.
why: Blurry or distorted images do not look appealing.
check: image natural width >= rendered width x devicePixelRatio.

text: [T78] Use supportive images that reinforce the message (credit-card visual for "The simplest way to pay your bills") instead of irrelevant stock (a wallet in a hand).
why: Irrelevant images fail to support the story and meaning.
check: visual / alt text matches the headline.

text: [T10] Show the user where and why an error occurred: red "!" inside the offending field and a small red message directly below it ("Username not valid!"); bad shows only a "1 error found !" summary above the form.
why: Users must locate the error and know the reason to correct it.
check: error text adjacent to its field and linked (`aria-describedby`).

text: [T27] Show the steps of a procedure visually: pagination dots under the button and copy "We just have one question" instead of "We have a few questions".
why: Users do not know how many steps remain.
check: progress indicator present.

text: [T52] Make selected items pop: selected row filled with primary gradient and white text vs unselected white rows (bad: only a tiny checkmark changes).
why: Users cannot tell that something happened.
check: selected state differs by fill from default.

text: [T60] Error/offline screens must name the error and suggest a solution: illustration, "You're offline" and a full-width "Retry" button with a refresh icon.
why: A bare spinner looks incomplete and gives no recovery path.
check: network failure state has message + retry action.

text: [T62] Use skeleton loading (grey blocks mirroring the layout with a shimmer sweep) instead of a spinner for content areas.
why: Skeletons are perceived as faster; spinners make loading feel slower and show nothing.
check: loading state has skeleton matching final layout.

text: [T63] Keep important guidance visible: show password rules as an inline checklist under the field ("More than 8 characters" met in green, "Include special characters or numbers" unmet) instead of a "?" tooltip.
why: Required info hidden under a tooltip is missed.
check: requirements rendered in the DOM, not in a hover-only tooltip.

text: [T97] Show a glimpse of an off-screen element in horizontal carousels (the next card peeks at the edge) rather than only a slider indicator.
why: Indicator alone gets ignored.
check: carousel item widths < container width with next item partially visible.

text: [T101] Create more than you consume: balance reading and inspiration with real designing.
why: More creation means more practice and better UI skill.
check: n/a. Not a UI rule.

text: [X1] Dark-mode recipe: base surface a dark grey not black (T15), accents at tones 200-500 (T2), separate palette from light mode (T3), elevation by lighter greys (T77).
why: These four rules together define dark theme tokens.
check: token audit of `.dark`.

text: [X2] Form recipe: one column (T14), left-aligned visible labels above boxed fields (T4, T64, T74), 8px label-to-input and 16px between groups (T93), titled groups (T90), focus ring (T91), errors under field (T10), rules inline (T63), masks (T38), full-width verb-labelled submit (T57, T98).
why: Collates the 10+ form rules into one build order.
check: run T-checks above.

text: [X3] Pricing recipe: highlighted best plan (T34), accent top rules to distinguish (T88), filled primary CTA (T28), consistent corner shapes.
why: Combines three pricing tips.
check: one highlighted card; visual.

text: [X4] Reserve the primary colour for CTA, active state and key accents (T55, T28, T92, T19) and keep everything else neutral.
why: Signal colour only works when scarce.
check: primary-coloured area share; sibling items have <= 1 coloured.

text: [X5] Do not rely on the book's mock pixel values as tokens; they are artboard numbers. Use the stated ratios (side padding = 2x vertical, 8:16 label gaps, inner radius < outer, 45-75 ch, 14pt floor).
why: The mocks use inconsistent sizes between good/bad (see section 7).
check: n/a

text: [team research] Count the high-signal cluster: centred or bottom-left hero stack; tiny uppercase or mono eyebrow; oversized tightly tracked sentence headline; vague support sentence; large rounded primary button + text-link secondary; floating rounded glass navigation; dark photographic or gradient background; acid, blue or purple accent; decorative grain/grid/radial light/cursor effect; later sections of equal cards or list rows; repeated reveal animation and dramatic microcopy. Any single item can be appropriate; five or more without a brand-specific reason create the tell.
why: The tell is the cluster, not one component.
check: count items in the first viewport (threshold in LAI-35).

text: [team research] Treat a choice as suspicious when several of the seven conditions (core idea 3) are true; the definition is contextual: a centred hero, pill, serif, glass layer, lowercase wordmark or giant headline can be right; the problem is reflexive combination and missing product reasoning.
why: Avoids banning techniques; bans reflex.
check: `visual`.

text: [team research] Before drawing a hero write: audience; offer; change (concrete before/after); objection; proof; action (verb + object); brand premise (three traits + one productive contradiction, e.g. "disciplined, nocturnal, restorative - but not mystical"); visual thesis; familiar frame; authored deviation.
why: Required design sequence.
check: `DIRECTION.md` has all ten.

text: [team research] When a hero feels generic do not add a new fashionable object; first remove the eyebrow, secondary action, ornamental container, decorative labels and redundant effects.
why: Default posture.
check: n/a (process).

text: [team research] Keep a tracked uppercase/mono eyebrow only when it identifies a real taxonomy, status, date, edition, location or sequence, that information would be useful without the styling, and the same label system is used consistently. Otherwise remove it and let the heading establish hierarchy, write a natural-language context line, integrate the category into the headline, or use placement/scale instead.
why: It creates the appearance of hierarchy after the fact and adds reading friction.
check: uppercase element <= 13px above the H1.

text: [team research] Do not enlarge a sentence headline until it fills most of the viewport with extreme tracking and forced breaks. Keep it only when language is the brand artifact, the words deserve the stage, letterforms and breaks were composed, and the hero stays balanced at intermediate and narrow widths. Better: medium display scale with image/grid/whitespace leading; one word or typographic detail carrying emphasis; a compact editorial title tied to evidence; reveal scale later.
why: Scale becomes the idea; it competes with the image and pushes support and action into the margins.
check: H1 size vs viewport (LAI-52).

text: [team research] Do not default to a floating pill dock (centred glass capsule with logo, segmented nav, white or accent CTA). Keep it only when floating solves a real spatial/persistent-tool need, the site has few destinations and the geometry belongs to the identity, the background makes translucency meaningful, and mobile stays clear. Better: edge-aligned header on the page grid; brand-specific masthead; quiet transparent header with no outer shell; conventional header distinguished by type, spacing or content.
why: The nav becomes a visual product demo; stacked edge treatments say nothing about the brand.
check: header container `border-radius` >= 999px or position detached with blur.

text: [team research] Do not build a "designed-to-look-designed" CTA (wide rounded rectangle with inner arrow chip, liquid fill, magnetic hover, rotating arrow). Keep inner structure only if it communicates a real state or split action, motion explains direction/progress, and the target stays stable. Better: a plain well-proportioned solid control with specific copy; a typographic link for low commitment; a brand-derived shape used consistently; a familiar button with a distinctive pressed/focus/material response.
why: Too many parts for a simple action; it performs "premium" instead of building confidence.
check: count of decorative behaviours on CTA <= 1; target does not move on hover.

text: [team research] Lowercase as borrowed personality: when wordmark, nav, buttons, headings and body are all lowercase there is no contrast between brand voice and functional language. Keep it only when the wordmark is intentionally drawn that way, the tone supports intimacy, and functional labels still follow coherent casing; otherwise preserve sentence/title case in nav and actions, reserve lowercase for the wordmark or one expressive role, use wording not casing for warmth. (Note: this is the exact voice Larpo's own site uses; see `larpo-brand-and-constraints.md` LBC-06 and conflict C2.)
why: All-lowercase can feel affected on a serious or physical service.
check: lowercase-initial share of nav/button labels (D-TYPE-6-style).

text: [team research] Do not add decorative technicality (mono labels, coordinates, rotated side notes, indices, temperature readouts, grids, status dots) to imply precision. Keep only when the data is real and decision-relevant, comes from the product's operating environment, and the user can act on or interpret it.
why: Borrows credibility from measurement systems without supplying measurement.
check: each label maps to a data field.

text: [team research] Atmosphere stacking: allow one primary atmospheric device and at most one quiet supporting material. If the photograph already establishes the world, effects should mostly protect legibility and motion continuity.
why: Photograph + dark grade + noise + glow + blend + parallax + cursor lens + loader means every layer says "mood" and none has a job.
check: count of atmospheric layers <= 2.
