text: [team research] Do not default to the template waterfall (hero, logo strip, three features, product card, metrics, testimonials, pricing, FAQ, final CTA). Map the page to six visitor questions: what is this? is it for my situation? how does it work? why should I believe it? what does it cost or require? what happens if I act? Include only the sections needed.
why: Sequence should resolve uncertainty, not mirror a theme demo.
check: section list mapped to questions.

text: [team research] Replacement order: remove the suspect element; identify the lost job if any; try to solve it via copy, hierarchy, proximity or real evidence; add a component or effect only if a job remains; adapt to the brand's type, shape, material and motion language. Removing a pill eyebrow and adding a handwritten annotation is not authorship; removing an orb and adding a WebGL blob is not originality.
why: The replacement trap.
check: n/a (process).

text: [team research] First viewport = familiar frame (recognisable logo position, usable navigation, readable message, obvious action) + one authored deviation (brand-specific break in composition, visual evidence, type, material or interaction). If everything deviates the visitor decodes the interface; if nothing does the page is forgettable.
why: Low complexity and high prototypicality scored well in first-impression studies.
check: `visual`.

text: [team research] Decide the single preattentive focal point (product state, human/physical subject, headline, result/proof, or interactive utility); every other high-contrast object must support or yield. A giant headline, bright CTA, acid eyebrow, luminous nav and moving cursor effect cannot all be primary.
why: Contrast, scale, position, colour, edge and movement register before reading.
check: squint test.

text: [team research] Group in this order: proximity; alignment; shared type or colour; divider; container.
why: Generated pages jump to containers and pills because they are easy to code.
check: n/a (process).

text: [team research] Ask three separate questions of any CTA or hero: can they see it? can they understand it? do they have a reason to believe and act? Do not solve the third by increasing the answer to the first (attention is not persuasion).
why: Scale, motion, saturation attract attention but do not create trust.
check: `visual`.

text: [team research] Integrate message, evidence and image into one composition; do not make the real offer look like a banner pasted over a background or isolate important information inside flashy ornamental treatments.
why: Banner blindness.
check: `visual`.

text: [team research] Present one dominant next step; a secondary path only for a meaningfully different visitor state (e.g. "Book a visit" vs "View the space"); keep the action close to the promise or object it affects.
why: Two equally styled buttons expose an unresolved priority.
check: primary CTA count 1; secondary visually weaker.

text: [team research] A hero reduces to: identity; specific promise or proposition; one line of mechanism or scope; one action; one piece of visual or factual evidence. Eyebrows, secondary actions, side labels, social proof, scroll cues and atmospheric effects begin absent.
why: Minimum truthful argument.
check: element count.

text: [team research] Emotion without theatre: write the specific desire with a credible service and time ("Swim, sauna, and recover after the last public session") instead of performative fragments ("Keep the night. Meet us after dark."). Emotion comes from subject, stakes, language, rhythm, cultural association and sensory specificity, not poetic fragments, glows or slow reveals.
why: The first performs a mood; the second gives the mood a service.
check: copy contains a concrete noun, time or number; `visual`.

text: [team research] No blank-prompt design: do not open an editor until audience, offer, action, objection, proof, brand premise, visual thesis, actual copy and asset plan are written. A fictional product still needs coherent operating facts first.
why: The 2026-08-29 miss was a fictional SaaS hero built in one pass with no file in the KB opened first.
check: `DIRECTION.md` complete before code.

text: [team research] Default-free first sketch: the first structural sketch contains no eyebrow, pill nav, secondary CTA, glass, gradient/glow, card grid, grain, entrance animation, cursor effect or decorative mono label; add any back only with a written reason. Sketch three different dominant geometries before coding.
why: Defaults enter through the first sketch.
check: first render lacks the listed items.

text: [team research] Name one authored deviation in a sentence specific enough that a different product could not reuse it unchanged. Weak: "Large type over immersive photography." Strong: "Availability and temperature are composed like the club's physical lane board, crossing the underwater photograph at the pool's real horizon." "Large type on a dark gradient" is not a move.
why: Gate 3.
check: sentence in `DIRECTION.md`.

text: [team research] Removal test: for each decorative or unusual element name its job, remove it mentally, identify what meaning/hierarchy/state/action/identity is lost; if nothing is lost remove it; if something is lost solve the job with the smallest existing means.
why: Gate 6 of the 14-gate critique.
check: list of elements with jobs.

text: [team research] Transplant test: replace the company name and hero copy with an unrelated startup; circle every element that still works perfectly; those are infrastructure or defaults, not identity. The design needs at least one coherent system of choices that fails this transplant. If every choice still makes equal sense, the design carries no identity (it may remain as infrastructure but cannot count as the authored idea).
why: Gate 5 (canonical) / Gate 12 (research).
check: DOM-mutation screenshot comparison.

text: [team research] AI-cluster count in the first viewport: tracked uppercase eyebrow; oversized sentence headline; extreme negative tracking; lowercase-everything voice; floating pill dock; nested rounded nav group; white or accent CTA capsule; arrow chip inside CTA; dark plus neon palette; photo + heavy grade + grain; rotated side label; decorative mono metadata; two CTAs by reflex; cursor lens or blob; loader before a simple page; generic poetic fragments (16 items). Three demand review; five or more require a structural reset unless the brief explicitly justifies the cluster. Diagnostic only, never a number to publish.
why: Gate 4 (canonical preflight) / Gate 5 (research).
check: count <= 2 to pass; 3-4 review; >= 5 reset.

text: [team research] Focal competition: list every high-salience element (largest type, brightest colour, highest-contrast surface, face or human subject, moving object, primary action, nav shell, glow/reflection); choose one first and one second focal point and reduce the rest until the squint test gives that order.
why: Gate 4 of the research list.
check: squint/grayscale.

text: [team research] Typography proof: typeface matches the written brand voice; headline shape composed at all target widths; H1 does not win over evidence accidentally; body and action copy comfortably readable; casing has semantic rules; tracking is optical not a trendy preset; line heights accommodate diacritics and zoom; font loading does not shift disruptively.
why: Gate 7.
check: `check.mjs` type section.

text: [team research] Navigation proof: labels predict destinations; header aligns to the page system; current state exists where needed; primary service action distinct but not ornamental theatre; no nested shell without a real grouping job; mobile nav deliberately composed; focus visible across every background.
why: Gate 8.
check: DOM audit.

text: [team research] CTA proof: label names the action and likely outcome; commitment understandable; only one primary; button/link semantics match behaviour; geometry belongs to the brand system; hover does not move the target; pressed, focus, loading and result states exist when relevant.
why: Gate 9.
check: DOM + state audit.

text: [team research] Colour proof: palette explained through brand, category, material and context; accent has a limited job; text and controls meet contrast; state not encoded by colour alone; dark mode has tonal hierarchy beyond black plus neon; photography and UI colours coexist intentionally.
why: Gate 10.
check: contrast + role table.

text: [team research] Effect budget: classify every effect as evidence, hierarchy, state, spatial continuity or atmosphere; allow one dominant atmospheric technique per viewport; if several effects occupy one class keep the strongest.
why: Gate 11.
check: list classified.

text: [team research] Ten-second critique: show the screenshot without explanation for ten seconds and ask what company/category it is, what you can do, what you remember visually, what felt generic or performative, what looked clickable; do not defend the concept before hearing the answers.
why: Gate 13.
check: n/a (process).

text: [team research] Rendered acceptance: inspect real output at desktop, tablet, mobile widths: first paint before animation, image and font loading, heading wrapping, browser chrome and safe areas, keyboard order and focus, touch targets, hover/active, reduced motion, 200% zoom and text spacing, slow device/network, contrast across changing imagery, actual destinations. Inspect at 100 percent for craft and 25 percent for social-feed hierarchy; confirm the idea survives platform cropping and read every number back against sample-data coherence.
why: Gate 14 / canonical Gate 7.
check: screenshots at the listed widths.

text: [team research] Critique in precise, correctable statements ("The 142px H1 covers the photographic subject and forces the action into the bottom margin"; "The accent is used for five different roles, so it no longer identifies the primary action"). Avoid "make it pop", "more premium", "more modern", "it needs wow", "the font is bad".
why: Specific diagnosis prevents the next revision becoming a different pile of trends.
check: n/a.

text: [team research] Sample-data coherence (canonical Gate 6): names belong to one organisation; dates run in a plausible sequence; totals add up; statuses agree across views; IDs use one format; the visual answers what is this, what changed, what action is available, how it supports the claim; label `sample workflow` or `demo data` when not a real environment.
why: The 2026-08-29 mock claimed 47 alerts collapsed into one incident while listing 49 silenced items.
check: reconcile totals.

text: [team research] Handover must state plainly: (1) which constraints the piece follows and which it knowingly departs from; (2) every invented number, logo or endorsement in the frame; (3) the Gate 4 cluster count and the Gate 3 authored move; (4) what has not been verified. Handing over a visual without this list is incomplete delivery.
why: Escalation checklist.
check: present in delivery message.

text: [team research] Gate 0: before styling read `context/constraints.md`, decide for each layer whether it belongs to the publisher or the subject, and read `context/brand.md` for the visual direction, motion budget and reference set ("ingredients, not templates"). The playbook may read, draft, render, critique and propose directions; it must escalate any departure from `context/constraints.md`, publishing/posting to a Larpo surface, and invented numbers/logos/endorsements.
why: The playbook triggers on any visual or public-facing output (page, hero, section, mockup, wireframe, component, social image, banner, screenshot, concept piece, copy for a larpo surface; any edit to .html .css .svg .jsx .tsx .astro .vue).
check: n/a (process).

text: [team research] Write the desired voice before browsing fonts (institutional or personal; engineered or crafted; contemporary or historical; restrained or expressive; warm or severe; familiar or specialist), then evaluate letterform personality, readability at real sizes, display behaviour at real headline size, family breadth/axes, italics/numerals/special characters, Lithuanian and required language coverage, licensing, performance, and whether the face is already a default signal in the category. Research supports typeface-personality associations but no universal "proper font".
why: Brand congruence.
check: voice sentence in `DIRECTION.md`.

text: [team research] Do not let one trendy family be the whole identity (wordmark, display, body, labels, metadata and buttons all the same popular face with only size changes). Create voice via intentional width/optical size/grade/weight; contrast through scale and measure not extreme tracking; one specialist role (display cut or editorial serif); custom lettering for the wordmark with familiar interface text; numerals/punctuation/capitalisation as signature.
why: A neutral grotesk is excellent infrastructure but generic when it is everything.
check: role/family table.

text: [team research] Headline size is relational (no magic `vw` value): the H1 should not overpower the main evidence unless language is the evidence; support text and action stay comfortably visible; the title keeps a stable shape across common widths; forced breaks are intentional and tested with real copy; tight tracking must not deform the face or cause collisions; never six mobile lines merely because desktop scale was fluid. For a photographic lifestyle hero start with a medium display range; for an editorial statement hero the title can dominate if wording and typesetting are unusually strong.
why: Gates for headline size.
check: H1 box vs evidence box area; H1 lines at 390 px <= 5.

text: [team research] Define type roles (display, page title, section title, lead, body, functional label, metadata), each with family, weight, size range, line height, tracking, measure, casing and allowed contexts; a visible difference between roles should come from at least two properties, not a two-pixel size change.
why: Role system.
check: role table.

text: [team research] Casing: sentence case for most actions and navigation unless the brand has a reason; reserve all caps for short real metadata whose shape benefits scanning; never combine all caps + mono + tiny size + wide tracking as a universal "premium" label; reserve lowercase for a deliberate verbal or identity role; keep capitalisation grammatically consistent.
why: Casing carries hierarchy.
applies: all (but see LBC-06 for Larpo's own surfaces).
check: casing class per label group.

text: [team research] Text measure and rhythm: roughly 45-75 characters for sustained Latin text; short hero support may be narrower. Avoid long centred paragraphs, `text-wrap: balance` on every paragraph, aggressive negative tracking on text fonts, body text made faint to look refined, line heights chosen without checking ascenders/descenders/diacritics, fixed heights that break under increased text spacing.
why: Readability.
check: ch count; fixed-height containers with text.

text: [team research] Assign spacing values to relationships (glyph/icon detail; control interior; label-to-value; heading-to-support; support-to-action; module-to-module; section transition; compositional stage); between-group space at least about twice within-group space. A base-unit grid (Carbon-style) provides rhythm and consistency, not "every margin divisible by eight": use a small coherent scale, distinguish component from layout spacing, keep keylines, make deliberate optical exceptions, change scale steps responsively rather than shrinking proportionally.
why: Spacing is relational grammar.
check: gap ratios.

text: [team research] Layout: define page grid and gutters, content measure, image safe area, focal object, reading path, alignment anchors, overlap rules and mobile recomposition first, then component styling; add surfaces only where a boundary communicates something. Asymmetry needs a counterweight (image mass, whitespace, colour, text density, alignment) and a clear reading start.
why: Generated pages choose cards, pills and shadows first.
check: `visual`.

text: [team research] Mobile is a new composition: decide the focal point, whether the image crop still contains the subject, whether nav becomes a menu/short list/contextual action, whether the headline needs new breaks or a smaller role, which secondary elements disappear, and how the first action stays reachable without covering content. Optical QA at 320, 375, 768, 1024, 1440, a wide desktop and 200% text zoom: cap/baseline alignment, mathematically-but-not-optically centred icons, widows and weak final headline lines, over-tight rounded letters, nav weight consistency, text measure over changing imagery, vertical rhythm after font load.
why: Do not stack the desktop DOM.
check: screenshots at the listed widths.

text: [team research] Reject one-word colour recipes ("blue means trust", "red means urgency", "green means growth", "black means luxury"). Choose colour through five questions: category expectation; brand stance (align or contrast); functional hierarchy; environment (light, display, photography, print, materials); culture and audience.
why: Meaning depends on context, culture, category, object, surrounding colours, lightness, chroma and learned associations.
check: rationale in `DIRECTION.md`.

text: [team research] Ensure contrast before emotion: readable text, identifiable controls, distinguishable states, usable focus indicators; check the actual rendered combination (weight, size, alpha compositing, gradient position, image variation, hover/focus/active/disabled, light/dark); do not use colour as the only state cue.
why: Nuance cannot compensate for faint text.
check: sampled contrast >= 4.5:1 / 3:1.

text: [team research] Build a job-based palette: primitives then semantic roles (canvas; raised and inset surfaces; primary and secondary text; subtle and strong borders; primary action; interactive text; focus; selected; success, warning, destructive, information; expressive image/illustration colours). The brand accent need not fill every interactive role.
why: An accent on everything stops directing attention.
check: accent-hue element count.

text: [team research] Treat chroma as an attention budget: allocate saturation to the most important state or action and keep surrounding chroma lower; the same saturated accent across many objects flattens priority and yields a generic "dark plus neon" scheme.
why: Highly saturated colour is preattentive.
check: share of saturated pixels near non-primary elements.

text: [team research] A convincing dark palette needs tonal separation between canvas and surfaces, a readable text hierarchy, borders/shadows appropriate to dark adaptation, image grades that preserve subject detail, a focus colour that survives varied backgrounds, accents whose chroma does not vibrate against near-black, and tested disabled/secondary states; for hospitality, culture or wellness neon-on-black suggests nightlife, gaming, crypto or futuristic software unless the physical brand earns it.
why: Dark mode is not black plus acid.
check: contrast of tiers.

text: [team research] Get palette distinctiveness from relationships, not rare hex values: unusual dominant-to-accent proportion; subject-tied temperature contrast; material-derived neutrals; photography and UI sharing a controlled grade; one signature interaction colour used sparingly; a palette that changes meaningfully across sections or states. A better brief: "The audience knows public pools through turquoise tile and clinical blue. Use mineral gray and off-white for institutional calm, then reserve a muted copper for heat and booking states."
why: Distinctiveness through relationships.
check: `visual`.

text: [team research] When colour may affect action, test meaningful systems (hierarchy, label, placement, surrounding contrast, perceived commitment) rather than isolated button hues; a different CTA colour may win because it is more visible in that composition, not because of a universal effect.
why: Test, do not mythologise.
check: n/a.

text: [team research] The primary navigation answers: where am I; what major destinations exist; which matters now; how do I reach the main action. Use descriptive labels with strong information scent; avoid "Explore", "Discover", poetic nouns when a concrete destination exists.
why: Navigation is information architecture, not hero decoration.
check: labels predict destinations.

text: [team research] Header composition: align to the hero grid unless a deliberate full-bleed masthead is the concept; wordmark, destinations and action have visibly different roles; do not wrap the nav in a capsule by default; no segmented-control shell inside another nav shell unless links behave as a stateful local control; stable active state; translucency only if the header crosses changing content; clear focus, contrast and target size on every background.
why: Header rules.
check: DOM audit.

text: [team research] Functional navigation usually uses sentence or title case; all-lowercase nav combined with lowercase logo, lowercase CTA and soft rounded containers becomes a familiar generated-brand package.
why: Casing and tone.
check: casing class.

text: [team research] Use a button for an action on the current page or application state and a link for navigation to another destination; a link may be styled as the primary call to action but its semantics must match its behaviour.
why: Semantics.
check: `a` vs `button` audit.

text: [team research] CTA copy: concrete verb + object ("View availability", "Book a night swim", "See the session timetable", "Request membership details", "Watch the workflow", "Compare plans"); avoid "Get started", "Learn more", "Explore", "Continue", "Join now" when the commitment is specific; short only when it stays predictive.
why: Predictability of outcome.
check: label not in generic list.

text: [team research] CTA hierarchy: one control represents the expected action; secondary actions are lower emphasis and serve a different need; do not give every nav item, hero action, sticky action and card action the same accent.
why: Similar appearance communicates similar importance.
check: accent-filled controls per viewport <= 1.

text: [team research] Button geometry belongs to the system: corner logic related to fields, cards, imagery and physical artifacts; padding that centres the label; icon scale and gap suited to the font; expands for longer copy; touch targets met without looking inflated; border, fill and shadow do not all define the same edge. A pill suits a compact action, filter or strongly rounded identity, not as the automatic premium shape.
why: Geometry coherence.
check: radius family; target size >= 24 px desktop / 44 px mobile.

text: [team research] An arrow should clarify direction, external navigation, progression or motion; do not add an arrow chip only to look designed; keep icons stable on hover (small translation/material response may reinforce direction; rotation and magnetic movement only if physical behaviour supports the brand).
why: Ornamental icons.
check: icon + label redundancy; hover transform.

text: [team research] Every primary action needs default; hover where applicable; visible keyboard focus; active/pressed; disabled only when necessary and explained; loading/pending if not immediate; success/error if state changes. Animation must not move the click target away from the pointer; the static control must already look usable. Place the CTA close to the promise, product state, form or content it affects. Hero-action test: cover styling and read only label, destination and nearby copy; can the visitor predict what happens, commitment level, whether money/signup/booking/contact is involved, and why it follows from the promise?
why: State and proximity.
check: state audit.

text: [team research] When the headline reaches 142 px (`9.4vw`, line-height .82, tracking -.083em) and occupies most of the lower-left, it overpowers the photographic subject: reduce to a medium display role so the subject leads. The audit's single highest-impact correction: delete the fashionable UI wrapper around the photograph and rebuild the first viewport from real venue facts; rebuild order: define venue facts and service model; rewrite hero and CTA with specific language; remove eyebrow, side note, dock shell, secondary CTA, cursor lens and liquid button; reduce H1 until the swimmer is first or co-equal focal point; redesign header as venue IA; establish a physical material and signage system; add at most one authored interaction; test desktop, intermediate, mobile, keyboard, reduced motion.
why: Tidehouse audit P1 findings (H1 142 px; nested pill nav; 11 px mono uppercase eyebrow tracked .15em; weak action language "Book a night" vs "Request access" vs "Try a single night").
check: H1 height vs subject.

check: `visual`/copy review.

text: [team research] Before choosing any font, gradient, shader or component library, write one thesis sentence naming the audience, the change the product creates, and the visual behaviour that supports the claim. Weak: "modern AI SaaS, dark with gradients." Strong: "Make operational complexity feel inspectable: a calm editorial shell around one live product workflow that progressively reveals cause and effect."
why: A style word is not a concept; without a thesis every later choice is drawn from the statistical default.
check: `DIRECTION.md` contains a thesis sentence with audience + change + visual behaviour.

text: [team research] Choose layout from the strongest evidence: interface proves value -> product dominates; transformation is emotional/physical -> art direction or photography; idea is unfamiliar -> explanatory diagram/sequence; trust is the barrier -> proof beside the promise; product already known -> less explanation, more immediacy. Never force text-left / screenshot-right by default.
why: The arrangement is right only when the content creates that hierarchy, not because a starter template used it.
check: `visual`; record the evidence type in `DIRECTION.md`.

text: [team research] Make one decision lead in every viewport (scale, type, image, product artifact, spatial reveal, grid break, or material contrast). Do not let headline, glow, 3D object, logo cloud, floating cards and animated background compete for first place. Use the squint test.
why: A page reads as designed when one decision leads and the others support it.
check: blur the screenshot; primary/secondary/tertiary order must remain obvious.

text: [team research] Choose type by voice and content, not trend; use the fewest families and roles that make hierarchy unmistakable; pair for meaningful contrast (texture, width, construction, historical character); tune the actual face (optical size, weight, tracking, line height, measure are not interchangeable presets).
why: "A strong type system can carry an entire site. Decorative effects cannot rescue weak typesetting."
check: count families and roles in `getComputedStyle`; `visual` for voice fit.

text: [team research] Keep body copy around 45-75 characters per line (short marketing copy may be narrower). Prevent accidental six-line hero headings by editing copy, changing measure, or choosing another composition. Use fluid display sizing with controlled minima and maxima and inspect every breakpoint rather than trusting one `clamp()`.
why: Long measures lose the eye; a six-line H1 means copy and composition were not matched.
check: `ch` count of `p` between 45 and 75; H1 line count <= 4 at 320, 375, 768, 1024, 1440.

text: [team research] Load only used font weights and formats; prefer WOFF2, set fallbacks, prevent layout shift; use optical alignment for icons, punctuation, caps and buttons instead of assuming mathematical centering looks centred.
why: Mathematically centred glyphs and symbols look off-centre; unneeded weights cost payload.
check: network panel font list; CLS from font swap.

text: [team research] Space by relationship: at least a 2:1 difference between intra-group and inter-group gaps as a practical starting rule. Build a small scale then assign semantic roles: micro (icon-to-label), control (internal padding, adjacent controls), group, region (between modules), section (page pacing), stage (intentional empty space around a dominant composition).
why: Spacing is not a uniform blanket; grouping must be legible before containers are added.
check: measure gap between sibling items vs gap between groups; ratio >= 2.0.

text: [team research] Use alignment and whitespace before adding containers. If every idea needs a card, the grouping logic is probably weak. Do not use a three-card grid for content with a clear hierarchy; repeated equal cards communicate equal importance.
why: Containers add objects the visitor must perceive; equal cards flatten priority.
check: count of bordered/filled boxes vs groups; `visual`.

text: [team research] Define content grid, gutters, max measures and full-bleed rules; let some elements escape the grid only when the concept earns it. Design reusable sections for their container (container queries), not only the viewport.
why: Grids guide, they must not flatten; container-relative responsiveness keeps modules reusable.
check: presence of `@container` on reusable modules; `visual`.

text: [team research] Separate primitive colors from semantic roles (text, surface, border, accent, positive, warning, destructive). A disciplined palette: background family, text hierarchy, surface hierarchy, one primary signal colour, semantic status colours, optional expressive colours reserved for illustration or data. Do not apply the brand accent to every button, icon, heading fragment, glow, badge and selection state.
why: An accent used everywhere stops directing attention.
check: number of distinct elements carrying the accent hue; accent confined to <= 2 roles.

text: [team research] Verify contrast on the actual rendered background, including alpha and imagery. Do not use light-gray text to manufacture hierarchy at the cost of readability.
why: Alpha and photographic backgrounds change the real pair.
check: contrast >= 4.5:1 body, 3:1 large, sampled from the render.

text: [team research] Use borders for separation, tonal shifts for grouping, shadows for elevation; do not stack all three automatically. Good shadows are layered and low-opacity (tight contact shadow plus broader soft layers); match softness to element size and distance; avoid coloured glow unless light emission is part of the concept. Nested radii should be optically concentric when insets are visible.
why: Random radii and stacked edge treatments read as components from unrelated kits.
check: per element: edge defined by at most 2 of {border, tonal fill, shadow}; radius inner = outer - inset.

text: [team research] Motion must clarify origin, destination, hierarchy, continuity or causality. Use transform and opacity for most transitions; short responsive feedback and slower composed page entrances; stagger by reading order, not every DOM child; springs for interruptible/physical interactions, easing for time and sequence; scroll-driven motion reversible and tied to a narrative; pause offscreen animation, cap ambient frame rates, honour reduced motion; never hide essential content behind an animation that can fail.
why: Decorative ambient motion competes with reading and can fail.
check: `prefers-reduced-motion` media query present; animated properties limited to transform/opacity.

text: [team research] A static screenshot must still communicate the core design.
why: Heroes are posted as stills; animation cannot carry the idea.
check: render with animations disabled and compare with the intended frame.

text: [team research] Before adding a shader, particle, blur, glass, noise, dither, 3D, marquee, mask or cursor effect, finish the sentence "This effect helps the visitor understand or feel ___ because ___." Reject it if the answer is "it looks cool". Provide a fallback image or CSS treatment and set a performance budget first.
why: Effects are materials, not concepts.
check: `DIRECTION.md` has the completed sentence for every effect.

text: [team research] For SaaS and AI sites show a believable workflow, state transition, input/output pair, data trace or result with accurate copy, realistic data and visible interaction consequences. A screenshot floating in a glass panel is not proof. Do not invent customer logos, testimonials, metrics, awards, dashboards or capabilities to fill a layout.
why: Proof is what reduces the visitor's objection; decoration does not.
check: `visual`; every number traces to a labelled sample dataset.

text: [team research] Study references by decomposing them into transferable principles (hierarchy, pacing, framing, type contrast, material, motion grammar, proof strategy) and combine several; do not copy distinctive copy, assets, branded colour combinations, signature illustrations or near-identical compositions. Keep a reference ledger recording what was borrowed at the level of principle; if one reference dominates, the synthesis is too narrow.
why: Originality comes from synthesis.
check: `DIRECTION.md` reference ledger lists borrowed principle per source, >= 3 sources.

text: [team research] Treat these as weak when reflexive (not forbidden): purple-on-black gradient blobs without brand logic; centred badge + huge gradient headline + two CTAs + floating dashboard + logo strip + three equal feature cards as automatic skeleton; glass inside glass; rounded rectangles around every sentence; random sparkle/dot-grid/beam/orb; "supercharge", "revolutionize", "seamless", "unlock the power"; many tiny uppercase mono labels; uniform section rhythm; mixed icon families or stroke weights; placeholder charts and fake terminal windows; scroll animation on every element; a trendy font not checked for Lithuanian characters, numerals, italics, licensing.
why: Each is a statistical default.
check: `tools/check.mjs` AI-tell list plus `visual`.

text: [team research] Build the system in seven layers: brand and content constraints; primitive scales (colour, type, spacing, radius, border, shadow, motion); semantic tokens (text, surface, action, state, focus, overlay); component contracts (anatomy, states, behaviour, responsive, a11y); section patterns (hero, proof, features, workflow, case study, pricing, FAQ, CTA); page composition rules (pacing, alternation, narrative, transitions); QA harnesses (realistic content, narrow widths, zoom, themes, reduced motion, keyboard, loading/error states).
why: Coherent work becomes easier without making every page identical.
check: `visual`; tokens file exists before components.

text: [team research] Accept a design only after checking: real copy and data; desktop, intermediate, mobile and zoomed widths; long and short headings; keyboard and focus order; hover, active, disabled, loading, error, empty, success states; overlays and scroll locking; light/dark when supported; reduced motion and touch; image and font loading; Core Web Vitals risks; originality against the reference set.
why: "A design is not finished because the code compiles or a desktop screenshot looks good."
check: `tools/check.mjs` plus manual list.

text: [team research] When a brief asks for one desktop social still, scope-limit the checklist in LDP-20 to what the deliverable actually shows; the full checklist applies to real pages.
why: The team measured the cost of over-scoping (see LHS-13, LHS-30).
check: delivery contract in `DIRECTION.md` names what is out of scope.

text: [team research] Use the nine-step study loop for any new craft area: observe strong and weak examples; describe without aesthetic adjectives; extract rules; recompose for a different brief; implement a narrow specimen; render with realistic content and stress states; critique against the thesis; record what survived and failed; convert repeatable wins into tokens/components/skills. Promote only repeated, verified patterns into the design system.
why: Reading builds vocabulary; repeated decomposition, reconstruction, critique and browser verification build judgment.
check: n/a (process).

text: [team research] For every shipped page save the brief, references, rejected directions and final reasoning; capture desktop and mobile results; record the techniques that worked with exact constraints and the failures with reasons.
why: "Larpo's own verified work should gradually become the strongest teacher."
check: project folder has brief + references + rejected directions.

text: [team research] Install or adopt a skill/repo only after reading its full contents, scripts, hooks, dependencies, update mechanism, licence and overlap. Do not stack several taste skills; use one primary skill plus at most one or two supporting skills. No external repo is adopted merely because it says "anti-slop". Verify the current licence and asset-level licences before reuse; public visibility is not permission to copy.
why: Agent skills are executable instructions; stacked taste prompts conflict and produce overdesigned work; one candidate (`video-to-superprompt`) was removed after the installer marked it high risk.
check: n/a (process).

text: [founder] Do not set the headline as an oversized generic grotesk that dominates most of the frame.
why: Rejected default in the 2026-08-29/30 hero exercises; scale became the idea and crowded the product.
check: H1 bounding box < 28% of frame height and the family is not Geist/Inter/Manrope/Space Grotesk-class without a written reason; `visual`.

Accepted direction Nacre: sculptural central product, spacious composition, restrained palette, elegant display typography, information placed around the image rather than inside a generic content block. text: [founder] Reject Baton-class output: sterile monochrome product proof with the publisher identity imposed on the fictional subject. Reject Linecheck-class output: industrial photograph + giant headline + right-side inspection panel + familiar blue CTA, because product-specific details do not rescue a familiar skeleton.

text: [founder] Take and Mise were "materially better received than Baton and Linecheck". The lesson is not their layout but that brand field, material, interface vocabulary, image, type and action reinforce one premise. Future work must exceed them rather than restyle them.
why: Ledger positive evidence; relative rating, not an unqualified accept.

section: 2a. Founder-feedback rules (hard guardrails for fictional hero concepts)

text: [team research] Larpo's website, captions, profile assets and any frame explicitly presented as Larpo follow Larpo's canonical system (geist, black/white/neutral gray, lowercase). A clearly labelled fictional product concept gets its own type, colour, layout, imagery and logo territory unless the brief explicitly asks for a Larpo-branded concept. The Larpo caption and truth boundary stay Larpo's.
why: The Baton weakness was caused by the preflight applying Larpo's publisher identity to the fictional subject.
check: `DIRECTION.md` states publisher layer vs subject layer; subject fonts/colours differ from the Larpo set.

text: [team research] Label fictional names, workflows and sample data as `concept` or `sample`/`demo data`; never present them as client proof. Keep the label legible at feed scale (an in-frame label alone does not survive feed scale; the post copy must also state it is a fictional concept).
why: Truth boundary; the evenbooks sidecar notes the in-frame label does not survive feed scale.
check: string "sample" or "concept" in the DOM; caption includes the word `concept`.

text: [team research] For "one desktop hero and screenshot for X" build exactly: one hero, desktop only, 1920 x 1080 composition, 3840 x 2160 lossless PNG export, browser-openable source. An explicit different X ratio from the user wins. Keep critical text and actions clear of a 96 px outer safe area.
why: Locked delivery contract (playbook status active, updated 2026-08-30).
check: viewport 1920x1080; export dimensions 3840x2160; text/CTA bounding boxes >= 96 px from edges.

text: [team research] Deliver three things: the source, the 4K PNG and a browser-openable preview. Binary files over 2 MB do not go in the Larpo KB (use JPEG fallback, e.g. `linecheck-hero-x-4k.jpg`).
why: KB pre-commit blocks binaries over 2 MB.
check: file listing.

text: [team research] Load at most three skills for a hero: `frontend-design` (subject-specific identity and spatial exploration), `product-proof-saas` (believable mechanism and coherent sample state), and one narrow finishing skill chosen from the actual need. Never stack several taste skills; a shader or image tool must solve a named problem.
why: Taste skills conflict and overdesign.
check: n/a (process).

text: [team research] Before styling write one line each: product and category; audience; expensive or frustrating moment; product mechanism; single visitor action; proof artifact visible in the frame; three brand traits and one useful contradiction; one visual behaviour native to the product world. If the answers could describe an unrelated startup unchanged, the subject is not specific enough.
why: A hero should not be transplantable.
check: `DIRECTION.md` has all eight lines.

text: [team research] Privately sketch three different dominant geometries before coding; they must change the spatial idea, not palette, corner radius or card order. Do not default to left copy + right dashboard, giant headline above a generated photograph, a photograph with one floating UI panel, or a decorative card collage. Structures that count as different: type integrated into a product canvas; one edge-to-edge workflow with copy in its controls; a split where the split is a real comparison/state transition; an editorial composition around one physical artifact; a modular identity system whose repeated units encode product behaviour; a cropped application world with nav and CTA in the same plane.
why: "Three directions are not different if all three keep the same DOM skeleton."
check: three structure names recorded; none equals a rejected skeleton.

text: [team research] Give the fictional subject its own wordmark or mark; choose typography from the brand premise not from the agent's usual stack; use sentence case unless the subject voice supports another; start headline exploration between 56 and 84 px at 1920 px and exceed that band only when the composition clearly benefits; treat mono and uppercase utility text as real data language.
why: Prevents the shared grammar; band keeps the rest of the composition alive.
check: `font-size` of H1 between 56 and 84 px at 1920; font-family differs from last 8 ledger entries.

text: [team research] Do not default to Geist, Inter, Manrope, Space Grotesk or a similar neutral grotesk for every fictional company; record why the display face belongs to the product.
why: Seven r5 concepts all used Geist for nav/body/UI and five also for the H1.
check: font-family list vs the five named families.

text: [team research] Define colour as functional roles: field, ink, secondary surface, signal, state and material colour. Use contrast to control attention. Avoid forcing Larpo monochrome on a fictional subject and avoid the dark-plus-neon and warm-cream-plus-serif clusters unless the subject makes them unavoidable and the composition is otherwise original.
why: Trend clusters read as generated.
check: palette roles listed; hue of leading accent differs from other batch entries.

text: [team research] Navigation: scan in one second (logo, three or four real destinations, sign-in or equivalent, one clear main action when appropriate); normal capitalisation and readable size; avoid the floating pill dock, nested rounded group and excessive empty space; it may be quiet but must feel designed (alignment, rhythm, hover, mark, CTA share one identity). CTA: one dominant by default, written from the visitor's point of view, add a secondary only when it resolves a distinct visitor question; check default, hover, focus, pressed without letting button work consume a screenshot brief.
why: Founder rejected the pill dock and generic CTAs (LHS-04, LHS-05).
check: nav links 3-4; primary CTA count 1.

text: [team research] Make the product the proof: show something the user creates, reviews, controls, compares or approves; show a decision or state transition not decorative analytics; label fictional material `sample` or `concept`; keep names, dates, statuses, measurements and totals coherent; never invent customers, endorsements, outcomes or security claims. The visual must answer what changed, what the user controls and what happens next.
why: Product proof is the evidence layer inside an authored brand.
check: sum of visible numbers reconciles; `visual`.

text: [team research] A shader, texture or real-time effect is used only when its behaviour expresses the product; provide a still fallback for the screenshot. A custom logo must come from the same premise as the layout; a generic symbol plus wordmark does not complete the identity.
why: Effects and logos must belong to the subject.
check: `visual`.

text: [team research] Render review: inspect at 100 percent (alignment, type, edges, image quality), at 25 percent (feed hierarchy, CTA clarity), in grayscale (focal order), and in a centre crop plus a modest top/bottom crop (platform resilience).
why: Hero stills are consumed in feeds.
check: screenshots at 100%, 25%, grayscale, crops exist in `reports/`.

text: [team research] Internal critique questions: could an unrelated startup use this skeleton by changing logo and copy? is the biggest element also the most meaningful? one idea or several disconnected effects? does the UI prove a workflow? are nav and CTA intentionally designed? does the font choice express the subject? did generated imagery become the concept? does it hold at 25 percent? did the work stay in scope? Any "yes" to the first or seventh, or "no" to the fourth through eighth, requires another pass; change structure before polishing the surface.
why: Codified in the runbook.
check: `visual`; transplant test (LAI-34).

text: [team research] After delivery append direct acceptance/rejection to the feedback ledger with the exact reason; do not call a rejected result a benchmark; preserve rejected artifacts as labelled negative evidence; do not silently promote a generated concept into canonical guidance; record exactly what was accepted without declaring the whole layout a template.
why: Ledger is system memory.
check: ledger entry exists for each verdict.

text: [team research] The playbook may alone: define a fictional concept, create its brand and interface, generate supporting assets, implement one desktop hero, render and critique. It must escalate: publishing/posting the result; presenting fictional material as client work; adding invented customers, endorsements, outcomes or security claims; changing Larpo's own brand system.
why: Playbook escalation rule (active).
check: n/a (process).

text: [team research] Acceptance at feed scale: at 25 percent size a viewer must identify (1) the company or product identity, (2) the main promise or product moment, (3) the focal visual, (4) the action if there is one. Reject if it becomes a gray block, a giant headline plus tiny UI, or a generic app screenshot.

text: [team research] Utility mono and uppercase labels only for authentic data or machine language; use sentence case unless the product's voice justifies another choice; tune width, weight, line height and measure together; "a large title is not a substitute for a visual premise."
why: Decorative seriousness is a tell.
check: uppercase/mono text count with non-data content.

text: [team research] Start from a proof artifact (what a user creates, reviews, controls, compares or approves); generated imagery must leave room for the intended layout and share lighting, crop and visual grammar.

text: [team research] A hero is the first compressed argument and must answer: is this for me? what changes for me? why should I believe it? what should I do next?

text: [team research] Do not polish a hero until you know: one primary audience, one primary action, the exact offer, visitor current vs desired state, strongest proof available now, main objection, traffic context and awareness, real assets, technical constraints (performance, CMS, framework, localisation, motion, accessibility).
