text: [team research] Never describe a concept name or mark as legally available or trademark-cleared; a web search is not a clearance review. For real brands search exact and similar names, alternative spellings/pronunciations, design codes, related goods and services, app stores, domains, company databases, common-law use, reverse image search as a screen; consult a trademark professional before adoption (USPTO guidance cited).
why: Originality and trademark gate.
check: concept note states "not cleared".

text: [team research] Avoid AI-logo failure modes: a generic geometric icon rationalised after drawing; a sparkle as AI shorthand; the first letter in a rounded square; four gradients before a monochrome test; perfect symmetry with weak optical weight; a logo that cannot be redrawn because it depends on texture; a custom wordmark made by deleting random pieces of letters; a mark too close to a well-known design defended as "inspired"; a concept presented as trademark-safe.
why: Failure list.
check: `visual`.

text: [team research] Invent an effect with: brand concept + visual primitive + transformation + input + constraint (e.g. reconciliation + braided paths + merge into one traceable line + scroll progress + never cross the copy column). Effect families and their generic failures: SDF (endless metaballs), domain warping (cloudy purple noise), flow fields (particle soup), Voronoi (tech-honeycomb), reaction-diffusion (decorative slime), advection (cursor goo everywhere), raymarching (chrome blob), refraction (glass-card distortion), dither/halftone (grain over everything), contour (random map lines), interference/moire (illegible vibration), image displacement (unrelated cursor ripple), particles (starfield "AI"), procedural material (texture hiding weak composition), grid/terrain (Tron grid).
why: Effects need a semantic job.
check: formula sentence recorded.

text: [team research] Choose one dominant effect lane: subtle depth field; system behaviour; object-centric 3D; cinematic world. Do not mix three or four heavy lanes in the first viewport; a SaaS home page usually needs subtle depth or system behaviour; pricing and high-intent pages need less.
why: Visual noise and cost.
check: lane named.

text: [team research] Effect composition: design the static poster first; reserve a quiet contrast region for copy; lower motion amplitude near text and actions; give pointer response a bounded purpose (never make visitors chase the CTA); one dominant frequency scale (not fine grain + medium particles + large blobs + moving grids); keep colours inside the brand tonal hierarchy; share geometry with logo or product model; stop the effect at a meaningful boundary.
why: Subordinate the effect to the page.
check: `visual`.

text: [team research] Anti-generic effect test, answer all eight: what product fact generated it; what would change if the company sold something else; what is the primitive; what is transforming; what user input matters; what constraint keeps it subordinate; can it be recognised in one still frame; can it fall back to a static image without losing the message. If the first two answers are weak it is decoration and stays simple.
why: Effect-as-decoration filter.
check: eight answers in `DIRECTION.md`.

text: [team research] Effect libraries: Three.js for full scenes; React Three Fiber for declarative React composition; OGL for a lighter WebGL layer; native WebGL2 for small full-screen fragment effects; WebGPU/TSL only with compatibility and fallback planning; The Book of Shaders, LYGIA (dual-licence, do not assume unrestricted commercial use), Inigo Quilez articles, MDN WebGL best practices as learning sources. Do not select from demo beauty alone: check licence, bundle weight, maintenance, framework fit, cleanup, fallback, tunability.
why: Library selection criteria.
check: n/a.

text: [team research] Build effects progressively: semantic content and layout; static poster or CSS background; capability and motion-preference checks; lazy-loaded renderer; interaction and animation; adaptive quality; cleanup and context-loss handling. Message and action must work before the renderer initialises and after it fails. Three DOM layers: `hero__fallback` (visible immediately), `hero__canvas` (decorative, usually `aria-hidden="true"`, non-interactive, `pointer-events: none`), `hero__content` (semantic). Never put essential text in Canvas/WebGL.
why: Progressive enhancement.
check: DOM layers present; hero readable with JS disabled.

text: [team research] Quality tiers: static (reduced motion, unsupported contexts, data-saving, low-power, failure); low (lower resolution, no post-processing, fewer particles, reduced update rate, no pointer history); standard (devicePixelRatio capped around 1.5, one or two meshes/passes, modest particles, bounded pointer response); high (capable desktops only, when it materially benefits). Never make the high tier the only art-directed version. Start with `min(devicePixelRatio, 1.5)` for continuous full-bleed effects; allow 2 only after profiling; render a smaller back buffer and upscale for soft/noisy effects.
why: Pixel budget.
check: `renderer.setPixelRatio(min(dpr,1.5))` or equivalent.

text: [team research] Render-loop policy: use `setAnimationLoop` where applicable; pause when not visible; render on demand for static scenes; no per-frame allocation; clamp delta time after tab suspension; stop observers/listeners at teardown; dispose geometries, materials, textures, render targets and renderer on route change; handle `webglcontextlost`.
why: Performance and leak safety.
check: code audit.

text: [team research] Fragment-background recipe: one screen-covering triangle; pass resolution, time, normalised pointer uniforms; correct aspect ratio; few noise octaves; consistent colour space; authored contrast mask behind the content column; quantise/dither/grain only if it belongs to the identity; capture a deterministic poster; use seeded randomness. Bind the visual to meaningful state (workflow stage, selected source/result, scroll progress, pointer proximity to a relevant object, completion/approval/conflict) mapped to one or two parameters.
why: Reproducible approved first frame.
check: poster capture exists.

text: [team research] Fallback is part of the design: capture at the approved composition (not a random frame); export AVIF/WebP plus a compatible option if needed; keep the same quiet copy region and contrast; separate desktop/mobile crops if composition changes; keep the poster loaded while the first shader frame compiles then crossfade only after a successful render; under reduced motion keep the still or a near-static low-amplitude state.
why: Graceful degradation.
check: poster asset.

text: [team research] Performance and accessibility gates for effects: no long task delaying navigation/CTA; no layout shift when the canvas initialises; no uncontrolled VRAM growth; no repeated shader compilation after load; no WebGL errors; avoid blocking calls (`getParameter`, readbacks); respect `prefers-reduced-motion`; preserve text contrast across every animated frame; avoid rapid flashing/high-frequency interference; provide a DOM/transcript equivalent for meaningful sequences; keep keyboard/pointer actions independent of canvas; never encode state only through hue or motion; zoom and text-spacing changes must not collide with a fixed canvas composition.
why: Gates.
check: profiling on a representative phone and laptop.

text: [team research] Route product situations to type direction, proof, logo territory, behaviour and bans (excerpt): developer infrastructure -> high-legibility grotesk, mono only for real code; proof request/route/trace/result; avoid black + neon grid + code wallpaper. Security/privacy -> calm sturdy sans; protected object/evidence/action/recovery; avoid shield/lock cliche and threatening red. Finance/operations -> stable proportions, excellent numerals; source values/reconciliation/approval/audit trail; avoid crypto gradients, fake growth. Creative collaboration -> expressive display + usable UI face; avoid rainbow blob, floating avatars. Climate/science -> transparent info-first type; avoid simulated data as evidence. HR/team workflow -> human not childish; avoid pastel people illustrations. AI writing/research -> strong reading face; sources, intermediate state, edit, citation, output; avoid purple orb, sparkle, fake typing. Healthcare -> quiet legible accessible type, conservative motion; avoid glossy wellness. Consumer productivity -> compact warm fast type; avoid gradient mesh + oversized rounded cards. Premium B2B service -> distinctive controlled display + sober UI; avoid generic serif + beige + thin rules.
why: Decision matrix (not a style generator; every row needs product-specific facts).
check: `visual`.

text: [team research] Five-question router: is the effect proof, explanation, interaction or identity; which product verb should it embody; which visual primitive carries that verb; what familiar structure keeps the page understandable; which one deviation makes the system difficult to transplant. Generate three systems that change type structure, composition, logo territory and signature behaviour together, not three colour variants.
why: Routing premise to system.
check: three systems recorded.

text: [team research] Fill the product-derived vocabulary worksheet before exploring: product nouns; verbs; user emotions before/after; physical analogies; structures; materials; time behaviour; inputs; outputs; human-control point; risk or objection; category cliches to ban; familiar page frame; authored deviation.
why: Product-derived visual vocabulary.
check: worksheet present.

text: [team research] SaaS hero preflight groups: product truth (all facts written; coherent sample data and a real limitation; labelled sample workflow; no invented logos/testimonials/certifications/metrics); typography (licence, coverage, axes, WOFF2; Lithuanian glyph test; 25% readability; role-based styles; no damaging layout shift); product visual (explains its own object, state change, action; believable density; coherent data; states exist); logo (3 territories + 20 thumbnails; one colour/reversed/16-32 px; custom kerning; preliminary conflict checks recorded; never "legally cleared"); effect (derived from a noun/verb; one lane; approved poster first; quiet copy region stable; reduced-motion/mobile/low-power/failure fallbacks; pixel ratio/iterations/pause/cleanup explicit); composition (1440 x 1024 directly; survives cropping; focal order survives squint/grayscale; nav and CTA geometry same brand system; one memorable deviation).
why: Preflight.
check: checklist.

text: [team research] Do not proceed to polish when: the product cannot be explained as a workflow; the chosen font lacks glyphs or web rights; the logo has not survived monochrome and small-size tests; the effect has no product-derived rationale; the screenshot uses contradictory or fake data; the static first frame is weaker than the animation; the CTA and navigation are generic components pasted over an unrelated visual.
why: Stop conditions.
check: n/a.

text: [team research] Use one primary skill plus no more than two supporting skills (routing table: product-led hero -> `product-proof-saas` + `better-typography` + `better-layout`; font system -> `better-typography` + `better-colors` + `better-accessibility`; generic-looking audit -> `audit-ai-design-slop` + `no-ai-design-slop` + `audit-reference-originality`; subtle WebGL hero -> `webgl-landing-steering` + `webgl-components` + `optimize-web-animations`; custom Three.js -> `threejs` + `webgl-3d-object`; final interaction critique -> `better-interface` + `web-quality-audit` + `review-animations`). Start from the concept, not the skill name; a skill that says "add particles" is a technique source, not authorisation.
why: Skill routing principle.
check: n/a.

text: Before producing anything, restate the brief in your own words (goals, objectives, audience, deliverables) and surface it for confirmation or correction.
why: Misunderstandings and missing points are far cheaper to catch before creative work than after.
check: an explicit "brief restated" artifact exists before the first design/code step; it lists goals and objectives.

text: Ask clarifying questions up front until you can say exactly what the client wants; do not start on an ambiguous brief.
why: "Understanding what they want is critical; else, you won't be able to offer it" (p.87).
check: list of open questions is empty or each has a stated assumption before build.
source: (p.87) [engine note: when the founder cannot be asked, write each assumption down explicitly]

text: Ask "Why?" repeatedly about each requirement to find the underlying problem, ambition and motivation. Examine requirements before committing to a solution or budget, because the client may not understand why they need the website/app.
why: The stated request is often a proxy for a business problem.
check: each major requirement has a recorded "why".

text: Write the scope down first: what is delivered, what is NOT included, and what costs extra.
why: An explicit boundary lets you go back to the client when scope creeps or they ask for things "that weren't in your original proposal" (p.82-83, 85).
check: a scope doc with an explicit exclusions list exists.

text: State deliverables concretely: what will be produced, by whom, by when, how many meetings, and what the client must do to keep the schedule on track.
why: Many clients have never commissioned design; the process must be explained to them.
check: deliverables list with owner and date per item.

text: Include a realistic schedule that accounts for other work running in parallel, to avoid bottlenecks. "Above all, avoid over-promising."
why: Missed deadlines damage trust more than a longer honest estimate.
check: schedule exists; no item lacks an estimate.

text: When estimating time, add a buffer: example 7 days of work -> quote 10 days (add 2-3 days). Deliver early against the quoted date.
why: Early delivery against a padded promise reads as speed and wins ratings; (the book cites Walmart/Amazon delivery padding as the same trick).
check: quoted duration = estimate + 2 to 3 days on a 7-day job (~30-40% pad).

text: Split large projects into small pieces and complete one or two pieces per day; do not postpone starting a big job.
why: Procrastination on large jobs is the failure mode; small pieces make progress measurable.
check: task list granularity: each task completable in about a day.

text: Cut a project into essential stages (design concept, development, implementation, etc.) and close each stage explicitly (invoice/sign-off on completion).
why: Each stage gets a clean sign-off and protects against late or non-payment; also helps cash-flow forecasting (p.83).
check: stage list with completion criterion per stage.
source: (p.83) [engine note: for an agent, stage sign-off = review gate before next stage]

text: Involve the client in design decisions and learn their business and customers before proposing solutions.
why: An involved client is receptive to new ideas; they know their own customers better than you do.
check: decision points listed with who approves.

text: Do not accept projects you do not know how to finish; confirm you can reach the finish line first. Prefer genres you know, master them, then move to the next topic.
why: Taking work to "get the job first" leads to abandoned projects and bad ratings (the p.22-23 story: a freelancer claimed grid/Bootstrap skill, had none, ghosted for three days then quit).
check: capability self-assessment before accept.

text: If you cannot finish or will miss a deadline, say so immediately; do not waste the client's time.
why: Early notice lets the client re-plan.
check: blockers raised at first occurrence, not at deadline.

text: Answer client messages promptly and professionally: balanced tone ("not too strict or too funny"). On disagreement stay patient and composed; prefer a call/face-to-face over text.
why: Calls de-escalate; text hardens conflicts.
check: n/a mechanically. visual/manual.

text: Use plain, complete sentences and full words in client communication; avoid slang/abbreviations ("u", "DIY") because clients from other countries may not understand them.
why: Non-native readers misinterpret shorthand.
check: grep for "ur", "u ", "DIY" style shorthand in outbound text.

text: Keep communication short and specific: enough information for the other person to understand fully, no excess or useless information; double-check before sending (spell/grammar checkers are "not foolproof").
why: Brevity plus precision prevents misreads.
check: manual re-read of each outbound message.

text: Keep timesheets / track time per task; base future estimates on similar past projects; use them to explain cost and to detect a project running over budget.
why: Past data makes quotes faster and more accurate; shows which work types are profitable.
check: time log exists and estimates reference it.

text: Before the first working session write answers to: your process; why you take the work; which projects you will/won't take (and that "no" is allowed); your role in the client meeting; what success means to you AND the customer; what makes you stand out.
why: Undefined process/success criteria cause drift; this is the book's #1 recurring theme ("Define").
check: written answers to the 6 items exist.

text: Learn when to say NO: no time/capacity, unrealistic expectations of budget/timescale/results (do not start until aligned), unethical activity or request to violate copyright, no chemistry.
why: Protects brand, client relationship and sanity.
check: explicit accept/decline decision with reason.

text: Choose one skill path ("hill") first; learn the latest tools, techniques, methods for it; then expand into related skills.
why: Depth differentiates; chasing whatever earns money this month (3ds Max, Android) scatters effort.
check: n/a (planning).
source: (p.9-10) [engine note: for an agent, prefer depth in the user's stack over adding tools]

text: Make the basics strong before advanced techniques.
why: Newbies "don't get much grip on the basics".
check: n/a.

text: Do not switch tools/technologies as soon as they appear; learn it well, account for the slow early learning curve, then switch.
why: Early switching is slow and shallow.
check: n/a.

text: Add only skills related to your major skill (e.g., HTML/CSS with UI design), not unrelated ones.
why: Related skills compound ("tree" metaphor).
check: n/a.

text: Allocate a daily block of time for learning; never stop learning.
why: Technology and tooling move fast.
check: n/a.

text: Be able to explain, on request, the process, rationale and daily workflow behind a project; developers must be able to explain method/code choices.
why: Interviewers (and clients) always ask.
check: n/a.

text: Use a wide range of design stakeholders: collaborate with management, test users, technical department; be able to explain design concepts (user persona, testing, layout) to marketers, engineers, business analysts.
why: UX/UI is collaborative even for a department of one.
check: n/a.

text: Be honest about methodology experience (Lean, Agile, Design Thinking). A critical view is fine if backed by logical arguments.
why: The recruiter is testing workflow fit and reasoning.
check: n/a.

text: In job-search answers, explain why a project was best or worst; difficulty that forced a new approach is a good story.
why: Shows motivation and problem-solving.
check: n/a.

text: Evaluate job postings against your own tolerance: lists of every imaginable duty; weird or impossible requirements; absurd tasks; lack of company diversity; unrealistic wages; who the UX team reports to.
why: Employers often don't understand UX/UI; flags show mismatch.
check: n/a.

text: Check job boards regularly (the book suggests once or twice a week for IxDA). Boards named: Dribbble (full-time + contract; freelance listings PRO-only), Behance (international, no extra fee for freelance), IxDA (~300 ads at time of writing, mostly US), RemoteOK (remote), Ideate Labs (0-2 years' experience; small hard-to-read font), Design Jobs Board (long-standing; vivid colours), Remotive (~2000 listings; can hide US-only), AngelList (startups), Interns.Design (internships).
why: Different boards serve different regions/seniority.
check: n/a.

text: Stay visible: attend local meet-ups and conferences, write about design experiences, be active on social platforms (Twitter, LinkedIn, Instagram, Medium, Facebook, Slack, Dribbble).
why: Visibility builds personal brand and online communication skill.
check: n/a.

text: Network and keep in touch with clients, peers and coworkers; they refer and are sources for rates of comparable jobs.
why: Referrals; "best method to get good work is to produce good work and have other people tell others".
check: n/a.

text: Final checklist for a successful UI freelancer: be honest; know your UX/UI process; love helping people; deliver on promises; take pride in work; don't sell yourself short; weed out bad clients; define the scope first.
why: Book's own summary.
check: n/a.

text: Put a written proposal in place before starting work: delivery details (what, when, by whom, number of meetings), the client's role in keeping the schedule, deliverables, cost, payment dates, what is excluded/extra, a realistic schedule, and T&Cs covering permissions/releases, copyright and ownership.
why: The proposal sets expectations; T&Cs are the fallback for late payment or mid-project cancellation.
check: proposal contains each listed item.

text: Explain the project stages and ways of working in plain language; many clients have never commissioned design.
why: A client who understands the process cooperates better.
check: manual.

text: Invoice on completion of each stage, not only at the end.
why: Protects you if a client doesn't pay; aids cash flow and forecasting.
check: n/a.

text: Base bids on expected hours (from timesheets) so you have room to go back to the client when scope creeps.
why: Hours-based bids tie price to scope.
check: quote lists hour estimate per stage.

text: Compute a minimum hourly rate = annual survival budget (living costs + business overheads) / billable hours. Example: 8 h/day, 5 d/week, 4 weeks off = 1,920 h/yr; ~40% for operations (finding clients, books, planning) leaves 1,152 billable h.
why: Time is what a service business sells; undercharging loses money.
check: n/a.
source: (p.80-81) (see open question: the book's result does not match its numbers)

text: Test a rate against client reaction: if more than 1 in 4 people wince, slow down (ease off the rate); if fewer than 1 in 4 wince, raise it.
why: Wince rate is a market signal (Reichelt quote).
check: n/a.

text: When a client wants a quote on the spot, it is fine to gather needs, take notes and return the next day with a proposal.
why: Better to examine requirements before committing to a budget.
check: n/a.

text: Do not undervalue yourself because a job took less time; value = skill and impact, not minutes.
why: Quoted verbatim in spirit: "you are valuable as a person with skills and qualities" (p.45-46).
check: n/a.

text: Track hours on long engagements and keep detailed notes; they inform future estimates and mistakes.
why: Learning loop for estimation.
check: time log.

text: Make exceptions on rate only for a portfolio-growing project, a client you really want, or a cause you believe in; be wary of clients who bargain you down in exchange for promised future work.
why: Design is competitive; many clients exploit this.
check: n/a.

text: Weed out bad clients and "don't accept every project" (see also `brief-scope-and-delivery-process.md`).
why: Protects brand and sanity.
check: n/a.

text: Pick a niche when founding an agency: a specific vertical gives authority, a shorter learning curve, and a differentiator; verify enough demand exists and will grow.
why: Generalists have no value proposition beyond "we do good work" (Racki quote, p.65).
check: n/a.

text: If you offer one service, form referral arrangements with non-competing agencies offering complementary services.
why: Partners send you work they can't do.
check: n/a.

text: Choose an agency name with checks for: existing trademarks; incorporation availability in your state; domain and social handles; long-term fit (not restrictive). Law differs by country; seek a business attorney.
why: Name drives all branding; conflicts are costly.
check: domain and handle availability.

text: List what you do as a freelancer and identify what you cannot do when scaled; hire for each gap: workload -> assistant; finding customers -> salesperson/account rep; technical -> technical co-founder; managing staff -> partner/CEO; running the business -> accountant, attorney, VA.
why: Defines hiring in order of need.
check: n/a.

text: Pick partners with complementary skills or the same skills according to your gaps; split workload evenly; collaborate on design decisions even if one partner owns suppliers/dev.
why: Complementary abilities widen services; uneven load breaks partnerships.
check: n/a.

text: Choose suppliers who are specialists (not salespeople), share your vision and ethics, and nurture them as an extension of your team.
why: Output quality depends on suppliers; good ones handle problems professionally.
check: n/a.

text: Remote staff: state in advance whether in-office work will be required; use time-tracking tooling rather than frequent check-ins (book describes Hubstaff: time tracking, optional random screenshots, activity detection, payroll, invoicing, tasks with weekly sprints/checklists/daily standups; free up to 5 team members).
why: Check-ins are inefficient; surprises on office policy upset staff.
check: n/a.

text: Seek advice from an accountant/lawyer on taxes, licences, overheads, invoicing before going full-time freelance; keep company expenses deductible.
why: Legal/tax exposure.
check: n/a.

text: Present each design inside a realistic context mock-up (device frame for an app/site, table scene for a card) rather than as a bare artboard; present the final result as one complete package.
why: "Mock-ups allow clients to see your design in context and in real world", which affects their imagination and thinking.
applies: landing page | SaaS app UI | mobile (deliverable previews).
check: deliverable preview shows the design inside a device/frame or real surface; visual.

text: Prefer high-quality (premium) mock-ups over weak free ones when the impression matters; the book names ThemeForest-type marketplaces.
why: Quality of presentation lifts perceived quality of the work.
check: visual.

text: For a reading-first document (resume, CV, case-study page), do not overdesign: no bright colours, no striking shapes, no unconventional layouts; use a "sober & direct" version; let content lead.
why: Reviewers are "most likely tired and uninterested in a remarkable visual experience"; anything that diverts attention from the text is frowned on.
check: palette is neutral (text on plain background); no layout deviating from a single-column or simple two-column grid; visual.
source: (p.105-106) [numeric thresholds are engine notes; book gives none]

text: Prioritize readability and a clear visual hierarchy; no long paragraphs, no confusing layouts; the viewer must grasp immediately what they are looking at.
why: Scanning reviewers decide fast.
check: headings differ visibly in size/weight from body; paragraph length short (book gives no number).

text: Write each project entry to show how: "Instead of 'I designed the navigation system', show how you did it: how did you pull it off, what did it take, why was it important."
why: Process evidence beats task statements.
check: entry contains method + reason, not only a verb + noun.

text: Describe achievements and learnings, not tasks: what you completed, how long it took, what you learned and why it matters.
why: Recruiters want evidence, not job descriptions.
check: each project entry has an outcome statement.

text: Let writing reflect the author's voice (laid-back/funny or serious/direct) while remaining objective and concise; avoid grammar/spelling errors.
why: Personality survives even in efficient layouts.
check: spell/grammar pass.

text: Tailor emphasis to the target role/audience (e.g., data-driven research for UX, Agile for process-driven teams) but do not lie.
why: One golden opportunity justifies re-framing.
check: n/a (judgement).

text: Pair a portfolio (visual skill) with case studies (thinking). Make case studies easy to read; start with the strongest project; keep it basic and to the point.
why: Visual-only showcases (Dribbble/Behance style) omit problem-solving, empathy, business approach, data analysis.
check: first project in list is the strongest; each case study exists, not just images.

text: A case study answers five questions: what made the project difficult; how you overcame it; your logic and thought process; what you learned and how you apply it now; what effect the work had.
why: This is the structure the book gives for case-study content.
check: page contains five labelled sections or equivalents.

text: Highlight awards, certifications and work for known companies prominently on resume/portfolio.
why: They raise credibility and make you the first pick among similar candidates.
check: visual: proof element above the fold.

text: Prepare to explain your design process and the idea behind a project, and why you chose a method; also be able to explain design choices to non-designers (why a persona, why more testing, why a layout is better).
why: Interviews and clients ask for the reasoning, not only the output.
check: each major decision has a written rationale.
source: (p.14-15, 112-118) [engine note: an agent should attach a short "why" to each design decision it ships]

text: Keep written messages "short and specific"; reread before sending; use spellcheck but do not rely on it.
why: Intended meaning must survive transmission.
check: manual.

text: Keep the portfolio updated with new finished work.
why: "How quickly you get work depends on how unique and experienced your profile is"; new projects fix a thin profile (p.54-56).
check: latest entry date.

text: Never let the generating model pick between its own candidate directions. Deal them from outside: a seeded script chooses which candidate index is built, plus 2-6 challenger forms from different tiers (graphic system / instrument language / atmosphere world); store the seed and allow reproducible re-roll.
why: Measured 30/35 identical concepts across 16 prompt framings when the model chose. Same logic reduces Larpo's "5 of 7 concepts use Geist".
check: seed present in output comment + `grep` in the built HTML (Impeccable requires the seed key to survive the production build).

text: Keep a persistent ledger of structural fingerprints (macrostructure, nav archetype, footer archetype, type voice, ground band, accent hue, CTA silhouette, headline size band) and make the next build differ on >= 1 declared axis from the last three. Write the stamp into the page and into `ledger/`.
why: Hallmark does this; it is the only mechanism found that addresses cross-run sameness.
check: compare stamp to last 3 ledger entries (script).

text: Use a separate evaluator agent that renders the page (Playwright), scores Design quality, Originality, Craft, Functionality against written criteria that explicitly penalise stock components and AI-generated patterns, and is calibrated with several few-shot graded examples drawn from the ledger. Allow the generator to pivot aesthetic, not only refine. Cap iterations (5-15) and keep the best iteration, not the last.
why: Anthropic's harness; originality and design quality needed explicit weight; scores plateau; middle iteration sometimes better.
check: evaluator transcript + per-criterion scores stored with the ledger entry.

text: Before layout, produce >= 7 candidate world-references for the audience, including print/instrument/notation/identity-system artifacts from before the web; delete the category default and its predictable opposite; let the dice pick.
why: Forces source material that is not the web median; Arc/Irwin precedent.
check: artifact list present with one line each; no more than 3 of 7 share one material.

text: Write the direction contract (<= 150 words) as an HTML comment at the top of `<body>` in the emitted markup: THESIS (one idea + the category default refused), OWN-WORLD, FIRST VIEWPORT, signature interaction, seed. Grep the built output to prove it survived the build.
why: Makes the commitment auditable and lets a reviewer diff promise vs behaviour.
check: `grep` built HTML for seed key.

text: When generating options, ask for 5-8 with self-estimated "typicality" and require the build candidate to be low-typicality but high audience-fit (Verbalized-Sampling style).
why: Targets the preference-data typicality bias.
check: record the list in the ledger; run E-2.

text: Pre-build plan = 4-6 named colours, type roles, one-sentence layout concept + ASCII wireframe, "what makes it unique"; a review step compares it with the default look for that category and logs what changed.
why: Catches convergence before code exists, when changing is free.
check: plan file exists; diff vs the fingerprint ledger.

text: Write criteria wording deliberately and test it: adjectives such as "museum quality" or "premium" steer toward one look.
why: Observed convergence side effect in Anthropic's harness.
check: A/B the criteria on 3 briefs and compare fingerprints.

text: Use image-first exploration only when the comp is treated as a spatial contract and the code is verified against it; otherwise the code drifts back to template.
why: Taste-skill `image-to-code` (one image per section, extract layout/type/spacing/colour values, build, compare in a real browser) and Impeccable "comp is king" both flag that "generic coded reinterpretation after the image step" is the failure mode. Impeccable requires a pixel-overlap reproduction check of the first viewport (saved as `.impeccable/review/hero-repro.png`) before building further.
check: screenshot-diff vs comp at the comp's dimensions.

text: Bounded verification: build fully, inspect once in a batched round (desktop + mobile), fix everything in one batch, confirm with at most one more round, then stop; hand the remaining finds to a fresh-context reviewer.
why: Open-ended self-QA "burns the user's money doing worse what the finish handoffs do better"; a fresh reviewer finds more than the builder.
check: round counter in the run log.

text: Capture validity before critique: settle or disable entrance animation first, capture full-page from the document top, open every file and confirm it shows what its name says. An invalid capture invalidates the review.
why: An element hidden by animation timing reads as missing and gets "fixed" into a regression.
check: screenshot sanity (no blank/black regions; non-zero variance).

text: Do not use a font or palette because an "anti-slop" list recommended it. For every typeface and every ground/accent pair, check it against the current overused sets (Section 3) and against the last N builds; a recommendation list is a prior, not a decision.
why: The anti-slop skill ecosystem seeds Geist, "cobalt and cream", "terracotta and slate" into thousands of agents (Core idea 4).
check: D-FONT-1, D-COLOR-3, B-AXIS-*.

text: Ban lists must always be paired with a positive, specific, non-listed destination derived from the brief's own world; never "avoid X" alone.
why: Negative-only instruction relocates the mode (Space Grotesk after Inter; terracotta after purple; Anthropic cookbook line quoted above). Impeccable's self-check: "if someone could guess your aesthetic from the category alone, or from category-plus-avoidance, rework until neither answer is obvious" [verified-local, reference/new-work.md].
check: visual + guess-the-aesthetic blind test (process note P-7).

text: Treat the cream ground, italic/high-contrast serif display, and terracotta/coral accent as ONE combined tell, and near-black + single neon accent as a second. Allowed only if the brief pins it; otherwise the free axis must not be spent on them.
why: Named by Anthropic's own skill, Impeccable ("cream-palette" rule + "calibration" paragraph), and press coverage of "Claudian sameness".
check: D-COLOR-3 (cream bg test), D-FONT-3 (italic serif H1).

text: Keep display tracking at or above -0.04em (prefer -0.02 to -0.03em) and display size at or below 96px (6rem); a full-sentence H1 at >=72px that covers >=28% of viewport height or >=25% of viewport area is flagged.
why: Impeccable craft-floor: "display max 6rem, tracking floor -0.04em"; its detector fires `extreme-negative-tracking` at <= -0.05em and `oversized-h1` at >=72px with >=40 characters and viewport dominance. Larpo's observed -0.052 to -0.064em at 62-83px sits on the wrong side of both.
check: D-TYPE-1, D-TYPE-2.

text: No tracked all-caps eyebrow/kicker, no "WORD - fragment" labels, no middle-dot meta strings, no arrows appended to links and buttons, no monospace small labels as decoration, unless they encode real information.
why: Anthropic SKILL.md lists these as "template chrome". Impeccable `kicker-above-heading` is an outright ban ("no brief earns it back"). The reflexive arrow on the CTA is on Anthropic's list and was one of the rejected-yet-recurring Larpo items.
check: D-LAYOUT-5, D-CTA-1.

text: Do not accent a single word in the headline by switching font, italicising, or recolouring it.
why: Anthropic SKILL.md names it a tell; slop-cop `hero_font_mix` fires when the biggest heading near the top mixes two families, roman+italic, or two text colours (min 32px, <=140 chars).
check: D-TYPE-3.

text: Count tells per page and per batch; use pattern-count tiers (0-1 / 2-3 / 4+) as a triage signal, not a score to maximise.
why: In 1,590 Show HN pages 22% hit 4+ patterns; tiers are what the only open measurement used. False-positive rate 5-10%, so a single hit proves nothing.
check: run detector (Section 3 of detector note).

text: A page where **three or more sections end on a short rebuttal or manufactured contrast** ("X. No Y.", "Not a feature. A platform.", "Stop guessing. Start winning.") fails the copy check; one is fine.
why: Impeccable `aphoristic-cadence`; ban lists across several secondary sources flag "It's not X, it's Y", "No fluff. No filler. Just results.", manufactured-suspense hooks ("The secret?", "Here's the thing"), and openers ("In today's fast-paced...").
check: D-COPY-1..4.
source: Impeccable registry [verified-local]; Gartner community and other lists [secondary, anecdotal].

text: Numbers must be sourced or labelled sample. "Fake-perfect" stats (`99.99%`, `4.1x`, `10K+ users` rows) are tells.
why: taste-skill bans fake-precise numbers; slop-cop `stat_banner_row` (3-6 sibling cards, number font >=22px, text <=10 chars, row >=300px wide); Anthropic SKILL.md: don't default to big number + small label + supporting stats + gradient accent.
check: D-LAYOUT-6.

text: Do not add a FAQ accordion, numbered 1-2-3 steps, or a logo/stat strip by template habit; add only if the visitor's actual objection requires it.
why: Both are slop-cop patterns (`faq_accordion`: >=3 `<details>` or "FAQ"-headed uniform question items in the lower half; `numbered_steps`: >=3 ascending numeric markers). Larpo's playbook covers the template waterfall in prose; these are the measured forms.
check: D-LAYOUT-7, D-LAYOUT-8.

text: Style the browser-owned surfaces: text selection, caret, scrollbars, focus ring, underline offset, tabular numerals.
why: Impeccable craft-floor: the cheapest signal that a page was built rather than assembled, "the one models skip most reliably". Not on any other list.
check: D-CRAFT-1 (`::selection`, `caret-color`, `scrollbar-color/width`, `text-underline-offset`, `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` present in computed/stylesheet rules).

text: Pick light vs dark from a physical use scene (who, where, ambient light), not from category.
why: Impeccable: "Dark or light is never a default." Perma-dark + grey body is a slop-cop pattern.
check: visual; D-COLOR-4 for the grey-on-dark half.

text: Build the app shell as sidebar 238 px (237 + 1 px right hairline #eeeff1) on #fbfbfb, main canvas #fff, and stack the main area as 48 px bands each closed by a 1 px #eeeff1 hairline (title bar, view bar, sort/filter bar 46 px), with the table directly under them.
why: Equal bands separated by hairlines give a calm, scannable chrome; the sidebar tint is the only surface change.
check: sidebar width 236-240; hairline y positions at 48/96/142 (+/-1) in a 563 px tall view; sidebar bg within 2 levels of #fbfbfb.

text: Make sidebar nav rows 32 px pitch with a 14 px icon at x 15, the label at x 35 (gap 6, row padding 8), 14/20 weight 500 tracking -0.28 px in #242629.
why: One pitch and one icon column make 15 nav items read as a single list.
check: consecutive nav label tops differ by 32.0 px; icon left edge 15 +/- 1; label left 35 +/- 1.
source: img/data-sales-screen ink bands 106, 138, 170, 202, 234, 266 [R]; hero window rows 24.6 = 28 x 0.88 with padding 0 8 gap 6 [M]

text: Mark the active sidebar row with a #f4f5f6 fill, radius 9, inset 6-8 px from both sidebar edges, and nothing else (no accent bar, no bold, no icon tint).
why: Selection is a state; a neutral fill keeps colour reserved for data.
check: active row bg rgb(244,245,246) or rgb(238,239,241); no border/outline; font-weight unchanged.
source: img/data-sales-screen (Deals row) [R]; hero window Home row bg rgb(238,239,241) r9 [M]

text: Group sidebar sections under 12/16 weight 500 labels in #75777c with a 12 px chevron at x 19 (collapsible), sentence case, never uppercase, with 8 px extra space above each group.
why: Sentence-case grey labels with a disclosure chevron are quieter than uppercase eyebrow labels and show the groups can fold.
check: section label fontSize 12, weight 500, text-transform none, colour rgb(117,119,124) or 55% black; chevron present.

text: Give each record type in the sidebar a 14 px solid colour tile, radius 4, with a white filled 10 px glyph (People and Companies #266df0, Deals #fd9038, Partnerships #0eb472, Invoices #dba600); use outline 14 px icons for app sections (Notifications, Tasks, Notes, Emails, Reports, Automations).
why: Filled tiles mark "data you own" and become the object's identity across views, chips and filters; outline icons mark tools.
check: record-type icons 14x14 radius 3.5-5 with solid bg and white glyph; tool icons are stroke icons with no fill.
source: img/data-sales-screen colour probe [R]; hero window object tiles 14 r4.8 with 5% border [M]

text: Put the workspace switcher in a 48 px header: 24 px logo tile radius 7, 8 px gap, name 16/600 tracking -0.3 px, a 16 px chevron, and a sidebar-collapse icon (18-20 px, #75777c) right-aligned at 15 px from the edge.
why: The switcher is the only 16/600 element in the sidebar, which anchors the column without a big logo.
check: header height 48 +/- 1, logo 24 px, name 16/600.

text: Put "Quick actions ⌘K" and a search icon button with a "/" keycap as two 28 px white buttons (radius 9, gap 8) directly under the workspace header; widths about 161 and 50.
why: Keyboard entry points are the first thing in the sidebar; keycaps teach the shortcut without a tooltip.
check: two buttons, height 28, radius 8-9, each with a kbd chip 18 high radius 6 and 11 px grey text.
source: img/data-sales-screen [R]; hero window Quick Actions 167x24.6 r8, kbd 24x17.6 r6 border 5% [M]

text: Show presence in the title bar as 24 px avatar rings overlapping by 8 px (1 px ring in a distinct colour per person, 1 px white gap, 20 px photo or initial) followed by a 22 px "+1" circle in #f8f9fa with a #e6e7ea border.
why: Coloured rings make a collaborative product visible at 24 px without a "Share" call-out.
check: avatar 24 px, negative margin -8, ring colour differs per avatar, overflow chip 22 px 10 px text.

text: Set table rows to 36 px pitch with a 1 px #e6e7ea bottom and right grid line on every cell, the header row 35 px plus its hairline, and cell padding 0 8 px; omit the last column's right line.
why: A full grid in a very light grey reads as a spreadsheet you can edit, which is the product promise; 36 px holds a 22 px chip with 7 px air.
check: row text bands repeat every 36.0 px; grid colour rgb(230,231,234); cell padding-left 8.

text: Write column headers as 14/500 ink (not grey, not uppercase) with a 14 px attribute-type icon 6 px before the label; the first column carries the select-all checkbox and a 12 px "+" (add column) right-aligned.
why: The icon tells the data type (tag, currency, person, select) so the header can stay the same size and colour as the cells.
check: th fontSize 14, weight 500, colour equals cell ink, text-transform none, one icon per header.
source: img/data-sales-screen ("Deal +", "Type", "Potential value (USD)", "Point of contact", "Source") [R]; measure-home-table headers 14/500 rgb(36,38,41) with 13 px icons [M]

text: Make the primary column a 16 px checkbox (radius 5, 1 px #ccc border in rows, #e6e7ea in the header), 10 px gap, a 16 px company logo, then the record name with a 1 px #e7e7e7 underline offset 2-3 px under the baseline.
why: The light underline says "this opens a record" without link-blue; logos make each row a real company at a glance.
check: first-column cell contains checkbox 16 px, img 14-16 px, underlined name; underline colour lightness >= 90%.

text: Right-align currency and numbers in ink 14/500 with 9-10 px right padding, keep the unit in the header ("Potential value (USD)"), and let magnitudes vary naturally ($3,200 to $100,200).
why: Right alignment lets the eye compare magnitudes; putting the unit in the header removes repeated noise from 10 cells.
check: numeric cells justify-content flex-end; currency code appears once in the header.

text: End the table with a 26 px aggregate row: "2,813 count", "$83,560,165 sum" (value in #111, label in #75777c, 8 px gap, right-aligned) and "+ Add calculation" in #75777c in every other column.
why: Aggregates prove the table is a live database, and the grey "+ Add calculation" shows the capability without a button.
check: footer row present; value darker than its label; empty columns show an add affordance.

text: Fill a demo table with 10+ rows of real-looking records (recognisable company logos, photographed contacts, varied amounts, mixed statuses) and label it as sample data in the surrounding page.
why: Believability comes from variety and real faces/logos at 12-16 px; uniform rows or grey bars read as a wireframe.
check: >= 8 rows; >= 4 distinct chip values per select column; avatars are photos or initials with colour, not grey blobs.

text: Render select and status values as chips 22 px high, radius 7, padding 0 5 px, 1 px border one step darker than the fill, text 14/500 in the deepest shade of the same hue (blue #e5eeff/#d6e5ff/#183c81, green #ddf9e4/#c7f4d3/#075a39, purple #f5eeff/#e8ddfe/#4711bb, cyan #daf4fc/#c3edf9/#0a5a70, yellow #fff3cc/#ffebad/#705500, pink #feecf1/#fddde7/#6f065d, grey #f4f5f6/#eeeff1/#5c5e63).
why: The darker border crisps the chip edge on white at 1x; the deep same-hue text passes contrast without turning the chip into a badge.
check: chip height 22, radius 6-8, border colour differs from fill by 1 step of the same hue, text contrast >= 4.5:1 on the fill.

text: Use the same chip height and text size as the cell text (22 px chip in a 36 px row, 14 px text); never shrink chip text to 11-12 px inside a table.
why: Same-size chips keep one baseline across the row; smaller chip text is what makes generated tables look fiddly.
check: chip fontSize equals neighbouring cell fontSize.
source: img/data-sales-screen; measure-home-table score chip 22 px 14/500 green rgb(0,125,83) on rgb(224,252,237) border rgb(203,247,225) r7 [R][M]

text: Render a person/relationship value as a pill: 22 px high, radius 11, #fbfbfb fill, 1 px #e6e7ea border, 12 px round photo at 5 px left padding, 6 px gap, name in #75777c.
why: A pill (not a chip) says "this is a linked record"; grey text keeps a column of names quieter than the status chips beside it.
check: relationship cell uses full-round radius, avatar 12 px, text colour lighter than ink.

text: Give each attribute type one rendering and reuse it in table, kanban card, record page and filter builder: name = logo + underlined text, select = chip, person = avatar + name, currency = "USD" grey + amount ink, date = ink text, email = blue chip, stage = 8-12 px dot + label.
why: Consistent type rendering is what lets a dense CRM feel learnable; the eye learns the vocabulary once.
check: the same attribute renders with the same component in every view.
source: img/data-sales-screen, slices/home-05 (kanban "USD $20,800"), crop-home-record (email chip), img/help-lists (stage dots) [R][M][V]

text: Show an AI-filled or computed attribute with a small sparkle icon in its column header (Industry ✦, Research agent ✦) and keep the cell itself styled like any other value.
why: The provenance is in the schema, not in every cell; the data stays calm.
check: AI columns marked once at the header; cells unchanged.
source: img/help-lists, measure-home-table ("ICP Score" and "Research agent" headers with 13 px sparkle at 40% black) [V][M]

text: Build toolbar buttons 28 px high, radius 9, white, with the soft-halo shadow `0 0 2px rgba(28,40,64,0.18), 0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,0.04)` and no border; 14 px icon, 6 px gap, 14/500 ink label, 6-7 px left and 9-10 px right padding.
why: The 2 px blurred halo gives a crisp-but-soft edge that a 1 px ring cannot; asymmetric padding optically centres icon + text.
check: button height 28, radius 8-9, box-shadow contains a 0 0 2px layer at alpha 0.15-0.2 and no 0 0 0 1px ring.
source: measure-home-hero-window and measure-home-workflow (same shadow token on buttons and nodes) [M]; edge ramp at 4x [R]

text: Make the primary in-app button #266df0 with a 1 px rgba(0,0,0,0.1) border, white 14/500 text, 28 px high radius 8, and a blue-tinted shadow `0 2px 4px -2px rgba(15,107,233,0.12), 0 3px 6px -2px rgba(15,107,233,0.08)`; one per view.
why: A tinted shadow keeps the blue from looking pasted on white; one primary per view keeps it meaningful.
check: at most one bg #266df0 button per view; its shadow colour is blue-tinted.
source: measure-home-table ("New person") [M]; img/help-lists ("Add Company"), img/sequences-preview ("Enroll recipients") [V]

text: Show the active view as a white 28 px dropdown button whose leading 14 px tile encodes the view type (green 2x2 grid = table, orange columns = kanban), followed by the view name and a chevron; put "View settings" next to it or at the right with "Import / Export".
why: The tile tells the layout before you read the name, and the switcher lives where the data is, not in a tab bar.
check: view switcher has a coloured type tile + name + chevron.
source: img/data-sales-screen ("All deals"), img/help-create-new-view ("Candidate Pipeline" orange, "All Applications" green), measure-home-table ("All Companies" 12 px green icon) [R][V][M]

text: Make the view-switcher dropdown a white r12 popover with a "Search views..." input row, views listed with type tile + name + ⋮ (active view in blue text, not filled), a hairline, and a "+ Create new view" footer row on a grey fill.
why: Search first scales to dozens of views; marking the active view by text colour avoids a second selection style.
check: popover radius 12, first row is a search input, active item uses accent text colour only.
section: 2.4 Controls, view switcher, sort and filter

text: When no sort or filter is set, show "Sort" and "Filter" as dashed ghost chips: 28-29 px, radius 9, 1 px dashed #e3e3e6 border, #fbfbfb fill, 14 px icon + 14/500 #75777c label, separated by a 1 px x 20 px #eeeff1 divider.
why: Dashed outlines read as "empty slot you can fill", which invites use without adding visual weight.
check: empty sort/filter controls use border-style dashed and grey text.
section: 2.4 Controls, view switcher, sort and filter

text: Build the filter editor as rows of 32 px segment pills (Where | attribute ▾ | operator ▾ | value ▾ | ⋮), nested groups inside a #f8f9fa inset panel radius 12, a toggleable "And ⟲" connector pill, and text actions "+ Add filter", "Delete group", "Clear all filters"; show an applied advanced filter as a chip with a count ("Advanced filter 3") plus an attached ⋮ segment.
why: Each clause reads as a sentence; nesting by inset panel is clearer than indentation; counts make hidden filters visible.
check: filter rows are sentence-ordered segment controls; groups have an inset bg; applied filters show a count.
section: 2.4 Controls, view switcher, sort and filter

text: Render keyboard hints as keycaps 18 px high, radius 6, 1 px #e4e4e8 border, 11/16 #75777c, 3.5-4 px side padding, inside the control they trigger (⌘K, /, T, N, ↵).
why: In-place keycaps teach shortcuts continuously; they also signal "keyboard-first" at a glance.
check: kbd height 17-20, radius 5-6, fontSize 11.
source: img/data-sales-screen, measure-home-hero-window (kbd 24x17.6 r6, 11 px, 40% black), img/cl-cmdpalette [R][M][V]

text: Build kanban columns 272 px wide with white-80% fill, radius 12 12 0 0, padding 8, a header of 12 px colour dot + 14/600 title + count chip (16 px, radius 5, 4% black fill, 6% border, 11/500) + "+" icon button, and cards 248 px wide with 8 px gaps.
why: The stage colour lives only in the dot; the column itself stays neutral so the cards carry the data.
check: column header dot 8-12 px; count chip 16 px; column bg neutral.

text: Make a kanban card a white r12 box with a 1 px rgba(0,0,0,0.06) border and no shadow at rest; inside, attribute rows at 32 px pitch (14 px grey icon + 14/500 value), then a footer of three 28 px ghost icon buttons (notes, tasks, comments) and a right-aligned age chip ("12d", 12/500 50% black with a clock).
why: Cards are mini record pages: the same attribute rows, a fixed footer for actions, and an age that shows staleness without a colour alarm.
check: card radius 12, border alpha 0.05-0.07, row pitch 32, footer icon buttons 28 px.
source: measure-home-kanban (rows at y 137/169/201/233/265; buttons 28 r8; "12d" 12/500 rgba(0,0,0,0.5)) [M]

text: Show a dragged kanban card rotated 2-4 degrees, lifted with a larger soft shadow and slightly scaled, while its slot stays open in the source column; on drop update both column counts.
why: Rotation plus shadow reads as "picked up" physically; updating counts closes the loop.
check: visual: drag state has rotation and an elevated shadow; counts change on drop.
source: motion/kanban-contact.png (live homepage, 1.6-3.2 s), img/cl-kanban-video-poster (blue 2 px outline + tint when dragged in the 2022 version) [V]

text: On multi-select, float a bulk-action bar at the bottom centre: count chip ("2 selected"), white 32 px action buttons (Add to collection, Send email, More ▾) and a close ×, on a white r12 surface with a soft shadow.
why: Bulk actions appear only when relevant and stay out of the toolbar the rest of the time.
check: bulk bar is hidden with 0 selected and appears bottom-centre with a count.

text: Lay out a record page as a left column (~340 px) with logo/avatar 40 px, name 20/600, an action row (one labelled button such as "Compose email" or "Add to list" + 28 px ringed icon buttons + ⋮), a collapsible "Details" list of attribute rows (14 px icon + 12-14 px grey label in a fixed ~140 px column + 14/500 value), and a right area with tabs (Overview, Activity, Emails 12, Notes 4, Tasks 6, Files, Calls 6, Deals 4).
why: Attributes left and activity right matches how people scan a record: who is this, then what happened.
check: label column fixed width, labels grey and truncated with ellipsis ("Last intera..."), tab labels carry count chips.

text: Put count chips on tabs and section headers as 16-18 px grey chips (4% fill, 6% border, 11-12 px) right after the label, never as coloured badges.
why: Counts inform without competing; coloured badges are reserved for unread or overdue.
check: count chips neutral unless signalling urgency.

text: Write activity rows as "Avatar Name verb object" with the name in ink, the verb in grey and the object underlined ("Michael Chang attended an in-person meeting"), the relative time right-aligned in grey 12-14 px, and a 20 px ringed type icon on a vertical connector line.
why: Sentence-shaped events scan faster than columns; colour separates actor, action and object without bold.
check: event rows mix ink and grey in one line; time right-aligned; timeline connector present.

text: Group the activity timeline under time headings ("Upcoming" in amber, "This week", "Today"/"In 2 days" right-aligned in amber for future items) and render meetings as r12 cards with a 3 px green left bar, title, time, participant avatars and a blue "Join meeting" button.
why: Amber marks the future, green bars mark meetings; everything else stays neutral.
check: future items use one warm accent; meeting cards have a coloured leading bar.

text: Show highlights on a record as a grid of r12 cards (1 px #eeeff1 border, padding 12-16) each with a 12/500 grey label + 14 px icon top-right and a 14-16 px value (Summary with sparkle, Upcoming with a date tile "THU 29", Company with logo, Sales Outreach with a segmented 4 px progress bar).
why: Each card answers one question; the label/icon/value grammar is identical so the grid reads as one instrument.
check: highlight cards share label style, radius 12 and border; values are real data.
source: crop-home-record (cards r12, border rgb(238,239,241), segments 4 px pills) [M]

text: Put each chart in a white r12 card with a 14/500 title, an info icon, an object chip (People/Companies tile + name), a ⋮ menu top-right, and the card shadow `0 0 1px 1px rgba(0,22,62,0.01), 0 4px 12px -1px rgba(0,22,62,0.04), 0 1px 3px -1px rgba(0,22,62,0.18)`.
why: Naming the data source on the card makes every chart traceable to records, which is the CRM's credibility.
check: chart card has title + source chip + menu; radius 12.

text: Use saturated categorical colours in charts (blue #266df0, amber #f5a300, red #ff5454, green, purple, cyan) with 1-2 px white gaps between stacked segments, dashed 1 px grid lines, 10-12 px grey axis labels and a 12 px "Count" axis title rotated; legends as 8-10 px dots + 12-14 px labels centred above the plot.
why: Charts are the one place colour is allowed to be loud; white gaps and dashed grids keep loud colour from looking heavy.
check: chart series colours are saturated hues; grid dashed; segment separators white.

text: Offer a time-range segmented control (7D 30D 3M 6M 12M All) as a grey track with a white selected segment, and a "Refresh data" secondary + "Add report" primary at the top right of a dashboard.
why: Range is the most-used dashboard control; a segmented track makes the current range obvious.
check: range control is a segmented track with one white thumb.

text: Under a report, show "Calculated values" as a collapsible grey-header table (dot + category, count) with a download-as-CSV icon button and a tooltip; offer report types as a list of r12 option cards (32 px icon tile + 14/500 title + grey description).
why: The numbers behind the chart are one click away, which builds trust; option cards explain choices in one line each.
check: chart has an adjacent data table; type picker items have title + description.

text: Design empty states as a quiet line illustration (isometric, grey strokes with one accent-blue element) above a 14/500 ink title and a 14 px grey instruction ("Input needed to display chart / Select a data source").
why: The empty state tells the next action in five words; one blue element ties the drawing to the UI accent.
check: empty state has title + instruction; illustration grey with <= 1 accent colour.

text: Build the command palette as a two-pane r12-16 dialog: a 48 px search input ("Search quick actions and records..."), a left list grouped by 12/500 uppercase grey labels (NOW, COMPANIES, QUICK ACTIONS) with 24 px ringed icon tiles and right-aligned keycaps, the selected row a #f4f5f6 r8 fill, a right pane previewing the highlighted record, and a footer with "↑ ↓ Navigate" keycaps plus a secondary and a primary(↵) button.
why: The preview pane turns search into action without leaving the keyboard; group labels make a long list scannable.
check: palette has search, grouped list, preview pane, footer with keycaps.

text: Use the same dialog footer everywhere: "↑ ↓ Navigate" at left, then a white secondary ("Create note", "Start from scratch") and a blue primary with an inline ↵ keycap ("Open Meeting ↵", "Preview template ↵") at right.
why: One footer grammar across overlays makes every dialog operable the same way.
check: dialog footers share layout and include a keycap on the primary.

text: Slide side panels (compose email, record preview) in from the right over the table, r12, white, with the soft card shadow and their own header ("Send email" 12/500 grey label + 16-18/500 title + grey summary), leaving the table visible and dimmed by nothing.
why: The panel keeps the list in context; no scrim means the user never loses their place.
check: side panel overlaps content without a backdrop; radius 12.

text: Show AI work as product objects: a collapsible "2 tools used ▾" line, a shimmering "Thinking" label while streaming, answers as numbered records with inline record chips (logo + name in a bordered row), and thumbs/copy/regenerate icon buttons; never a coloured chat bubble.
why: The AI proves it read the CRM by returning records you can open; a grey streaming state reads as work, not decoration.
check: AI output contains linked record chips; tool use is disclosed.
source: crop-home-charts ("2 tools used", "Brightloop" chip), slices/home-07/09, fold-home ("Thinking" gradient text) [M][V]

text: Draw workflow canvases on a dotted #f4f5f6 field with white r15 nodes (216x74, 26 px tinted icon tile r7, 15/500 title, 12/500 grey subtitle), 1 px grey connectors with rounded corners and small arrowheads, output ports as 6 px dots, branch labels (True/False) at the node edge, and a blue "Trigger" tab plus green "✓ Triggered/Completed" status chips above nodes.
why: Nodes reuse the card and chip vocabulary, so the builder feels like the same product; status chips show the run, not just the graph.
check: nodes radius 14-16; connectors 1 px with radius corners; run status uses the green chip recipe.
source: measure-home-workflow (nodes 216x74 r15, icon tile 26 r7, title 15/500, sub 12/500 55%, chip #e0fced/#cbf7e1/#007d53), crop-home-workflow [M][V]

text: Set product UI in Inter with exactly two weights: 500 for everything (labels, values, buttons, nav, headers) and 600 only for page title, workspace name, record name and kanban column titles.
why: With size fixed at 14, a single 600 step is enough hierarchy; 400 body text looks thin next to 500 controls at this density.
check: distinct font-weights in the app = {500, 600}; 600 count <= 6 per screen.

text: Use 14/20 for all content and controls, 12/16 for labels and meta, 11/16 for keycaps and counts, 10 for avatar initials and chart axes, 16/20 (600) for page and workspace titles, and 20/24 (600) for a record title; no other sizes.
why: Six sizes with 14 carrying 60-90% of text is what keeps a dense screen calm.
check: font-size set within {10, 11, 12, 14, 16, 20}; share of 14 px >= 60% of text nodes.

text: Track 14 px UI text at -0.28 px (-2%) in the app shell and sidebar and -0.14 px (-1%) in marketing-scaled tables; track 12 px at -0.16 px or 0 and 16 px titles at -0.2 to -0.3 px.
why: Inter at 14/500 is wide; -2% tightens it to the Attio texture; the recreation's text widths only matched after switching 14 px to -0.28.
check: letter-spacing on 14 px text between -0.3 and -0.13 px.
source: measure-home-hero-window (-0.28 on sidebar), measure-home-table (-0.14), round-1 -> round-2 text-band match [M][X]

text: Colour text with a four-step neutral ramp: ink #242629 (rgb 36,38,41), secondary #505155, muted #75777c, faint #9fa1a7 (or 55% / 40% black on white); use #111 only for aggregate figures.
why: A fixed ramp holds hierarchy at one size; four steps cover value, label, meta and disabled.
check: text colours outside chips <= 5 neutrals.

text: Use two hairline greys: #eeeff1 for chrome separators and card borders, #e6e7ea for the table grid and relationship pills; never a darker border on a resting surface.
why: Two close greys separate "frame" from "data grid" without any line being noticed on its own.
check: border colours on resting elements in {#eeeff1, #e6e7ea, rgba(0,0,0,0.05-0.06)}.

text: Keep one accent (#266df0) for primary buttons, links, selected-in-list text, checkboxes and toggles; give every other hue a job in data (chips, tiles, chart series, avatar rings).
why: One blue for "act here" plus many hues for "this is data" is the opposite of a brand-colour-everywhere dashboard.
check: accent used only on interactive elements; chrome contains no other saturated colour.
source: measure-home-table (#266df0 on button, checkbox, ring), img/help-lists, img/cl-timeline toggles [M][V]

text: Use three depth levels only: resting card = 1 px hairline, no shadow (kanban, highlight cards); floating control = soft halo `0 0 2px rgba(28,40,64,0.18), 0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,0.04)`; popover/panel = halo + `0 4px 12px -1px` at 4% navy.
why: Depth tells what you can grab; flat cards keep the board calm, haloed controls look pressable.
check: distinct box-shadow tokens <= 3 per screen; kanban cards have no shadow.

text: Size icons at 14 px with a 1.25 px stroke in rows, headers and buttons (12 px for chevrons, 16-20 px only for the sidebar toggle and header icon buttons), coloured ink in headers and nav and 40-55% black for trailing affordances.
why: 14/1.25 matches the stem weight of Inter 14/500; heavier strokes look clip-art at this density.
check: icons in rows 13-14 px; stroke-width 1.2-1.4 effective.
source: measure-home-table (13 px svgs), measure-home-kanban (40 x 14 px svgs), round-2 stroke fix [M][X]

text: Animate state with short, plain transitions: colour and background 0.3 s cubic-bezier(0.4,0,0.2,1), opacity 0.2 s, transform 0.3 s; reserve choreography for demos (card drag, panel slide, streaming text, edges lighting in sequence).
why: The product feels fast because hovers and toggles barely move; motion is spent where it explains a workflow.
check: transition durations <= 0.3 s on controls; no entrance animation on static chrome.

text: In marketing demos, animate the product doing one job per block: rows appear then a side panel slides in with a drafted email (table), a card lifts, tilts and lands in the next stage (kanban), the AI streams "Thinking" then an answer with record chips (AI), connectors light up node by node with status chips (workflow).
why: Each loop proves a verb (send, move, ask, automate); generic fade-ins prove nothing.
check: each animated product block demonstrates one user action end to end.

text: Before rebuilding a reference, measure it at its native scale: scan for hairlines (exact y/x of every separator), ink bands (text cap/baseline per row) and colours at chip centres and edges; build only from those numbers.
why: Round 1 built from eyeballed values was 5.18% pixels off; after building from probes the same layout reached 2.0% in one round.
check: a measurements table exists before code; recreation diff < 2.5% pixels off by round 2.

text: Render a static build for overlay through an HTTP server (or an in-process one), never file:// with type="module" scripts.
why: Round 1's first render was a blank white page: module scripts are blocked on file://, and a blank render silently invalidates the comparison.
check: render is non-blank (pixel variance > 0) before computing diffs.

text: Track Inter 14/500 at -0.28 px for Attio-grade app text; the engine's default -0.14 px made every label 1-2 px wider and pushed chips, keycaps and right-aligned values out of alignment.
why: Width error accumulates along a row; at 14 px, 1% tracking moves "Quick actions" by 1.7 px.
check: ink-band left/right edges of labels within 0.5 px of the reference.

text: Replace the engine's 1 px ring + drop shadow on white controls with Attio's 2 px blur halo; check the edge at 4x: the reference ramps over 2 px (251 -> 239), a ring jumps in one pixel (250 -> 235).
why: The hard ring was the single most "generated-looking" detail in round 1; the halo is softer and still crisper than no edge.

text: Use a 1.25 px stroke at 14 px for line icons and pick glyphs per meaning (equalizer-with-knobs for Filter, arrows for Sort, tag for select, circled $ for currency, person for relationship); the engine's default 1.5-2 px stroke and generic sliders read heavier than the type.
why: In round 1 every icon was the darkest thing in its row; at 1.25 px icon and text share one stem weight.
check: icon stroke visually equals the 14/500 text stem; no icon darker than its label.

text: Size small chips by measured padding, not by feel: Attio chips are 5 px side padding (engine used 6) and relationship pills 5/6 px (engine used 5/8); recheck right edges with an ink-band scan.
why: A 1 px per-side error is invisible alone but shifts 20 chips in a column into a visibly different rhythm.
check: chip right ink edge within 0.5 px of the reference.

text: Sample every categorical colour from the reference instead of reusing a palette (Companies is the same #266df0 as People, Deals #fd9038, Partnerships #0eb472, Invoices #dba600), and use filled glyphs in object tiles.
why: Round 2's guessed tile colours and outline glyphs were the largest remaining sidebar error; filled white glyphs on solid tiles are Attio's object identity.
check: tile colours match sampled hex within deltaE 2.
source: round-3 sidebar pair crop, colour probes [R][X]

text: Stop iterating when the remaining diff is font rasterisation and proprietary glyphs (here 1.78% pixels off, mean abs 2.19/255, every edge within 0.5 px); record the residue instead of hand-drawing icons to close it.
why: Attio ships its own icon set; the founder rule bans hand-drawn SVG icons, so the nearest professional glyph is the correct stopping point.
check: residual diff map shows only glyph interiors and text AA, no edge offsets.
source: round-6.png difference panel; founder-taste icon rule [X]

check: `contrast(accent-text, page|card|accent-soft) >= 4.5 and |Lc| >= 60`.

text: Gate text on WCAG 2.2 AND APCA: body/secondary text >= 4.5:1 (7:1 for ink-2 targets) **and** |Lc| >= 60 (75 for the primary reading colour). Large text (>= 18pt = 24px, or >= 14pt bold = ~18.7px) may use 3:1 under WCAG.
why: WCAG's formula treats light-on-dark mid-greys too generously; APCA models polarity (Lc 32 for the 4.5:1 grey on `#0f0f0f`) [computed]. Myndex thresholds: Lc 15 invisibility point for some viewers, 30 minimum for any spot/non-text use, 45 large fluent text or sub-fluent minimum, 60 medium text >24px, 75 minimum body text, 90 preferred body [verified]. Rounding is not allowed in WCAG: 4.499:1 fails [verified].
check: per pair: `wcag >= T && |apca| >= A`.
