text: Size form controls at 44px tall with 16px text below 640px and 36px with 14px text from 640px, keeping line-height at 24px in both.
why: 44px meets touch targets and 16px stops iOS focus zoom; dense desktop rows stay scannable; a fixed 24px line keeps vertical rhythm.
check: computed height of `button, input, select` at 375px = 44 and at 1280px = 36 (+-1).

text: Draw control and card borders as the foreground colour at 10% alpha (hover 20%), and in dark mode white at 10% (hover 20%), never as a fixed grey.
why: Alpha borders keep the same perceived contrast on white, tinted and dark surfaces, so one rule covers every container.
check: computed border-color of inputs/cards has alpha < 1.

text: Give every nested rounded layer a radius of outer radius minus the inset (Catalyst: `calc(var(--radius-lg) - 1px)` for 1px insets).
why: Concentric corners look machined; equal radii on nested shapes look pinched at the corners.
check: for element with border-radius R and child inset d, child radius = R - d.

text: Show the focus indicator only for keyboard focus: a 2px outline at 2px offset in one accent (Catalyst blue-500) on every interactive control.
why: One consistent ring is learnable; hiding it for pointer clicks removes the main reason teams delete focus styles.
check: keyboard-tab each control: outline-width 2px, outline-offset 2px, same colour across controls.

text: Pair coloured fills with a dark shade of the same hue for text when the fill is light (amber-400 + amber-950, lime-300 + lime-950) instead of forcing white text.
why: White on mid-light hues fails AA; same-hue dark text passes and keeps the colour feeling unified.
check: contrast ratio of label vs fill >= 4.5.

text: In app UI keep page headings small (20-24px, weight 600) and let layout, not size, carry hierarchy.
why: Large display headings waste vertical space in tools and compete with data.
check: `h1` font-size <= 24px inside app shells.
source: catalyst docs/heading (opinion: this is Catalyst's taste for app screens; marketing pages differ.)

text: When building on the Tailwind default theme, change at least the font family and the neutral family (e.g. zinc -> taupe/mauve/olive/mist) before shipping.
why: System font stack + zinc/gray is the most common SaaS surface on the web; neutral tint and type are the two cheapest identity levers.
check: `--font-sans` is not the default stack and neutrals are not zinc/gray/slate unless overridden in DIRECTION.md.

text: Animate a toggle only when its state changes (`duration-0` at rest, 200ms on change), never on mount.
why: Mount animations make settings pages flicker on load and misreport state.

text: Reference colour only through role tokens (`bg-weak-50`, `text-sub-600`, `stroke-soft-200`, `error-base`); allow raw palette steps only for named one-offs, and keep them under about 5% of colour references.
why: The role layer is what dark mode, theming and re-branding re-point; a raw step in a component is a place where the system cannot reach. AlignUI's starter holds 97% role references.
check: In project CSS/TSX: count colour utilities and variables per layer; raw hex or palette steps outside `tokens.css` should be 0 (or each listed in the spec).

text: Build light and dark as two assignments of the same role names; write zero per-component dark overrides.
why: One mapping to maintain and test; guarantees that every component has a dark state the moment it uses roles.
check: `grep -c "dark:"` in component source is 0 (except dark-only illustrations); the `.dark` block redefines roles only.

text: Name role tokens `{group}-{intensity}-{lightStep}` with a fixed intensity vocabulary (white/weak/soft/sub/surface/strong for fills, strong/sub/soft/disabled for text, strong/sub/soft/white for strokes).
why: The name carries meaning and the light value, so review and code search work without a lookup; intensities are comparable across fills, text and strokes.
check: token file: every role key matches `^(bg|text|stroke)-[a-z]+-\d+$`; no `gray-3`, `color1`, or per-component colour names.

text: Give every semantic state family the same four tones (dark, base, light, lighter) and the same dark-mode behaviour (dark -> 400 step; light and lighter -> 24% and 16% alpha).
why: Any badge, alert, status or chart can use any family without special cases; dark mode tints become translucent so they sit on any surface.
check: each family in tokens has exactly `dark|base|light|lighter`; dark block defines all four.

text: Keep a complete alpha ramp (10, 16, 24 percent) for every hue and use it for hover tints, focus halos and dark-mode tints; never invent a one-off opacity.
why: Alpha tints stay correct on any background and in both themes; three stops is enough to cover tint, hover and halo.
check: no `rgba(` or `/ 12%` inside components; only `*-alpha-{10,16,24}` tokens.

text: Define typography as named composites that bundle size, line-height, weight and letter-spacing; ban raw `font-size`/`line-height` in components. Tighten tracking as size grows (about -1.5% at 18-24 px, -1.1% at 16, -0.6% at 14, 0 at 12 and below) and widen it for uppercase labels (+2% to +6%).
why: Optical size correction is baked in once; components cannot drift to arbitrary sizes. The 1.0 changelog says tracking was re-derived from the Inter creator's geometric calculation; the values for 12/14/16/18 px (0, -0.6%, -1.1%, about -1.5%) match Inter's dynamic-metrics curve `tracking = -0.0223em + 0.185em * e^(-0.1745 * size_px)` (computes +0.05%, -0.62%, -1.10%, -1.43%) [E, computed], then clamp at about -1.5% and -1% for large titles. Derive tracking from a formula, not by eye.
check: computed (font-size, line-height, weight, letter-spacing) tuples on the page map to <= the spec's named styles (AlignUI marketing home measures 23 distinct tuples on 12 font sizes at 1440, 16 tuples on 9 sizes at 390).

text: Pair every size with a role in the type list (label = interactive text, medium weight; paragraph = reading text, regular weight; subheading = small uppercase caps with wide tracking; title = headings; doc = long-form).
why: Weight is part of the role, so a button label and a body line of equal size still look different on purpose.
check: controls use `label-*`, descriptions use `paragraph-*`; button text is weight 500, paragraph weight 400.

text: Build focus as a two-layer halo (2 px gap in the page-background token, then a 2 px halo ring in a role-matched alpha) and add a strong 1 px ring on form fields. Our engine must raise the halo to >= 3:1 against the surface (AlignUI's 10% alpha halo measures about 1.14:1).
why: The gap keeps the ring separable from any fill; but a 10% alpha halo alone fails non-text contrast. Copy the structure, not the opacity.
check: computed `:focus-visible` box-shadow has two spread layers (2px/4px) and its outer colour contrast vs surface >= 3:1; or an outline of >= 2px at >= 3:1.

text: Before building any page, reconcile the design's h1/h2/h3/p values (mobile and desktop) against global base styles; style tags once, never per component.
why: One source of type truth stops drift; Kargul Studio's starter makes this "rule 1".
check: computed font-size/line-height/letter-spacing of every `h1-h3,p` equal across all pages within 0px; no `text-[..px]` utilities on headings.

text: Express section vertical padding as 3-4 named tokens (sm/md/lg/page) plus one global gutter token; every section uses a token.
why: Section rhythm becomes auditable; measured kargul.studio has `--padding-section-sm 2rem / md 3.5rem / lg 3.5rem / page 7.375rem`, `--padding-global 1.1875rem`.
check: list of distinct section padding-top/bottom values <= 4; gutter identical on every page.

text: Give headings `max-width` in `em`, paragraphs in `em` derived from px/font-size.
why: Line length scales with the type size across breakpoints. Kargul h1 max-width measured 626.08px at 52px = 12.04em.
check: `parseFloat(getComputedStyle(h).maxWidth) / parseFloat(fontSize)` is constant per heading level across breakpoints; source CSS has no px max-width on headings.

text: One tracking value for display type (about -0.03em at 18-72px) and one easing family for interactions; record both as tokens.
why: Uniform micro-values read as intent. Measured: heading letter-spacing -0.03em at 18, 36, 52, 72px; easing cubic-bezier(0.76,0,0.24,1) 0.3s.
check: set of distinct `letter-spacing/font-size` ratios on h1-h3 has size 1 (+/-0.002); set of transition timing functions <= 3.

text: If the shell is neutral, put colour and personality in the work shown (screenshots, illustration, imagery) and make that work per-client distinctive.
why: Neutral frame + distinctive content is how a studio looks consistent and not templated. (This does not make a neutral shell a good brand site for a product with no portfolio; see `fully-specced-bar.md`.)
check: visual.

text: Evaluate each interaction against three things: the specific action performed (for example entering text into a web form), the physical attributes of the device (size, shape, weight of a phone), and how the user interacts with information on the device in context (p.84).
why: These variables determine whether a product lets users work quickly and efficiently (p.84).
check: process: each flow lists device, action, and context.

text: Size touch controls to reduce incorrect actions; if testing shows users struggle to hit certain buttons, enlarge them. Measure the error rate during user testing (p.84-85).
why: Mobile ergonomic design aims to reduce the possibility of incorrect actions (p.85).
check: touch target width/height from computed layout; process: error rate in test. The book gives no minimum size; see section 5 engine note.

text: Internal consistency: apply the same conventions and visual appearance to all UI elements throughout the interface (p.85-86).
why: A consistent design lets users transfer an acquired ability to other parts of the product; it is essential for pleasant encounters (p.85).
check: computed style variance for components of one role across all pages (button height, radius, font-size, colour); the set of distinct values per property should be small and tokenised.

text: External consistency: use the same design for the product on all platforms, desktop and mobile alike (p.86).
why: Same reason as internal: skills and expectations transfer (p.85-86).
check: compare component styling, labels and flows across breakpoints; same label strings, same iconography.

text: Use one name and one appearance per concept across screens (see also PU-DIF-06 in why-systems-fail.md) (p.47, 85).
why: Inconsistency forces rote learning (p.47).
check: synonym clustering of labels.

text: Prefer familiar concepts and metaphors; do not reinvent conventional patterns for novelty's sake (Jakob's Law). Full rule: PU-MOD-02 in memory-models-learning-effort.md (p.86).
why: Users get accustomed to conventions from other products and expect them (p.86).
check: see PU-MOD-02.

text: Give proper feedback: use visual and audio cues so users comprehend the present state of the system (p.87).
why: Control of information by the user is at the heart of HCI design; the user, not the system, should be in charge (p.87).
check: every async action has visible in-progress and completed states (spinner/skeleton/disabled/toast); focus, hover and active states exist on interactive elements.

text: Let users control system operations, including interrupting or terminating them (p.87).
why: Control is the user's, not the system's (p.87).
check: long-running operations (upload, export, generation) have cancel; modals and flows have close/back; no auto-advancing content without pause.

text: Personalise content using what you know about the user, to give the appearance that the system responds to their requirements (p.87).
why: Perceived responsiveness raises the sense of control (p.87).
check: process: personalised content has a visible, changeable source (e.g. shows name, recent items, saved settings) and a way to reset or control it.

text: Break difficult tasks into simple steps (p.88).
why: Simplifies decision-making and reduces complexity (p.88).
check: count fields/decisions per step; long forms are sectioned or stepped. No number in the book.

text: Remove every unnecessary action and keep navigation paths to a minimum so the user's attention and brainpower go to the task, not the interface (p.88).
why: Interaction should not take a lot of brainpower (p.87-88).
check: click depth from landing to each core task; count of optional fields and interstitials.

text: Give users the information they need to learn the system up front, and anticipate where they will need extra help (p.88).
why: Reduces learning cost at first use (p.88).
check: help text, empty states and contextual hints exist at known confusing points (format requirements stated before input, not after).

text: Combine related information and arrange UI elements so the most critical information is highlighted; use Gestalt principles to organise information on screens (p.88-89).
why: Grouping and emphasis cut search and cognitive effort (p.88-89).
check: see PU-PER-01/02/06.

text: Offer shortcuts for experienced users, for example keyboard shortcuts that perform tasks without a mouse (p.89).
why: Raises seasoned users' productivity (p.89).
check: visible shortcuts for repeated actions (command palette, kbd hints in menus); focusable controls in logical order.

text: Prevent errors where possible: map user journeys and analyse them to find places where users are likely to have issues (p.89-90).
why: Errors are human; the way a system handles them strongly affects users (p.89).
check: input constraints and formatting hints present (input type, masks, inline validation); process: journey walkthrough.

text: Stop users from making deadly mistakes with protective layers: confirm dialogs for deleting files or an entire account (p.90).
why: Fatal error states should be unreachable by accident (p.90).
check: destructive actions (delete, remove, cancel subscription, overwrite) trigger a confirmation that names the object, or are undoable.

text: Support "undo": allow actions to be reversed (p.90).
why: Reversibility makes trial and error safe (see PU-DIF-05) (p.46-47, 90).
check: delete/archive/edit actions expose undo (toast with Undo, trash, history).

text: When an error occurs, write messages that help users resolve it (p.90).
why: Users need to regain control (p.89-90).
check: error text states what is wrong and how to fix it, is adjacent to the field, uses no codes or jargon only; no "Error" alone.

text: Never hold users responsible for errors; treat them as the design's defects (p.90).
why: User-centered design: it is not the users' fault but design defects that cause mistakes (p.90).
check: copy lint on error text: no "you entered an invalid", "you failed", "your mistake"; phrase as what the system needs.

text: Design every decision point for three to four items held at once, not seven; treat Miller's 7 +/- 2 as an outdated upper bound (p.59-60).
why: The book reports estimates declining from Miller's seven and a half to three to four items (Koyani et al., 2004) and falling with age (p.60).
check: count items users must hold or compare simultaneously (steps in a flow visible at once, options in a primary choice, items in a nav level); flag >4 ungrouped.

text: Do not make users remember information across screens or steps; keep everything needed to complete the job in close proximity (p.62-63). People can only recall a few items for 3 to 4 seconds (p.62).
why: Short-term storage lasts 5 to 30 seconds (lower likely) (p.60) and is erased by competing activity (p.60-61).
check: multi-step flows repeat or summarise prior choices needed later; inputs with instructions put the instruction adjacent, not on another screen.

text: Place information that must be compared next to each other (p.63).
why: Avoids straining memory (p.63).
applies: landing page (pricing plans), SaaS app UI (tables, diffs).
check: compared items (plan features, before/after) appear in the same viewport and aligned rows.

text: Do not require working-memory tasks while the user needs to read fast: when screen-reading speed is critical, avoid asking for other jobs that use memory (p.63).
why: Short-term memory is overwritten by thinking, reciting or listening (p.60-61).
check: visual: no instruction text that disappears (auto-dismiss toast carrying required info; placeholder-only labels).

text: Organise, structure and present knowledge meaningfully and in familiar terms; give the user control over how information is presented (p.62).
why: Structured, meaningful, familiar information transfers to long-term memory and reduces demand on short-term (p.61-62).
check: headings/groups present; data views offer sort/filter/density control where tables exceed the chunk budget.

text: Make significant items unique or unusual (highlight crucial elements) to increase the chance they are remembered (p.63).
why: Distinctiveness aids recall (p.63).
check: one or two highlighted elements per section; if more than that are highlighted none is (see section 5).

text: Prefer recognition to recall: present lists of alternatives (menus, selects, suggestions, recent items) instead of requiring users to produce names or commands from memory (p.61-62, 80).
why: Active vocabulary (recallable) is about 2,000 to 3,000 words, passive vocabulary (recognisable) about 100,000; recognition provides memory cues for searching long-term memory (p.61-62). A GUI cut cognitive load by replacing commands to remember and format with menu commands only recognised (p.79-80).
check: free-text inputs where a finite option set exists (country, plan, role, date) should be a select/combobox/picker; commands exposed in menus not only via typed syntax.

text: Use words from the user's passive vocabulary: familiar words recognised at a glance; chunk size depends on the user's familiarity (p.60-62).
why: Familiarity enlarges chunk size (p.60).
check: copy review; jargon list.

text: Match the user's existing mental model: use familiar visual and usage expectations from other systems; a design that follows existing models is much easier to learn (p.73-74, 86).
why: Users carry expectations and prejudices from other systems and daily tasks; when the system matches, the model is reinforced and use feels intuitive; if not, interference arises (p.73-74).
check: compare nav placement, icon semantics, form patterns, checkout, auth flows to common conventions; deviation requires a stated reason.

text: Use familiar concepts and metaphors rather than inventing new ones (Jakob's Law): users spend most of their time on other products and expect conventional patterns; reinventing lengthens the learning curve (p.86).
why: Unfamiliar usage forces more time learning (p.86).
check: visual/pattern review: standard patterns for navigation, search, cart, forms.

text: When the existing mental model does not fit your goal, do not bend the design to it; give the user a clear and consistent new model to learn (p.74).
why: "Never compromise your goals or design to fit into pre-existing mental frameworks" (p.74).
check: process: new concept has one consistent name, one visual treatment, introduced once with onboarding.

text: Make targets for critical functions large; time to acquire a target depends on its distance and size (p.75-76).
why: Larger or closer targets are acquired faster (p.75); large buttons beat small buttons because they give a broader target (p.76).
check: computed bounding box of primary actions and touch targets; primary action larger than secondary actions; no numeric minimum is given in the book.

text: Use the screen's sides, top, bottom and corners ("pinning") for frequent controls, and let controls extend ("bleed") to the screen edge instead of leaving a one-pixel non-clickable border (p.75-76).
why: The edge stops the pointer at the control, so movement is much faster; a one-pixel edge needs careful positioning (p.76).
applies: SaaS app UI (toolbars, sidebars, top bars), desktop.
check: edge-docked bars: clickable area reaches the viewport edge (no padding between hit area and edge).

text: Size touch controls to reduce the possibility of incorrect actions; in testing measure error rate and enlarge buttons users miss (p.84-85).
why: Physical ergonomics: touch targets that are too small cause errors (p.85).
check: touch target dimensions and spacing; process: error rate in test.

text: Do not justify a complex design by users' ability to learn; where a simpler pathway exists, use it (p.76-77).
why: Humans can learn almost anything given time (the tightrope example), but unproductive learning time is usually avoided (p.76-77).
check: process: for each flow, compare the actual number of concepts to learn to the minimum.

text: Support jump-in, explore-and-experiment use: let people act immediately and discover; do not front-load massive amounts to learn (p.77).
why: People prefer to be active and experiment; the prospect of learning massive volumes deters some from using a system at all (p.77).
check: time/steps to first meaningful action; mandatory tutorials before first action are a flag.

text: Keep interface changes between versions or screens minimal; people are very sensitive to even modest changes (p.77).
why: Such changes cause problems when switching systems (p.77).
check: diff across screens/versions for moved or renamed primary controls.

text: Make the location of recurring items predictable by design consistency, so experienced users can start moving the cursor to a target before it appears (p.78).
why: Anticipating location is a by-product of learning; achieved through consistency, detailed and timely feedback, and phased learning (a person need only know what is required at that point) (p.78).
check: the same control occupies the same position/size across screens (compare bounding boxes of header, primary CTA, nav across routes).

text: Transfer skills: where possible let abilities learned in one setting apply in a similar situation elsewhere (p.77).
why: Learning is boosted by transfer (p.77).
check: same component = same behaviour everywhere.

text: Design screens so skilled performance can grow: allow gradual learning of shortcuts and better ways of working, and keep consistency so lower-order skills become automatic (p.78-79).
why: Skill is precise execution in exact time sequence; skills are hierarchical and lower ones become automatic (p.78-79).
check: frequent actions have keyboard shortcuts or quick paths; shortcut shown in menus/tooltips.

text: Cut cognitive load: keep screens free of noise and superfluous information; format and organise information properly; provide tools that rely on recognition not recollection; automate memory-intensive tasks (p.80).
why: The greater the effort required, the less likely a task is completed (p.79).
check: visual: count of distinct elements/weights per viewport; autofill/defaults/remembered values for memory-heavy fields.

text: Cut kinematic load: reduce the steps to complete tasks, minimise control actions and movements, automate mundane jobs (p.80).
why: Physical effort has a cost like mental effort; the GUI replaced multi-letter commands with one click (p.80).
check: click/keystroke/field count per task; pointer travel distance between consecutive controls.

text: Make the first use feel low-effort: a quick first impression that effort is not worth the reward ends in rejection, and so does merely believing it will take a lot of effort (p.81).
why: Perceived effort drives adoption as much as actual effort (p.81).
applies: landing page (above the fold), SaaS signup.
check: visual: first screen shows the job and one clear entry step; required fields at signup minimised (no number in the book).

text: Put related items closer to each other than to unrelated items; use gap size to encode relatedness (proximity) (p.55).
why: Near items are perceived as belonging together (p.55); this is the primary grouping cue.
check: measure inter-item gap within a group vs between groups; within-group gap < between-group gap for every adjacent pair (ratio of the two is the metric; book gives no number).

text: Give items that function alike the same visual feature (colour, size, shape, brightness, orientation) and give items that function differently a different one (similarity) (p.55).
why: Shared visual feature reads as belonging together (p.55).
applies: all (buttons of the same level, cards, nav items, tags).
check: computed style comparison across sibling components of the same role: same font-size/weight/colour/radius; differing roles differ in at least one property.

text: Do not draw every grouping explicitly; let closure and continuity complete shapes and lines, but enclose items with a border or container when they must read as one unit (unity) (p.55-56).
why: Perception creates logical wholes even from incomplete closed shapes; closed shapes are viewed as groups (p.55-56).
check: visual: groups containing 2+ related controls share a container or alignment axis.

text: Prefer vertical, horizontal and right-angle alignment for structure and keep layouts balanced (p.56).
why: These angles are "most visually pleasing and easy to look at"; people seek stability or equilibrium (p.56).
check: share of elements whose edges align to a small set of x/y axes (count distinct left edges per section); visual for balance.

text: Use depth cues consistently: overlapped, smaller or darker objects read as further; shadows and shading imply light from above (p.56).
why: Top-down lighting is natural; other orientations are unnatural (p.56).
check: computed `box-shadow` offset-y > 0 (shadow falls downward) for raised elements; inset shadows shade top.

text: Make the important element (the signal for the user's current task) distinguishable from its surroundings; reduce similarity between signal and background noise (p.57-58).
why: "Noise obstructs signal perception to the extent that they are similar to one another" (p.58); even an important signal can be obscured by noise.
check: contrast of primary CTA / key data vs adjacent elements (colour, size, weight, whitespace); visual: a squint/blur test should still reveal the primary element.

text: Let element prominence follow task phase: screen title is the signal when a screen first appears, data becomes the signal during use and the title recedes (p.58).
why: Elements change role between signal and noise as user needs change moment to moment (p.58-59).
check: visual: page title is smaller/quieter than the data region once content is on screen; heading is not the loudest thing in a data view.

text: Give every element on a screen a clear function; remove elements without one (p.64).
why: Reducing interface noise makes crucial details less likely to be overlooked; excessive, repeated stimulation causes habituation and the user can no longer tell important from irrelevant (p.64).
check: for each visible element: label its function; unlabelled elements are candidates for removal; count of distinct visual-weight levels per viewport.

text: Do not repeat attention-grabbing stimuli (repeated banners, pulsing badges, constant alerts) so often that users stop seeing them (p.64).
why: Habituation: sensory storage becomes less alert and cannot discriminate crucial from irrelevant information (p.64).
check: count of simultaneously animated or flagged ("new", red dot, pulse) elements per viewport; the book gives no number.

text: Treat the zone around the fixation point as a small "visual chunk" and make screen groups roughly that size or smaller; screens contain very few such chunks (p.64-66).
why: Relative acuity is half at 2.5 degrees from fixation; the optimum area is a 5-degree diameter circle (p.64-65). At 19 in (475 mm) viewing distance this is 1.67 in (41.8 mm) in diameter, holding 88 characters (15 on the widest line, seven rows) (p.65). Optimum viewing distance with modern screens is roughly 24 inches (p.66).
check: visual; angular-size calculation is possible: diameter = 2 x distance x tan(2.5 deg).

text: Avoid fill patterns of closely spaced lines or dots (hatching, fine dots, moire-like stripes) that shimmer; choose fill patterns carefully (p.66-67).
why: Eye tremor aids edge detection but makes close line/dot patterns shimmer, which is "distracting and upsetting" (p.66-67).
check: visual; flag repeating patterns with period under a few px. The book gives no number.

text: Use peripherally visible patterns, shapes and alignments to lead the eye through a screen in a methodical order (p.67-68).
why: Peripheral vision gives hints of where the eye should go next in visual search (p.67-68).
check: visual: consistent alignment axes and repeated shapes create a path; count distinct left-edges (fewer = stronger).

text: Do not put moving or dynamic content beside content the user is actively reading or working in (p.68).
why: Mori and Hayashi (1993): with peripheral windows present, performance on the foveal window deteriorates, and degradation is greater when the peripheral information is dynamic or moving (p.68).
applies: landing page (auto-playing carousels, tickers beside copy), SaaS app UI (live feeds beside forms).
check: detect CSS animations/autoplay media/marquee within the same viewport as primary text or forms; require pause control or reduced-motion respect.

text: Make each screen visually distinct in shape and structure so familiar users can recognise it with a glance instead of reading it. Avoid cluttering screens until they lose individuality (p.69-70).
why: Lower-level processing handles familiar information quickly without conscious effort; clutter forces slower, thought-interrupting reading (p.69-70).
check: visual: blur test, each page type has distinct layout skeleton; repeated layout across pages of different purpose is a flag.

text: For unfamiliar screens, give concrete identifying aspects: a title, the controls and the information it provides (p.69-70).
why: Unfamiliar users must use higher-level processing and rely on these cues to check "this is the right screen" (p.69-70).
applies: SaaS app UI (new users), landing page (h1).
check: each route has an `h1` or title that names its purpose.

text: Do not use colour that contradicts meaning (stop interference): no green for stop/destructive, red for go/confirm (p.71).
why: Naming the colour of a word printed in a different colour takes longer; a green Stop sign with a red Go sign creates mental conflict (p.71).
check: destructive buttons/states use red-family hue; success/confirm use green-family; no reversed semantics; label text colour does not name a different colour.

text: Avoid code combinations that cause distraction, such as colour and iconography meaning different things (p.72).
why: Interference arises when perception and cognition must reconcile opposing mental processes (p.71-72).
check: visual: icon meaning and its colour agree (e.g. no green "x" for delete).

text: Follow the conventions of previously learned systems; do not reuse a familiar pattern with a different meaning, and expect old habits to interfere with new rules (proactive interference), and new learning to disturb old (retroactive) (p.71-72).
why: Prior interaction procedures hamper learning new ones; learning a new system disturbs a learned one (p.71-72).
check: compare controls (icons, gestures, shortcuts) against platform/industry convention; flag reuse of a standard icon for a nonstandard action.

text: Before designing, write a problem statement that is about the user and their need, not about technology, revenue or product specs. Book's example: not "boost food sales to seniors by 5%" but "elders need meal delivery to have access to nutritious meal alternatives" (p.17-19).
why: A human-centered statement steers every later decision toward the user; a business-metric statement steers toward the company's bottom line (p.19).
applies: all (landing page: the hero/offer; SaaS: each screen's job).
check: process: brief contains a one-sentence user-need statement; it contains no KPI percentages, tech names or feature specs.

text: Keep the problem statement in a middle band: broad enough not to prescribe the solution or include technical requirements, narrow enough to be manageable. "Improve the human condition" is too broad (p.18).
why: Too narrow kills alternative solutions; too broad overwhelms the team (p.18-19).
check: process: statement does not name a UI pattern or technology; statement could be tested with a concrete task.

text: Evaluate any design on three axes at once: human attractiveness, business viability, technical feasibility. Failing the first means the other two cannot rescue it (p.11-12).
why: An unappealing product to its audience cannot generate profit (p.12).
check: process: critique output scores all three; visual for attractiveness.

text: Build an empathy map with four quadrants (Says, Thinks, Does, Feels) around the user before the first web design phase, and give *Does* (observed behaviour) more weight than *Says* (p.1, 9).
why: Cover tagline: attention to what users do. Stated and actual behaviour diverge.
check: process: four filled quadrants exist; each design claim traces to one.

text: Ask what users want, how they behave, where their pain points are, what their online habits are, and which wants must be met, before choosing a direction (p.9). Empathy techniques listed: What-How-Why, the 5 Whys, empathic interviews, photo/video studies, brainstorming, engaging users, journey map, analogies (p.11).
why: Answers give a strong start and prevent solving the wrong problem (p.9, 12).
check: process: list of the above answers present in brief.

text: Lay aside assumptions and own biases; examine what you see instead of rejecting it and do not seek only evidence that confirms prejudices (p.8, 10).
why: Biases enter how we interpret the world and the scenarios we investigate (p.10).
check: process: critique step lists at least one assumption that was tested rather than assumed.

text: Generate many candidate directions before selecting one; judge viability only afterwards. Ground rules: one conversation at a time; quantity over quality; encourage wild ideas; no judgment during generation; visualise (p.20-24).
why: Creativity appears when volume is prioritised; judgment blocks it (p.20, 23).
check: process: more than one distinct direction logged before commit. The book gives no number.

text: When mapping ideas, use keywords not long sentences, link every item to the central problem, and use images, colour and radial hierarchy for emphasis (p.25).
why: A map must give a quick cue to the concept; reading long statements wastes time (p.25).
check: visual.

text: Start with low-fidelity prototypes (storyboarding, drawing, Wizard of Oz, card sorting; paper-based, cheap). Use high-fidelity, computer-based prototypes when the product nears completion, because they give more genuine performance data (p.28-29).
why: Cheap models test many concepts without extra money, time or effort (p.31).
check: process: low-fi artefact precedes hi-fi render.

text: Test early and often, and treat test findings as grounds to revise the problem statement and loop back; do not treat the process as linear (p.33, 36).
why: Planned products rest on designer assumption until tested; later insights change earlier decisions (p.33, 36).
check: process: at least one render-critique-revise iteration recorded.

text: In moderated usability testing, let the moderator ask clarifying questions and ask participants to think aloud; most valuable with a high-fidelity prototype (p.34, 92).
why: Reveals why participants act the way they do (p.34).
check: process.

text: Use focus groups of six to nine members to study attitudes toward a specific solution (for example how onboarding makes users feel) (p.34).
why: Group debate surfaces feelings, not task performance.
check: process: group size 6-9.

text: Critique with precise, practical recommendations (constructive criticism) rather than verdicts (p.34).
why: It is the most effective way to give input on design solutions (p.34).
check: process: each critique item carries a concrete fix.

text: Use testing to find where cognitive load is high; if high, the experience gets less pleasurable (p.34-35).
why: Load is the amount of brainpower required (p.34).
check: visual + process (task walkthrough).

text: Pick method by phase: Wizard of Oz in user research (p.91); cognitive walkthrough in prototyping, working through tasks from the user's perspective (p.92); moderated testing with hi-fi prototype (p.92); contextual inquiry after launch, observing users in their natural setting (p.92).
why: Each keeps focus simple or realistic for its phase (p.91-92).
check: process.

text: For every user goal, make all three stages visible: (1) what the goal can be, (2) what controls carry it out, (3) what the outcome was. After any control activation, show a perceivable outcome that can be compared with what the user expected (p.40-43).
why: The user perceives the result, interprets it by expectation, then compares it with the goal (p.42); if any step is opaque, cycles repeat or goals are dropped (p.43).
check: for every `button`, `a[role=button]`, form submit: a DOM or visual state change within the interaction (loading/disabled/success/toast/navigation); script a click and diff DOM.

text: Minimise the steps and time the interface adds to a task's action cycle; design for the cycle to finish quickly and precisely (p.43).
why: Cycle length ranges from seconds to hours; interface should not add to it (p.43).
check: count clicks/fields from landing to goal completion; compare against baseline of the simplest flow.

text: Give each goal one obvious route, or if several routes exist, make them behave identically. Do not make the same outcome depend on when or how an action is performed (p.43, 46).
why: "Exceptional differences" (different results from the same action depending on timing) are minor, hard to notice and cause errors (p.46).
check: same-label controls resolve to same destination/behaviour across the site; visual.

text: Do not cram functionality in when user needs are not understood. Each added function adds complexity; "as a system's versatility grows, its usability declines" (p.44-45).
why: Higher complexity needs more learning and lowers performance efficiency (p.45).
applies: SaaS app UI, landing page (feature lists).
check: count of top-level actions per screen and nav items; flag screens where primary action is not distinguished from the others.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)

text: Use the user's vocabulary, not system jargon. Book's examples of opaque terms: filespec, abend, segment, boot (p.45).
why: Learning a system should not require learning a new language (p.45).
check: lint copy against a jargon list; nav and button labels use words a first-time user would produce; visual/copy review.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)

text: Make cause and effect evident: show results immediately and visibly; avoid hidden prerequisites and invisible overall architecture (p.45-46).
why: Unexpected design is non-intuitive; results are then not linked to the acts that produce them (p.45-46).
check: every state-changing control has visible result; disabled controls state why (text or tooltip adjacent).
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)

text: Avoid distinctions that have no practical importance and make the important distinctions at the point where they matter (p.46).
why: Book's example: a user said difficulties came from pressing Enter "in the wrong way" (p.46).
check: visual: no two near-identical controls with different outcomes.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)

text: Support trial-and-error: let people act, observe, and correct. Do not rely on them reading instructions first (p.46-47).
why: People learn by practice, often do not read instructions, and solve problems by "error-correcting" (p.46). Early systems used an "error-prevention" approach assuming people would act only when sure, which left people in one-way situations that were hard or impossible to escape (p.47).
check: every destructive or navigational action offers undo, cancel, back or an exit; no modal without a close/cancel; keyboard Esc closes.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)

text: Use one label, one behaviour, one information order per concept. Bad: "Save" vs "keep", "write" vs "list" for the same action; "not legal" vs "not legitimate" for the same outcome; same data in different order on different screens (p.47).
why: Inconsistency turns learning into rote memorisation; meaningful learning becomes very difficult (p.47).
check: collect all button/link/label strings; cluster synonyms; same concept = one string. Table columns/fields in same order across screens.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)

text: Treat every error, delay or confusing state as having outsized weight: users remember what went wrong, not what went right (p.47-48). Budget polish accordingly: error states, empty states, slow states.
why: Problems get abnormally high priority in memory (p.47-48).
check: each flow has designed error, loading and empty states; no raw browser/stack error visible.

text: Never let a response to an action be irreversible and unexplained; frustration rises when an unanticipated response cannot be reversed or what happened cannot be determined (p.49).
why: Named cause of frustration (p.49).
check: destructive actions: undo or confirmation; result messages state what happened.

text: Avoid the named causes of annoyance: roadblocks to tasks or requirements, design inconsistencies, slow response times, difficulty accessing information fast, outdated information, visual screen distractions (p.48-49).
why: Annoyance becomes frustration when annoyances accumulate or goals cannot be communicated (p.49).
check: performance budget (slow responses); stale content/date check; visual for distractions.

text: Do not leave users waiting under pressure without response: long response times while the user has a deadline or an unhappy customer create panic and anxiety (p.49). Also avoid underload: slow pace and long download times cause boredom, and "a bored person is more likely to make mistakes" (p.49-50).
why: Both overload and underload harm concentration (p.49-50).
check: measure interaction latency; any wait has a loading indicator; visual.

text: Keep perceived effort below perceived reward. When effort plus negative emotions exceed the reward, people abandon the system, use only part of it (the easiest or highest-benefit tasks), use an intermediary, change the task, add compensatory work (manual reformatting), abuse the system, or reprogram it (p.50-52).
why: People want the advantages to outweigh the expense or effort (p.50).
check: visual + process: for each task, list effort (fields, steps, reading) against reward; flag features that will be "partly used".

text: Never trust designer intuition about user skill. Assume users lack the context clues and system knowledge the designer has; assume they will not "think" the system is usable just because the designer can use it (p.44, 52-53).
why: Specialised knowledge creates a false sense of security; the designer cannot imagine someone unable to use the system they built (p.44, 53).
check: process: test with a naive task walkthrough ("first-time user, no context").

text: Design for users whose main goal is to get a task done, who are busy and may be hostile or technically unsophisticated. Do not require them to learn technology (p.53).
why: "He or she would rather use a computer than learn how to utilise one" (p.53). Many people also now expect a certain amount of design expertise (p.53).
check: visual: primary task visible without scrolling/explanation.

text: Treat visual design (colour patterns, typography, buttons, interactions) as the UI deliverable, and apply it to a structure and content plan that already exists. Do not invent information architecture while styling; if the structure is missing, define it first (sections, content priority, flows) and then style it.
why: UI without UX structure is arbitrary decoration (p.15); the UI designer's job is to receive "all of the needs and structure" and present them attractively (p.24).
check: process: a written section/content structure exists before visual styling begins.

text: Make the interface express exactly what the company/product is, through the UI itself (the interface carries the brand: colour, type, tone), without turning the task into logo/brand-identity design.
why: The UI designer "implements" the brand; they are not a branding designer but are closely tied to it.
check: visual: a viewer can name the brand/product category from the UI with logo covered.

text: Design for every screen size and resolution the product will be viewed on (the book names desktop, mobile device and an Xbox 360); the layout must "look good on each".
why: Adapting to every screen size and resolution is part of the UI designer's responsibility.
check: render at multiple viewports (e.g. desktop and mobile) and verify no overflow/broken layout. Specific breakpoints are not given in this chapter.

text: Include inner animations, interactivity and prototyping in the UI scope, not only static visuals.
why: "Nowadays it's a standard for UI designers to also think about inner animations, interactivity, prototyping."
check: visual/process: interactive states (hover, press, transitions) are defined for interactive elements.

text: Cover the full GUI element set: menus, tabs, widgets, input controls, navigational components and informational components.
why: This is the book's enumerated list of what UI/UX designers design.
check: inventory of components present vs this list.

text: Do competitive/market research (what is standard in the related market) before settling the look and feel, so the product "makes sense" in its category.
why: Look and feel is the biggest UI element; the designer analyses market standards "to insure that the product make sense".
check: process: reference set exists (and see examples/ layer).

text: Put the user first in structure and content decisions ("always user comes first... ALWAYS"), and strategize how content is applied and received, since "content is king on the web".
why: UX is a user-first discipline; content strategy is a large part of the UX role.
check: process.

text: Close the loop with the people who built and who use the product: incorporate customer feedback, usage metrics and usability findings; collaborate with developers so what ships looks and works as designed.
why: The designer is responsible for the voice of the customer and for design-to-build fidelity.
check: process.

text: Make the purchase/engagement journey feel personal and appealing to the particular user (the book's example: a customer looking for shoes should find the experience equally appealing to engage with; the purchase "must be a delightful one").
why: UX is about how the experience makes people feel, not only how it looks.
check: visual/process (user-journey walkthrough).

text: Use the UI/UX/CX lens as a checklist of qualities beyond appearance: UI (colour theory, typography, design patterns, interactivity and animations) inside UX (desirable, valuable, findable, accessible, credible) inside CX (attraction, awareness, advocacy, purchase, discovery, cultivation).
why: Scope diagram, p.13.
check: process: review a design against each ring.

text: Design the layout in grayscale first; only then choose a single brand colour, then choose the other colours that suit it.
why: Greyscale "forces a layout of the elements and a renewed focus on spacing" and makes a complex visual element simpler (p.57).
check: visual (render the page with `filter: grayscale(1)`; hierarchy and grouping must still read).

text: Choose colours that are consistent with the brand's personality; never use colours that contradict what the brand is trying to portray.
why: Colour sets the brand's mood, tone, concept and meaning, and the user connects it to the brand only if it agrees with it (p.36, p.57).
check: visual / brief review: each palette colour can be justified by a brand attribute.

text: Before committing to colour, define: brand personality, likely customers (the book names gender), tone to project, value proposition, and company age ("fresh and exciting" or "tried and true").
why: The goal is a hue that becomes synonymous with the company later (p.58-59).
check: the brief records these five answers before a palette is chosen.

text: Keep the goal as "a simple UI with sensible colors" rather than maximal colour.
why: Stated as the overall objective of colour selection (p.59).
check: visual; count distinct hues (see 2.2).

text: Match each hue's connotation to what the brand or product says (see the table in section 3): trust/security = blue, calm/regeneration = green, excitement = orange, joy = yellow, wealth/royalty = purple, energy/passion = red, mystery/modern = black, purity/clarity = white.
why: Hues provoke particular emotions and "help to get the desired response" (p.38); technology brands choose blue to establish trust (p.42).
check: visual / brief.

text: Keep in mind that meaning depends on culture and context; the same colour can mean opposite things (red = love and anger; black = mystery and death; warm colours = comfort or rage).
why: Each colour has "a unique meaning and connotation", partly culture-dependent (p.38, p.39-40, p.46).
check: visual; confirm with target-market review.

text: Run colour options past potential clients/users before launching a website or a new corporate logo.
why: Cheap validation; the book frames it as "never a bad idea" (p.70).
check: process (ledger of the review).

text: Take colour inspiration from nature and art (e.g. the many greens of grass); natural-looking colours are chosen by people and "appear to be user-friendly".
why: Colours that appear natural feel familiar and friendly (p.69). (opinion)
check: visual.

text: Use a deliberate UX palette to help readability, strengthen CTA buttons, improve navigation and meet subconscious aesthetic needs.
why: Appropriate colour aids information readability and elicits intuitive responses (p.37).
check: visual.

text: Distribute colour 60% / 30% / 10%: 60% a neutral ("any justifying neutral color"), 30% the secondary brand colour, 10% the main brand colour. The book writes it as 6:3:1 and calls it the Golden Rule / Golden Ratio of Colors.
why: Produces a neat, harmonious interface, soothes the eye, and lets the viewer flow from one place to the next naturally (p.59, p.60).
check: sample rendered pixels by colour family (neutral share about 60%, secondary about 30%, main brand colour about 10% of visible area).

text: Use no more than three primary colours.
why: Keeps the design from becoming jumbled and maintains equilibrium, especially with 60/30/10 (p.60).
check: cluster dominant hues on the rendered page; non-neutral hue families of brand role <= 3.

text: Apply it as: neutral for 60% of the design, secondary brand colour for 30%, main brand colour for 10% of the UI (the book's wording for a logo and for UI).
why: Same proportion, stated for both logo and UI (p.60).
check: as above.

text: Reference pattern (Amazon, p.61): white page background = 60%; blue (dark navy in the screenshot) header/footer = 30%; yellow buttons and star ratings = 10%. The accent colour sits on actions and ratings, i.e. the elements the user should act on.
why: The book presents it as good UI using the rule "to arouse people" (p.61).
applies: SaaS app UI | e-commerce landing page.
check: the 10% colour appears only on CTAs/key signals.

text: Avoid overcrowding and disorder; minimalism is "always preferable in user interfaces"; do not ignore colour combinations entirely.
why: Crowded colour use produces a disordered interface (p.59).
check: visual.

text: Prefer a simple scheme: two contrasting hues, or a monochromatic scheme. Do not put many colours in many locations.
why: Simple schemes are less distracting to the eye and make material easier to assimilate; too many colours "generates a convoluted interface that confuses the user". If the mind finds an app easy to look at, "half of a designer's job is done" (p.68).
check: count distinct non-neutral hues on a screen (target <= 2 in the book's "simple" version; <= 3 in the 60/30/10 version).

text: Monochromatic: use tints, shades and tones of one hue, including black and white. Expect lower contrast than other schemes; compensate so the result is not lifeless.
why: Full spectrum of one colour is cohesive but "the contrast is often lower ... making our creations appear lifeless" (p.50).
check: contrast ratios between element tiers (see 2.7).

text: Triad: three colours equally spaced on the wheel, used when the design needs more colours; make one colour prominent and the other two accents.
why: Keeps balance in a three-hue scheme (p.51).
check: one hue family covers the majority of coloured area; others limited.

text: Complementary: pair colours directly opposite each other for significant contrast. It is "the polar opposite of similar and monochrome". Example: an orange button on a blue background is difficult to overlook.
why: Opposite hues give maximum contrast and so make a CTA stand out (p.52).
check: hue difference about 180 degrees between CTA and its surroundings.

text: Analogous: use hues immediately adjacent on the wheel where there is little need for contrast, such as page backgrounds or banners.
why: Adjacent hues give "comparable harmony" with low contrast (p.53).
check: hue spread of the scheme narrow (adjacent wheel segments).

text: Tetradic (rectangle): four colours as two complementary pairs forming a rectangle on the wheel. It is the hardest to balance and "reserved for skilled designers"; works only if synchronised well.
why: Many hues compete; payoff is rich result when done well (p.54).
check: visual; keep one hue dominant.

text: Square: four colours evenly spaced around the wheel. Works best when one colour dominates; also balance warm and cold hues.
why: Evenly spaced hues have equal weight unless one is made dominant (p.55).
check: one hue holds the largest area share; both warm and cool present.

text: Split-complementary: base colour plus the two colours adjacent to its complement. Same high visual contrast as complementary but "less tense".
why: Keeps the contrast while softening the tension of an exact opposite pair (p.56).
applies: CTAs/accents where complementary feels too harsh.
check: hue offsets of accent colours about 150 and 210 degrees from base.

text: (figure-derived, not stated in the text) In every scheme mockup the type-and-button kit is built the same way: title and subheading are set in the scheme's darkest hue (near-black tinted with the scheme), body text is a neutral grey, the primary button is a solid fill in the strongest hue, the secondary button is a second hue (or a lighter tint) fill, and the tertiary button is an outline (or text-only) in the same hue.
why: Visible across pp.50-56: hierarchy is carried by fill > tinted fill > outline.
check: at most one solid fill per button group; lower tiers use tint/outline/text.

text: Create variants of a hue on the wheel by: adding white = tint; adding black = shade; adding a mix of black and white (grey) = tone.
why: These give systematic, harmonious variants of one hue ("extremely useful indicators for guiding the human brain to specific conclusions") (p.62, p.63).
check: tokens derive from one base hue by mixing with white/black/grey.

text: Use shades, tints and tones to enhance major design elements "in a subtle way", not as new unrelated colours.
why: Keeps the palette cohesive while giving emphasis (p.62).
check: visual.

text: To make a dark variant, increase saturation while lowering brightness; to make brighter variants, do the opposite (HSB terms).
why: Stated as the way to make dark/brighter colour variations (p.63). (Note: this is the HSB model shown on p.35.)
check: HSB of dark variants: S up, B down vs the base.

text: Use strong contrast (colours on opposite sides of the wheel, black next to white) to create tension and make viewers focus; use light contrast for delightful, relaxing, laid-back feel. Decide by intent.
why: Contrast between opposite hues is "always the most noticeable"; strong contrast creates tension and focus; light contrast relaxes (p.63, p.64).
check: visual; contrast of focal element vs surroundings higher than of non-focal elements.

text: Contrast is also a way to create a simple interface and elicit emotional responses.
why: Stated as a "simple approach" (p.63).
check: visual.

text: Combine a highly saturated hue with less saturated colours; do not saturate everything. "Saturation overload kills color vibrancy"; less is nearly always more.
why: One saturated colour among muted ones looks vivid (the Instagram logo is the example); many saturated colours cancel each other (p.64).
check: only one hue family has high saturation; rest neutral or desaturated.

text: Use interactive colours for anything the user touches or clicks (links, buttons, other controls). Keep primary interactions to a single hue.
why: "For the user, that color will begin to have a single meaning" (p.64).
check: all primary buttons/links share one hue (computed `background-color`/`color` of `a`, `button`).

text: Provide the interactive colour in dark and light variants and use these shades for states: pressed/hover (darker), disabled (lighter/washed).
why: Shades express status of UI elements; pressed and hover are named examples (p.65). The figure (p.64) shows default = saturated violet gradient, hover/pressed = darker indigo with cursor, disabled = pale lavender; loading = pale blue with spinner or progress bar.
check: four states exist per interactive component with the same hue.

text: (figure-derived, not stated in text) Purchase actions can have their own colour language. The p.64 figure shows a dark charcoal pill with yellow label ("ADD TO CART"), yellow pills with dark labels ("CHECKOUT", "PayPal" logo) and a blue pill ("Submit"); the pairs are high-contrast (yellow on charcoal, charcoal on yellow).
why: Shown, not explained; the text only says to keep primary interactions to one hue.
check: visual; each button's label/fill pair is a strong contrast.

text: Define a state palette: error, success, warning (the figure also has info). Red, green and (in the figure) yellow/amber and blue are used. Each status card has a tinted background, a tinted border, a solid-colour circular icon with white glyph, bold title, grey description, and a close X.
why: Denotative colours "have meaning" and must be defined for states (p.65).
check: tokens `--success`, `--warning`, `--error`, `--info` exist; each pairs colour with an icon glyph.

text: If a brand colour is red, do not use that red for error messages.
why: A brand colour carrying a status meaning makes errors indistinguishable from branding (p.66).
check: error colour differs in hue from brand primary.

text: When picking the disabled-state colour, make sure it has sufficient contrast; users must be able to read it.
why: Disabled does not mean unreadable (p.66).
check: contrast of disabled text/label vs its fill (see 2.7).

text: Check the contrast and accessibility level of the palette while choosing colours, so colourblind users can use the product. Use contrast checkers and accessibility checkers (WebAIM contrast checker, noCoffee, Accessibility Scanner).
why: "You are creating an interface for the use of public" (p.66, p.67).
check: computed contrast ratio per text/background pair. Book's own reference figure: WebAIM result 4.83:1 for a light violet foreground (about #9095FE) on a dark grey background (about #323232), which shows WCAG AA Pass and AAA Fail for normal text, AA Pass and AAA Pass for large text (p.67).

text: Do not rely entirely on colour distinctions. Use light and dark hues (value difference) and techniques like cross-hatching to distinguish parts of the interface.
why: Colour-blind people cannot use products that depend on colour alone (p.67).
check: desaturate the screenshot; elements and states must remain distinguishable.

text: Let hierarchy survive greyscale: in the book's example the bad version fills both "Skip" (pink) and "Continue" (teal) buttons, which become two near-identical grey fills in greyscale; the good version keeps "Skip" as an outline (pink border/text) and "Continue" filled, so greyscale still shows outline vs solid.
why: Colour-blind users and greyscale rendering lose hue, so primary vs secondary must differ in form (fill vs outline) too (p.66 figure).
check: greyscale screenshot; the primary and secondary controls differ in fill/weight, not hue only.

text: (claim) Treat colour as a primary driver of first impressions: the book cites the "Institute for Color" saying customers assess online purchases in about 90 seconds, that colour influences 62% to 90% of product evaluations on a subconscious level, and "up to 85%" of customers say colour is the most important purchase factor.
why: Used to justify care in logo, brand and packaging colour (p.36, p.57). No primary source given.
check: n/a (motivation only).
section: 2.8 Claims about colour effectiveness (source-stated; weak evidence)

text: Judge balance by perceived visual weight, not by element count, pixel area alone or real-world object weight.
why: The eye weighs distinctiveness and attention-pull; similar-looking competition means balance even when the "real" weights differ (basketball vs bowling ball).
check: visual (squint / blur test).

text: When two elements should feel equal, make them compete for attention equally; to make one dominant, raise its weight on purpose through size, color, contrast or density.
why: Visual weight is a metric of how distinctive an element is compared to its surroundings.
check: visual; mechanical proxy: compare area, background-contrast ratio, saturation and ink coverage of the two elements.

text: Size: the larger element carries more weight (book's figure: a large rounded square left of a roughly half-width rounded square of the same pink, bottoms on a shared baseline, left clearly dominant).
why: Most obvious weight lever.
check: bounding-box area ratio of the elements flanking an axis.

text: Color: saturated/hot colors (the book's hot pink-red) carry more weight than a pale yellow-lime of the same size on a light neutral ground. Treat this as a tendency, not a law.
why: Perception of a color depends on the colors around it; the red "commands our attention".
check: visual; compare saturation/chroma against the surrounding background.

text: Contrast: weight follows contrast against the element's own background. Darkening the background behind an element reduces its contrast and its weight; raising contrast on a neighbour shifts focus to that neighbour.
why: Figure p.75: same pink and yellow squares on a mid pink-red panel. The pink square (low contrast vs panel) fades, the lime-yellow square (high contrast) now wins. The reverse was true on the light background (p.74).
check: contrast ratio of each element vs its immediate background.

text: Density: when two elements share size, color and contrast, the denser one (more ink, less internal gap) is heavier. Open up gaps/white space inside the heavier one to bring it back into balance.
why: Figure p.75: two squares built from identical grids of small pink squares; the left grid has visible gaps, the right grid is nearly solid. Right looks heavier. "White space can help to achieve equilibrium."
check: ink-coverage ratio (non-background pixels / area) per element; icon fill vs outline.

text: Combine levers: tiny changes in size, color, contrast or density visibly change weight; use them together to tune balance.
why: The levers are additive.
check: visual.

text: In a centered hero, do not load one half of the page. If centered text keeps vertical-axis symmetry, the left and right halves still need similar weight (logo + a left-hand CTA vs nothing on the right reads lopsided).
why: Figure p.76: purple hero (logo top-left, four nav items top-right with the last wider, centered headline "The Conversion Platforms for Marketers", 3-line centered paragraph, ONE outlined CTA "PREVIEW THE PAGE BUILDER" sitting left-of-centre). The text is centered, but the single CTA makes the left half "visibly heavier", producing tension and a sense that "something appears strange".
check: compare ink/weight left vs right of the page's vertical center line; visual.

text: Fix the lopsided hero by adding a counterweight on the light side of the same visual size: a second outlined CTA to the right of the first ("HOW UNBOUNCE HELPS YOU"), so the pair sits symmetrically about the center line.
why: Figure p.77: same hero, now two equal outlined buttons side by side, centered as a pair; the page is "evenly balanced on both sides". "Our brains prefer balance over stress."
check: the pair's combined center aligns with the text's center axis; visual.

text: Create hierarchy between a primary and a secondary button without breaking balance: make the primary stronger through color/fill, but give the secondary a comparable *density* (a solid fill, e.g. white) rather than leaving it as a thin outline next to a solid primary.
why: Figure p.78 shows three attempts, each a pair "Secondary Button" (left) / "Primary Button" (right): (a) "Insufficient Contrast": secondary = dark navy outline, white fill, dark text; primary = outline only in the brand purple, purple text on light. Primary is harder to read, and the secondary now looks heavier. Wrong. (b) "Too Much Tension": secondary unchanged (dark outline); primary = solid purple/blue gradient fill with white text. Contrast fixed, but the primary is now "significantly too heavy" next to a thin outline. (c) "Balance & Tension": secondary = solid white filled pill/rounded rect, no outline, dark text; primary = solid purple fill, white text. The densities match and the color difference carries the hierarchy. Correct.
check: both buttons filled (or both comparably dense); primary differs by color, not by fill vs outline; visual.

text: Use tension deliberately and sparingly: avoid visual strain from accidental loss of equilibrium; use visual tension only "with care and purpose" to get a desired effect.
why: Brains prefer balance; deliberate tension can direct attention.
check: visual; ask whether each point of imbalance is intentional.

text: Symmetrical/formal balance: mirror the visual weight across the axis (vertical, horizontal or any line through the middle). Use it when you want stability, order and a clear, strong message.
why: Equal weight on both sides makes the composition stable and orderly and gives the viewer a stronger sense of what is being communicated.
check: reflect the layout across the axis; compare bounding boxes and colors.

text: In a symmetrical layout, keep value (lightness) matched on both sides; a light-valued side opposite a dark-valued side breaks the balance even if shapes and positions mirror exactly.
why: Figure p.80: top = three purple squares left and three purple squares right of a tall light-grey bar, dashed center axis through it ("perfectly balanced"); bottom = the identical layout with the left three squares in pale grey. Now the dark right side feels heavier.
check: compare mean luminance of left vs right of the axis.

text: Do not rely on pure mirror symmetry alone; mirror the weight but vary the techniques on each side to keep the design from being boring.
why: "Symmetrical balance doesn't always relay an interesting design."
check: visual.

text: Asymmetrical/informal balance: use unequal elements on each side, balanced by position and stacking, like a seesaw or beam scale. Options: several small elements against one large; smaller elements placed further from the center.
why: Weight times distance. It keeps balance while adding visual interest, movement and tension.
applies: all (hero with big illustration vs stacked small items, feature sections).
check: visual; weigh each side by area x contrast x distance from the axis.

text: In an asymmetric layout one side may feel heavier, as long as the whole is still balanced; expect to experiment because the two sides cannot be matched exactly.
why: Perfect matching is impossible, feel must be tuned.
check: visual iteration (step back, blur).

text: Radial balance: arrange objects, colors or textures at equal distances around a single point (usually the center, not always), like a snowflake or seesaw about a pivot.
why: Equal distribution about a point balances without any left-right axis.
applies: all (logo marks, orbit/diagram layouts, circular galleries).
check: radial distribution; equal radii for equal weights.

text: Mosaic/crystallographic balance: for "organized chaos" with no focal point, give all elements some uniform emphasis so it works together on close inspection.
why: Uniform emphasis across many parts replaces a focal point.
applies: all (dense galleries, pattern backgrounds, icon walls).
check: no element outweighs the rest; visual.

text: Step back and judge the whole composition; if one piece draws too much attention, redistribute weight by changing size, color, contrast, density.
why: Balance is a whole-composition property.
check: blur/squint test; thumbnail view.

text: Combine types of balance (e.g. symmetrical frame with asymmetrical content) for a more dynamic, lively design.
why: Single-type compositions are static.
check: visual.

text: Align elements to shared edges or center-lines; every element should line up with something else on the page.
why: Shared lines give the eye predictable stops, reading as organised, professional and unified.
check: collect the left/right/top/bottom/center coordinates of sibling elements (getBoundingClientRect); count distinct x-positions per column and distinct y-positions per row; flag near-misses of 1-3 px.

text: Connect related items by aligning them in the same row or column, as a table does; use this to make information scannable.
why: Row/column alignment signals relatedness without borders or labels ("without the need for external helpers").
applies: SaaS app UI, tables, forms, pricing.
check: items in a group share one x (column) or one y (row) edge.

text: When a list repeats a pattern (marker + title + description), start every row's marker on one x and every row's text on one x.
why: Figure p.98: left = "In Alignment": four rows, each a blue dot + bold title bar + two grey description lines; dots all on one dashed vertical guide, title bars all start at the same x. Right = "Out of Alignment": the dots are staggered on the guide (row 2 shifted right, row 3 slightly right, row 4 shifted left of the guide) and the text start moves with each dot, so the left edge zigzags. The book states the aligned version is "more pleasing to look at".
applies: all (lists, feeds, settings rows, notification lists).
check: `left` of the icon/avatar element identical across rows; `left` of the text block identical across rows.

text: Elements that belong to one brand/identity block (logo + slogan, heading + subheading) should share one alignment edge (both left-aligned) and sit close together.
why: Figure p.99: left = Pixsel Academy logo (round icon + wordmark) with the two-line slogan "Teaching the foundations of design" left-aligned beneath, left edges flush with the logo; right = same pair but the slogan is right-aligned (ragged against the logo), "looks like elements of different designs". Goal: "bring unity in the branding" and show both elements are one design element. "Common alignment and proximity with design elements can unify them."
check: left edge of subline == left edge of logo/wordmark block.

text: Align a row of items on a common top, bottom or center line; you need not align all three.
why: One consistent horizontal line is enough to read the row as ordered. Figure p.89: three identical cards (image-header on top, text lines below) with three dashed horizontal guides at the top edge, image/text boundary, and bottom edge; all three cards coincide on all lines.
check: equal `top` (or `bottom` / vertical center) across siblings.
section: Vertical alignment (items on a shared horizontal line)

text: If the items' heights differ dramatically, align by top (or bottom).
why: Figure p.90: main body (tall) and sidebar (short) share the top edge, and their headings align too, which establishes the connection. Tops-align avoids a floating short block.
applies: main + sidebar layouts, columns of unequal length.
check: `top` of both containers equal and first heading baselines equal.
section: Vertical alignment (items on a shared horizontal line)

text: If heights differ only somewhat, align by center.
why: Figure p.91: header nav bar with a round logo, three text links and a filled CTA, all centered on one dashed horizontal line across the bar even though the pieces have different heights.
applies: headers/navbars, icon + label rows, buttons with leading icons.
check: vertical center of each item within the row within 1 px (`align-items: center`).
section: Vertical alignment (items on a shared horizontal line)

text: Align items on a common left, right or center vertical line; again one of the three suffices.
why: Figure p.91: 2 x 3 grid of identical cards. Guides show the left edge, center and right edge of each card as vertical dashed lines: columns line up across both rows.
applies: card grids, sections stacked vertically, forms.
check: same `left` per column across rows.
section: Horizontal alignment (items on a shared vertical line)

text: Set a max-width on all content from the start; content then aligns to the same left and right edges regardless of push left/right.
why: The "invisible box" guarantees consistent edges. Figure p.92: whole landing-page mock with two vertical guides marking the content column; logo, nav end, hero text, hero image, cards, banner, and footer columns all start/stop at those two guides, while the header and footer bars extend full width.
check: every section's content box shares the same container left/right (same max-width and padding); no section uses a different gutter.
section: Horizontal alignment (items on a shared vertical line)

text: Use center alignment only when there is a single element in the row (the standard case: a call-to-action block: heading, short paragraph, button, all on one center axis).
why: Figure p.93: one purple panel with a dashed vertical center line passing through "Call to Action" heading, 3-line centered paragraph (bold "Lorem ipsum", "Cras nulla risus") and a white pill "Button"; all pieces share the center axis.
applies: landing page CTAs, empty states, hero.
check: items' horizontal centers equal the container center (+-1 px).
section: Horizontal alignment (items on a shared vertical line)

text: Left-align body text and multi-line text when the audience reads left to right.
why: With left alignment the eye jumps from the end of one line to the start of the next predictably; after a few lines readability degrades with centered or right alignment.
check: computed `text-align` on `p`, `li`, multi-line blocks is `start/left` (or `right` for RTL); flag `center` on paragraphs of more than ~3 lines.
section: Horizontal alignment (items on a shared vertical line)

text: Media objects (icon + text rows): center each icon on a common vertical axis and left-align all text on a second vertical axis; align like items with like items.
why: Icons of variable width otherwise cause misalignment. Figure p.94: "PROPERTY FEATURES" card: small caps label top-left; three rows each with an icon of different width (pin, key, car) centered on one dashed vertical guide, and to the right a bold title ("Beautiful Waterfront Location", "Fast check-in experience", "Free secure parking") plus 1-2 grey description lines, all text starting at one dashed guide. The result "gives a perfect look and balance".
check: icon center x equal across rows; text block `left` equal across rows.

text: Use edge alignment: anchor one or more corners of neighbouring blocks to shared horizontal and vertical lines (top edge of the text block with top edge of the image, bottom of the button with bottom of the image, inner edges with container edges).
why: Anchoring items "in each corner" guides the eye from one piece to the next. Figure p.94: purple banner; left = headline bar, two description lines, a white "Button" pill; right = wireframe image placeholder. Horizontal guides: headline bar top == image top; button bottom == image bottom. Vertical guides: text/button left edge and image right edge sit on the container's content edges.
applies: hero sections, split sections, cards with media.
check: `top` of text block == `top` of media; `bottom` of last element == `bottom` of media; left and right edges on container.

text: Where exact geometric alignment looks wrong, optically align: nudge the shape until it looks centered/aligned, rather than trusting the numbers.
why: An element's uneven visual weight distribution makes a mathematically centered shape look off. Figure p.95: two circular buttons with a play triangle. Left, "Center Alignment": the triangle's bounding box is centered, so the gaps left and right of the triangle (marked x and x) are equal; it looks shifted left. Right, "Optical Alignment": gaps marked x (left) and y (right), unequal: the triangle is deliberately moved right (by roughly a tenth of its width, measured from the figure; no number in the book), so the visual mass sits at the circle's center.
applies: icons in circles/buttons, play/arrow glyphs, asymmetric logos, text inside pills.
check: visual; compare bounding-box centering vs centroid centering and nudge by eye.

text: Left-aligned text is the easiest to read; default to it.
why: Figure p.96: three identical paragraph cards (8 lines each) labelled Left / Center / Right Alignment. Left is easiest; center "not so bad but a bit odd"; right is difficult.
check: `text-align`.

text: Center alignment is acceptable for short text of a few sentences: headings and slogans.
why: Few lines remove the ragged-start problem. (The paragraph in the figure was nevertheless judged harder than left.)
check: centered blocks <= ~3 lines (book: "after a few lines" it suffers).

text: Do not right-align running text in LTR languages; right alignment is the default for right-to-left languages, where left alignment would look weird.
why: Right-ragged starts make each new line hard to find; but RTL scripts invert the convention.
check: `dir` and `text-align` consistent.

text: Justified text is for print/multi-column text composition; the justification acts as the separator between columns. Avoid on short web columns.
why: Newspaper columns use it; long unseparated lines make readers lose their place. Figure p.97: two narrow columns of lorem ipsum in a rounded outlined box with both edges flush; uneven word and letter spacing is visible (line 3 of column 2 is visibly squeezed, lines in column 1 widely letter-spaced), showing the cost.
check: `text-align: justify` only with hyphenation and wide columns; visual rivers.

text: Right-align numeric columns (prices, totals); also align decimal points.
why: Units, tens, hundreds (and cents) stack in the same columns so magnitudes are comparable at a glance; with left alignment the decimals become confusing.
check: `text-align: right` on numeric cells and `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`; decimal-places constant.
