text: Use one of the three fundamental gradient types deliberately: linear (straight axis, one colour fading into another, horizontal, vertical or diagonal; builds momentum, e.g. Apple Music logo ring pink to blue on a diagonal), radial (starts at a point and fans out, or the reverse; frequent in logos; good for structurally or chromatically simple designs), reflected (a conventional gradient mirrored across an axis so it seems enclosed; middle has a dash of a different shade, same colour at start and end; used by premium brands such as the Audi emblem).
why: The type determines the visual effect: direction, focal glow, or enclosure.
check: CSS `linear-gradient` / `radial-gradient`; reflected = symmetrical stops (A, B, A).

text: Pick one light direction for the whole interface and keep it; every shadow's X/Y offset points the same way.
why: Mixed directions break the illusion of a single light source.
check: compare sign of offset-x/offset-y across all `box-shadow` values in the stylesheet; they must agree.

text: The higher an element is on the z-axis, the wider and more diffuse its shadow: raise blur and spread (and offset) with elevation.
why: Mimics real life: lifted objects cast larger, softer shadows.
check: shadow blur radius increases monotonically with layer level (card < dropdown < modal).

text: Treat X, Y and Blur as the three values that matter most; spread is a refinement. A negative spread makes the shadow look cast by a smaller piece (e.g. Y 20, Blur 0, Spread -10 shows a thinner crescent than Spread 0).
why: These three drive the look and are the first to tune.
check: visual.

text: Blur 0 gives a hard edge; N blur spreads N pixels in and out from the shadow's edge, and higher values give larger and more diffuse shadows.
why: Definition of the blur property.
check: `box-shadow` blur-radius value.

text: Hard offset-only shadows (blur 0) are an available style: offsets of 2 in each axis produce an edge/outline-like shadow on one or two sides; the six combinations are (0,2), (2,0), (2,2), (0,-2), (-2,0), (-2,-2). Multiple shadows can be stacked on one object, e.g. three hard shadows at Y 4, 8 and 12 in progressively darker tones (blue, light blue, orange in the figure) for a layered, extruded look.
why: "Very intriguing effects" via stacking.
check: `box-shadow` list with several layers.

text: Default to outer (drop) shadows for elevation; a standard one uses an offset (x, y or both from the centre), a blur and an opacity.
why: It is the most frequent UI effect and matches stacked layers.
check: `box-shadow` without `inset`.

text: Use inner shadows only for form inputs (fields, checkboxes, radio buttons) and for extruded objects in neumorphism, and sparingly.
why: Most interfaces are layers piled on one another, so an outer shadow makes sense; an inner shadow breaks the structure of the stack by suggesting a hole.
check: `box-shadow: inset` appears only on input-like components.

text: Use shadows to show interactivity: on hover a button gets a shadow to stand out from the background; on press/tap the shadow gets smaller (the element "pushes down"), the way a real button's height falls and its shadow shrinks.
why: Feedback that the action was carried out.
check: `:hover` has a larger/stronger shadow; `:active` has a smaller shadow than default state.

text: When stacking components on top of each other (flat style excepted), separate them with shadows on the z-axis: dropdowns and modals appear "above" page content while remaining distinct from inputs under them.
why: Layering by depth.
check: overlays (menu, popover, modal) have a shadow; page layer doesn't.

text: Use stacking order plus shadow to set visual hierarchy: decide what the user should focus on first and put it on top, with a shadow per layer; especially for menus appearing above content in mobile apps, and for items you want engaged with such as cookie or privacy notices.
why: Users attend to objects in the order depth presents them.
check: the topmost layer has the strongest shadow.

text: Never ship the design tool's default shadow (Sketch, Figma, Adobe XD alike); always alter it.
why: Default presets look dated; custom ones look "sleek and contemporary".
check: no `box-shadow: 0 2px 4px rgba(0,0,0,.5)`-style defaults (the book's "bad" example: X0, Y2, Blur 4, 50% opacity).

text: Make shadows softer: opacity 10-30% and blur 16px-40px. Book example (good): X 0, Y 8, Blur 24, 25% opacity; (bad): X 0, Y 2, Blur 4, 50% opacity.
why: Gentle shadows are generally the most attractive.
check: parse `box-shadow`: alpha in [0.10, 0.30], blur in [16px, 40px] for card/overlay elevations.

text: Consider building the shadow as a separate layer with a blur effect instead of a standard shadow style when you want to stand out; this gives more control over the shadow's position and size.
why: Layer shadow lets you offset/scale freely beyond the shadow-style limits.
check: visual.

text: Do not use pure grey shadows (except in a pure black-white theme); tint the shadow with the neutral colour of the UI's tone. Book example on a slate card: X 0, Y 16, Blur 40, #758EFE at 20% opacity.
why: Real-world shadows always carry a faint colour.
check: shadow colour has chroma > 0 (not r=g=b) unless the theme is pure black/white.

text: Take shadow colour from the object's material: semi-transparent real-world objects transfer their colour to their shadow, so use the object's own colour tones, including a gradient shadow/fill (example: #758EFE 100% to #495A7C 100%) to convey material.
why: Makes the object look physical and "brand new".
check: visual.

text: Observe real materials and light: look at the hues, blurring and angles of the shadows they cast, and borrow them. Example: neumorphic pair Light shadow X -4, Y -4, Blur 10, 13% and Dark shadow X 4, Y 4, Blur 10, 10%.
why: Exceptional results come from observation, not defaults.
check: visual.

text: A thin dark shadow can be swapped for a coloured diffuse one to make an interface more entertaining; experiment with settings to see how they change the mood.
why: Shadow colour/softness sets tone.
check: visual.

text: If using neumorphism: background colour must equal element colour; apply a light shadow at upper-left and a dark shadow at lower-right (light X -4, Y -4, Blur 10, Opacity 13%; dark X 4, Y 4, Blur 10, Opacity 10%), so the light source reads as upper-left and elements seem to emerge from the surface instead of floating.
why: Stacked shadows with negative X/Y create the extruded look.
check: two `box-shadow` layers with mirrored offsets and background-color equals element background-color.

text: Choose the right blur: background blur softens only what is behind the element (the element's own edge stays razor-sharp); layer blur blurs the whole element, including its edges and its background. Use layer blur to make a background element disappear so attention goes elsewhere, or as a decoration.
why: Different effects (frosted panel vs soft/vanishing object).
check: CSS `backdrop-filter: blur()` (background blur) vs `filter: blur()` (layer blur).

text: Use blur to focus attention: when a modal or mobile navigation opens, blur the existing background so attention goes to the opened item (iOS Control Center is the reference: the opened item is sharp, the background is blurred).
why: The most common use of blur in interface design.
check: modal/sheet overlay has `backdrop-filter`.

text: For text over images or video use either a hard background (good for subtitles) or a blurred background; a blur keeps the aesthetic without compromising accessibility, but the images behind the blur must share a similar colour palette, since text may be invisible on a blurred very dark or very light background.
why: Blur reduces detail noise under text but not luminance extremes.
check: contrast of text vs average of blurred region (4.5:1 body text is an [engine note]).

text: Blur background images in hero sections so imagery doesn't steal focus from graphic elements laid on top; also valid in animations and abstract elements.
why: Decorative but must not damage usability.
check: visual.

text: Do user research: find out what the target audience wants before designing.
why: Design decisions need a stated audience need behind them.
check: visual/process: brief states audience and needs.
section: Hard skills (definitions the book gives, p.577-578)

text: Do information architecture: structure data logically, including navigation, labelling and search tools.
why: Content must be findable before it is styled.
check: every nav/label/search has a defined place in the IA; visual.
section: Hard skills (definitions the book gives, p.577-578)

text: Wireframe (a blueprint of each screen) then prototype (testing the product's functionality) before final visuals.
why: Structure and function are validated cheaply before polish.
check: process.
section: Hard skills (definitions the book gives, p.577-578)

text: Command visual communication: images, typography, layout, icons, colour, design theory.
why: It is the craft layer of UI.
check: visual.
section: Hard skills (definitions the book gives, p.577-578)

text: Be able to state the reasoning behind every design decision, clearly and "boldly", to team members and clients.
why: "No one knows your thoughts better than you"; a good idea with no explanation fails in the presentation.
check: each output includes a short rationale (engine: attach "why" to each design choice).

text: Build empathy: understand the client's and user's wishes, needs, emotions, goals and thoughts, and fold those insights into the design so the result is relevant and useful.
why: A product cannot meet goals the designer does not grasp.
check: process: brief lists user needs.

text: Learn user needs through user interviews, usability testing, surveys, and observation.
why: These are the book's "greatest ways" to get at needs.
check: process.

text: Pursue unique ideas ("go outside the box") and see everyday objects in new ways; refine creativity by keeping up with current trends and being inspired by other designers' work.
why: Technical skill can be taught; originality is the scarce, sought-after skill, and it improves with exposure.
check: visual: compare against recent output for sameness.

text: Treat design as problem-solving: understand the exact brief, try options, pick the optimal solution after trial and error, address difficulties "from all perspectives", and stay calm when problems appear unexpectedly.
why: Design exists to make things run smoothly and easily for end users.
check: process.

text: Stay open-minded and adaptable: take on new ideas and others' opinions, adopt new design trends quickly, and expect clients to add requirements or change everything.
why: Narrow-mindedness blocks finding answers or excellent designs.
check: process.

text: Be passionate: a lack of interest "immediately reflects in the design of a product".
why: Careers include difficult workloads, strange hours, and heavy criticism; enthusiasm and desire to learn sustain quality.
check: n/a (opinion).

text: Accept constructive criticism and adapt designs in response to input; a flawless design does not exist.
why: There are no defined algorithms or mathematics for design and people's goals and requirements keep changing.
check: process: iteration log shows changes made from feedback.

text: Keep a list of apps/sites with outstanding UI and some with awful UI, and write down specifically why for each.
why: Making the unconscious map explicit turns taste into reusable principles.
check: process: list exists with a reason per entry.

text: Weekly: list **5 good-UI sites/apps and 1-2 bad-UI ones**, with the explanation in your own words.
why: It trains judgement of what works and what does not.
check: count = 5 good + 1-2 bad.

text: When collecting references, stay in your own field (e.g. a product designer working on data-heavy UI should seek data-heavy UI references).
why: Context-matched examples transfer; others do not.
check: visual.
source: (p.592; OCR on that page is garbled around this sentence, wording is from image: "it's important to note though, that in this exercise you should seek references from your field of work. If you're a product designer working with data-heavy UI.")

text: Agreement with the author is not the point; understanding why you feel the way you do is. Generalise each observation into a design philosophy you can reuse.
why: Principles generalise, opinions do not.
check: visual.

text: Reproduce an excellent existing design pixel-for-pixel in your design tool.
why: It forces you to redo every decision (typeface, size, layout, graphics, backgrounds, decoration), exposing choices you would not have made and tricks you would not have noticed by looking.
check: process.

text: Choose what to copy by what you want to improve: insane gradients or a bright palette for colour use; a prestigious "ritzy" site for premium branding; or copy very specific parts.
why: Targeted copying fills known gaps.
check: process.

text: Weekly: copy the UI of a decent site/app pixel-for-pixel, then write down the particular approaches the author used "to increase your design vocabulary". May be done as a **30-minute daily activity** instead of all at once.
why: Tracked uppercase gives a strong sense of alignment and "classiness" (the author notes he feels self-conscious doing it often).
check: `text-transform: uppercase` elements have positive `letter-spacing`.
source: (p.600) - Meta-lesson: the author had seen the design and thought it looked fantastic but did not internalise its techniques until replicating it (p.600-601).

text: Build a personal list of good fonts organically as you meet them in real sites/apps, not by Googling "best fonts" lists.
why: Lists with more than about 10 recommendations drift into niche-use or sub-par typefaces.
check: process.

text: For each font record: **font name; website/app it was found on; usages it would be good for (body font, title font, certain types of brands, etc.); a screenshot of it in use (especially if you cannot download it); price.**
why: Re-findable, usage-tagged knowledge makes selection fast later.
check: each entry has those 5 fields.

text: Organise fonts in a font manager (FontBase, cross-platform; or Font Book on Mac) into groups such as "Brush" or "Chunky heavyweights"; use multiple groupings for different font types and usage concepts.
why: Quick comparison and retrieval.
check: process.

text: If a font you like is free, download it immediately; keep fonts on hand and compare a paragraph of body text in font A vs font B as quickly as possible.
why: You must try a font to know if it fits; you will not want to download a thousand fonts noted last year at project start.
check: process.
source: (p.604-605) - Claim: "web design is 90% typography" may be an exaggeration but typography is an important talent; choosing from thousands of fonts is the easy part, styling them correctly is "far more difficult - and much more important" (p.602). Weekly: list fonts you enjoy, with when they work and where you saw them (p.605).

text: Use style tiles: small artboards showing the brand aspects under consideration (font, colour, form controls, logo). They preview the feel, not the final product, and are brief one-off explorations of one UI concept.
why: Cheap, concrete, debatable. A client and designer can say what is working and what is not "from a notion like this" instead of talking about brand in broad terms.
applies: landing page | SaaS app UI (brand direction).
check: artifact exists.
source: (p.605-609) - Style tile ingredients from the author's finance example (p.607-609): - **Logo**: for a first iteration just make a simple text wordmark (author tried about "a third of a dozen" = 4 typeface/style options, settled on Museo bold, a quirky sans that resembles a serif when small). (opinion: "for beginners, it'll suffice") - **Colors**: blue is the dull, predictable bank colour; the brief was "anything but blue". The author picked colours of **euro bills** because they read as "financial/money" yet are not blue. Logos of Merrill Lynch, Prudential, Barclays, Bank of America, Citi, Chase were shown as the blue-heavy pattern to avoid. - **Snippets of UI elements**: show a sample of items that may appear on the site (stock chart, user-submitted stock-tip card), not a full style guide. A button is typically one of the first things put on a style tile. **"Cards should be neat"** (the author regrets a dirty tan card colour). - **Font**: PT Sans, called a high-quality, free, underutilised Google Font. - **Copy snippet**: use real language that could appear on the site (e.g. "3 clicks and no hidden fees", a casual user-submitted stock tip) because how the site communicates is part of the brand.

text: The brief behind the example: finance platform where people feel comfortable depositing large sums, but "not anything too generic", must not look as tech-illiterate as a typical bank, must stand out (p.605).
why: Trust plus differentiation is the design tension for fintech.
check: visual.

text: Practise style tiles as a personal exercise: low-risk, quick, easy to try; no approval, UX limits, budget or bureaucracy. Example recipe: "perfect for a premium brand" font + classy Unsplash photographs + grayscale + gold, then play.
why: Fast idea/implement/assess cycles accelerate learning.
check: process.

text: Weekly: create **2-3 style tiles** for fonts in your database. Think of a site concept, then design a tile with: realistic font choices and text elements (headers, navigation, body text); an appropriate colour palette; example form controls or imagery; a logo (optional).
why: Applies the font collection in context.
check: tile contains those 3 required + 1 optional items.
source: (p.611) - Colour proportion figure (p.608): a bar labelled **60% Primary Colour, 30% Secondary Colour, 10% Accent Colour** (dark slate, periwinkle blue, light sky blue), captioned "Thinking outside the box for color palette inspiration" and introduced by "I notice pattern here" about the bank logos. The text does not name it the 60-30-10 rule or give application guidance; it is shown as the proportion pattern in the palette.

text: Do personal projects: unpaid, with you alone having complete creative control. Forms: build an app you wish existed; remodel an existing app/site you believe could be better; create a site for a non-profit/charity (you may send it to them).
why: Removes real-world constraints so you learn faster.
check: process.

text: Choose a project whose success criterion is "do I think it looks beautiful?" rather than one with a partner's heavy feedback.
why: With a partner you must also understand their feedback and converge on something both like, much harder for a beginner. The author notes (humorously) that the real world is not like this; it is a learning exercise.
check: process.

text: A good starting point: take a style tile you enjoyed and turn it into a fuller app/site.
why: Builds on work already done.
check: process.
source: (p.613) - Three scope levels, deciding how much design to finish before diminishing returns (p.613-614): 1. **Self-study project**: only for your education; may skip much of UX and real-world business limits; focus on visual skills (colour, font). Design the **primary screens** only: homepage, profiles, dashboards, feeds, articles (where users spend most time). 2. **Portfolio project**: design the entire app, including auxiliary experiences: **error states, loading pages, first-time-use flows**, etc. 3. **Real app/site**: if you or a partner can develop, it may become real; at that point "graduate to a real curriculum".

text: Weekly: design **1-3 screens** of the app/site you most want to work on using the style tiles from Exercise 4.
why: Ties together noted design details, lessons from copywork, collected fonts and styles.
check: 1-3 screens exist.
source: (p.614-615) - Closing: practise each exercise weekly; practice is the key (p.615).

text: Stage 1, Product Definition: gather user needs in the business context and inform UI/UX designers of the requirements **before** work begins. Design Team, Business Manager and Product Manager are all active; the whole team consults clients in their own surroundings; examine requirements within the context of the business.
why: This is when "the true extent of the product and its existence is realised".
check: a written brief with requirements exists before design starts.

text: Product Definition deliverables: **User Personas, User Stories, Use Case Diagrams.**
why: They fix who the users are and what they do.
check: the three artifacts exist.

text: Stage 2, Research (called "the most important aspect" for a designer): investigate how the current system functions for the customer proposal. Three primary functions: know what the competition is about; examine your current domain thoroughly; examine competitor strategy "to see what happens". Include the newest UI/UX trends, design principles and guidelines.
why: Design decisions need market and domain grounding.
check: competitor and domain notes exist.

text: Stage 3, Analysis: use the research to create **hypothetical personas** (to understand the types of people who will use the product and allow an accurate portrayal of the final product) and **user experience maps** (depict the flow of users through the final product, via visual representations and correct interactions with clients during product definition).
why: Turns raw research into usable models.
check: personas and a user flow/experience map exist.

text: Stage 4, Design: this is where final graphics begin. Key outcomes, in order: **Sketching** (hand-drawn sketches to visualise concepts simply, then pick one option); **Wireframes** (visual representation of page hierarchy and product aspects, the "backbone"/"skeleton" of the design, largely about overall appearance); **Prototypes** (look and feel and interaction experience, "similar to that of a simulator"); **Design specifications** (user flow and task flow diagrams, the overall working and stylistic requirements, procedures and graphical aspects).
why: Each step narrows from idea to buildable detail.
check: sketch, wireframe, prototype and spec artifacts.

text: Stage 5, Validation and Testing: testers list items needing improvement and send them back to the responsible team to fix. Distinguish **User Testing ("Do users need my app?")** from **Usability Testing ("Can users use my app?")**.
why: They answer two different questions: demand vs ease of use.
check: both questions were asked.

text: Final review checklist, four questions: Is the system **simple to use**? Is it **adaptable and simple to use** (sic; OCR/image both read this, apparently meaning adaptable/flexible)? Is it **effective in resolving the customer's problem**? Is it **trustworthy, and does it entice users to return** every time they need your services?
why: Covers ease, flexibility, effectiveness, and trust/retention.
check: answer all four per delivery.

text: Use a systematic, planned strategy (a UI/UX design process plan) to produce excellent interfaces.
why: Avoids repeated remodelling.
check: process.

text: Write content in plain language at about an 8th-grade reading level and avoid figures of speech, idioms and complicated metaphors.
why: Reading-level support (WCAG 3.1.5, AAA in WCAG itself though listed on the checklist).
check: run a readability formula (Flesch-Kincaid) on body copy blocks; flag grade > 9.

text: Link, button and label text is unique and descriptive within a page; no "click here" or "read more" alone.
why: Screen-reader users navigate by lists of links and buttons, where the text must stand alone.
check: collect accessible names of `a, button, label`; flag names in {click here, read more, learn more, here, more} and groups of identical names pointing at different hrefs.
source: a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Content ("Make sure that button, a, and label element content is unique and descriptive"), WCAG 1.3.1.

text: Left-align running text for left-to-right languages (right-align for RTL); do not centre or justify long text.
why: Centred and justified text is harder to read (WCAG 1.4.8).
check: computed `text-align` of paragraphs longer than 200 characters is `start`/`left`/`right` (not `center`, `justify`).

text: Validate HTML (no parsing errors such as duplicate ids, broken nesting).
why: Consistent AT behaviour; the checklist cites 4.1.1 (note: WCAG 2.2 removed 4.1.1 as obsolete [unverified, from my knowledge of WCAG 2.2]).
check: W3C Nu validator run: zero errors; duplicate `id` count 0.

text: Set `lang` on `<html>`.
why: Screen readers pick the right pronunciation (WCAG 3.1.1).
check: `document.documentElement.lang` matches `^[a-z]{2,3}(-[A-Za-z0-9]+)*$`.

text: Give every page or view a unique `<title>`.
why: It is often the first thing announced (WCAG 2.4.2).
check: `document.title` non-empty; across crawled routes titles are unique.

text: Do not disable viewport zoom, even in app-like web apps.
why: Text resize support (WCAG 1.4.4); native apps also respect OS text-size.
check: viewport meta has no `user-scalable=no` and no `maximum-scale` below 5.
source: a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Global code ("Ensure that viewport zoom is not disabled"). The "below 5" threshold is mine [unverified].

text: Use landmark elements for the main regions: `header`, `nav`, `main`, `footer` (and `aside`, `form`/`section` with names where needed).
why: Landmarks give screen-reader users quick region jumps (WCAG 4.1.2 per the checklist).
check: exactly one `main`; each `nav` has distinct `aria-label` if more than one; `header`/`footer` present at page level.

text: Keep a linear content flow: remove any `tabindex` value other than `0` or `-1`, and do not put tabindex on natively focusable elements.
why: Positive tabindex breaks natural order (WCAG 2.4.3).
check: `[tabindex]` whose value > 0: count 0; `a[href][tabindex], button[tabindex="0"]` count 0.
source: a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Global code ("Ensure a linear content flow").

text: Avoid the `autofocus` attribute.
why: Moving focus without permission disorients blind and low-vision users and burdens motor-impaired users (WCAG 2.4.3).
check: `[autofocus]` count 0 outside single-purpose input screens.
source: a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Global code ("Avoid using the autofocus attribute"). Conflicts with Vercel AGENTS.md; see section 5.

text: Let users extend, adjust, or turn off session timeouts well before they expire.
why: WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable.
check: if a session timeout exists: a warning dialog with an extend action appears before expiry.
source: a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Global code ("Allow extending session timeouts").

text: Remove `title` attribute tooltips as carriers of important information; legitimate use is naming an `iframe`.
why: `title` has poor keyboard, touch and AT support.
check: `[title]` on elements other than `iframe`, `abbr`, SVG `<title>`: count 0 where the text is not duplicated visibly.
source: a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Global code ("Remove title attribute tooltips").

text: Every interactive element shows a visible focus style when reached by keyboard.
why: Keyboard, switch, voice and screen-reader users must see where they are (WCAG 2.4.7).
check: Tab through the page; for each focused element, computed `outline-style != none` or `box-shadow != none` or border/background changes versus unfocused; screenshot diff of the element.
source: a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Keyboard and > Controls ("Ensure that controls have :focus states").

text: Keyboard focus order matches the visual order.
why: Meaningful sequence (WCAG 1.3.2).
check: list focused elements in Tab order with `getBoundingClientRect`; sorted by top then left, they should be mostly monotonic (flag reversals greater than 1 row).

text: Elements not currently discoverable (closed dropdowns, off-screen navigation, inactive modals) are not focusable (`display:none`, `hidden`, `inert`, or `visibility:hidden`).
why: Invisible focus stops confuse keyboard users (WCAG 2.4.3).
check: during a full Tab traversal, every stop has a non-zero visible rect within the viewport (after scrolling) and `elementFromPoint` hits it.

text: Every `img` has an `alt` attribute.
why: Without it a screen reader may read the file name (WCAG 1.1.1).
check: `img:not([alt])` count 0.

text: Decorative images use a null `alt=""`.
why: Hides noise from AT.
check: images inside buttons or links with adjacent text, or purely visual flourishes, have `alt=""` (and `role` not set).

text: Complex images (charts, graphs, maps) have a text alternative that describes axes, data points, labels and the overall point.
why: The whole visible message must exist as text.
check: each chart `svg`/`canvas`/`img` has an adjacent table, `aria-describedby`, or long description; non-empty.

text: For images that contain text, the `alt` includes that text (for example a logo with the word FedEx has `alt="FedEx"`).
why: Text content must not be trapped in pixels.
check: compare OCR or known logo text to `alt`; visual.

text: Use heading elements to introduce content, not for visual styling.
why: Headings build the document outline (WCAG 2.4.6).
check: every `h1-h6` is followed by content of the section it introduces; no heading used for large decorative text.

text: Use exactly one `h1` per page or view, describing the page's purpose; do not use `h1` for a fixed site name that does not change across pages.
why: Orientation.
check: `document.querySelectorAll('h1').length === 1` and its text differs from the site name on inner pages.

text: Headings follow a logical, descending sequence and never skip a level (no `h2` straight to `h4`); if a visual size is wanted, use a CSS class, not a different level.
why: Outline integrity.
check: iterate headings in DOM order: `level[i] - level[i-1] <= 1`.

text: Use list elements (`ul`, `ol`, `dl`) for list-like content, including card grids and sibling link groups.
why: Announces item count and relationship (WCAG 1.3.1).
check: runs of >= 3 sibling `a` or `li`-like elements outside a `ul/ol` flagged (nav link rows, card grids).

text: Use `a` with an `href` for links (including in SPAs); use `button` for actions (add `type="button"` where it must not submit a form).
why: Correct role and keyboard behaviour (WCAG 1.3.1).
check: `a:not([href])` count 0; `[onclick]` on `div/span` without role/tabindex count 0; `button` in a form without `type` flagged.

text: Links are recognisable as links without colour alone; underlines are the common, understood signal.
why: WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color.
check: in-text `a` computed `text-decoration-line: underline`, or non-colour cue plus 3:1 contrast against surrounding text.
source: a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Controls ("Ensure that links are recognizable as links") and > Appearance ("Make sure color isn't the only way information is conveyed").

text: Provide a skip link as the first focusable element, hidden until focused, that moves to the `main` content.
why: Bypass repeated navigation (WCAG 2.4.1).
check: first Tab stop is `a[href^="#"]` whose target exists and is `main` or contained in it; it is visible (non-zero rect, not clipped) when focused.
source:
a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Controls; /posts/skip-nav-links/ (example: `Skip to main content` before `nav`, with `
`).

text: Skip links work in Webkit: if the target is not natively focusable, add `tabindex="-1"` to it (older Webkit builds failed to move focus).
why: Focus must actually land at the target.
check: after activating the skip link, `document.activeElement` is or is within `main`.

text: Identify links that open in a new tab or window in the link text or an accessible label; ideally avoid them.
why: Advance warning of context change (technique G201; not strictly required for conformance).
check: `a[target=_blank]` has text or visually hidden text matching /new (tab|window)/i and `rel` includes `noopener`.

text: Use `table` for tabular data, `th` for headers (with `scope="col"` or `scope="row"` as complexity requires), and `caption` as the table's title.
why: AT relies on header associations and a caption (WCAG 1.3.1, 2.4.6).
applies: SaaS app UI | landing page (pricing tables).
check: each `table` has `caption` (or `aria-label`), `th` cells in header row/column, `scope` on `th`; no layout tables (`table` without any `th`).

text: Associate every input with a `label` using a `for`/`id` pair (highest support).
why: Name and larger click target (the checklist maps this to 3.2.2; 1.3.1 and 4.1.2 are the usual criteria [unverified mapping]).
check: each `input, select, textarea` (excluding hidden/submit) has `labels.length > 0` or `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby`; `label[for]` ids resolve.

text: Group related inputs in `fieldset` with a `legend` (radio groups, address blocks).
why: Group name is announced for each control.
check: radio/checkbox groups with the same `name` sit inside `fieldset > legend`.

text: Use `autocomplete` tokens on inputs asking for common personal data.
why: WCAG 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose.
check: fields for name, email, tel, address, card have valid `autocomplete` tokens.

text: After submit, list all errors in a block above the form with a link to each invalid field.
why: Quick overview, especially for long forms (WCAG 3.3.1).
check: submit invalid form: container with a list of `a[href^="#"]` exists, count equals invalid fields, each target id resolves.

text: Connect each error message to its input with `aria-describedby` (and set `aria-invalid`).
why: AT users hear the error with the field.
check: invalid inputs have `aria-describedby` that resolves to an element with the error text.

text: Error, warning and success states are not communicated by colour alone (add icon plus text).
why: Colour-blind and low-vision users (WCAG 1.4.1).
check: each state style (`.error`, `.success`) includes visible text or icon, not only border or background colour change.

text: Media does not autoplay.
why: Distracting for ADHD, can trigger vestibular and seizure disorders (WCAG 1.4.2).
check: `video[autoplay], audio[autoplay]` count 0, or muted, decorative and with a pause control.

text: Media controls use appropriate markup: a mute button exposes a pressed state (`aria-pressed`), a volume control is `input type=range`.
why: Roles and states (WCAG 1.3.1).
check: toggle buttons have `aria-pressed`; volume slider is an `input[type=range]`.

text: All media can be paused, with Space toggling playback when the player has focus, without breaking Space-scroll elsewhere.
why: WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard.
check: focus the player, press Space: playback toggles; focus body and press Space: page scrolls.

text: Videos have captions; audio has transcripts.
why: WCAG 1.2.2 Captions; transcripts for audio content (listed under 1.1.1 by the checklist).
check: `video` contains `track[kind="captions"]`; audio players have an adjacent transcript link.

text: Remove seizure triggers: nothing flashes more than three times per second.
why: WCAG 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold.
check: animation review for high-contrast flicker; `animation-duration` under 333 ms with infinite iteration on large areas flagged.
source: a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Video, > Animation. The 333 ms heuristic is mine [unverified].

text: Content stays legible and complete at 200% text size, with no overlap.
why: WCAG 1.4.4 Resize text.
check: set root font-size to 200% (or browser zoom 200%) at 1280 px width: no clipped text, no overlapping boxes (`scrollWidth > clientWidth + 1` on text elements flagged).

text: Check the page in specialised modes (Windows high contrast or forced colours, inverted colours): foreground still separable from background, and icons, borders, links and form fields still present.
why: WCAG 1.4.1.
check: emulate `forced-colors: active` (Playwright `forcedColors: 'active'`); buttons, inputs, focus rings and icons remain visible.

text: Keep related content close together so zoomed and magnified users can find everything (the "straw test").
why: WCAG 1.3.3.
check: visual at 400% zoom: labels remain adjacent to their controls.

text: Instructions never rely on sensory characteristics alone (position such as "on the right", or sound such as "after the tone"); name the element.
why: WCAG 1.3.3.
check: grep copy for /\b(on the (left|right)|above|below|after the tone|the (red|green) button)\b/.

text: Use a simple, consistent layout that reflows without a complicated structure.
why: WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow.
check: at 320 CSS px width there is no horizontal scroll (`scrollWidth <= clientWidth`).
source: a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Appearance ("Use a simple, straightforward, and consistent layout") and > Mobile and touch ("Remove horizontal scrolling"). The 320 px figure is WCAG's, not stated on the page [unverified on page].

text: Keep animations subtle and non-flashing.
why: WCAG 2.3.1.
check: see A11Y-40.

text: Provide a way to pause background video.
why: WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide.
check: hero or background `video` has a visible pause button reachable by keyboard.

text: All animation obeys `prefers-reduced-motion`; remove it when reduce is on, and if motion is essential to meaning, slow its duration down.
why: WCAG 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions.
check: with `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` emulated, computed `animation-name` is `none` and `transition-duration` is 0s (or longer-slower variant) on animated elements.
source: a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Animation; /posts/operating-system-and-browser-accessibility-display-modes/ (example uses `animation: none` inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`).

text: Normal-size text contrast is at least 4.5:1 (AA); the AAA level is 7:1.
why: WCAG 1.4.3.
check: compute luminance ratio per text node against its effective background (including images and gradients); fail < 4.5.

text: Large text contrast is at least 3:1; large means 18pt regular or 14pt bold and above.
why: Larger and heavier strokes stay legible at lower contrast.
check: font-size >= 24 CSS px (18pt), or >= 18.66 CSS px (14pt) with weight >= 700: threshold 3:1; otherwise 4.5.
source: a11yproject.com/checklist/ > Color contrast; /posts/what-is-color-contrast/ (18pt regular or 14pt bold).

text: Icons and input borders (text inputs, radios, checkboxes) have at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colours.
why: WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast.
check: compute ratio of input border colour versus surface, and meaningful icon fill versus surface: >= 3.

text: Text overlapping images or video stays legible; custom `::selection` colours also meet contrast; form placeholders also meet contrast.
why: WCAG 1.4.3.
check: sample the worst-case background under text at 9 points and compute ratio; check `::selection` pair; placeholder colour >= 4.5 on field background.

text: The site works in any orientation (not portrait-locked).
why: WCAG 1.3.4.
check: screenshots at 390x844 and 844x390; no orientation lock in the manifest or CSS.

text: Icon buttons and links (hamburger menus, social icons, gallery controls) are large enough to activate with ease for a range of hand and stylus sizes.
why: WCAG 2.5.5 Target Size per the checklist (the 2.2 AA criterion is 2.5.8, 24 px minimum).
check: target sizes >= 44x44 CSS px comfortable, 24x24 minimum. The page itself gives no pixel number [unverified on page].

text: Leave enough space between adjacent interactive items so users can start a scroll gesture without hitting a control (hand tremors).
why: Zero-gap stacks of controls make scrolling hazardous.
check: vertical gap between adjacent tappable rows >= 8 px [unverified threshold, mine].

text: Support dark mode with `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`; support users who set it at the OS.
why: Eye strain and photosensitivity.
check: emulate `prefers-color-scheme: dark`: body background and text computed colours change and pass contrast.

text: Where images or video are re-inverted for the inverted-colours mode, do it with `@media (inverted-colors: inverted) { img, video { filter: invert(100%) } }`.
why: Keeps photos natural while the UI inverts.
check: emulate or toggle inverted colours: photos look natural (visual).
source: /posts/operating-system-and-browser-accessibility-display-modes/ > Inverted Colors Mode. Safari already inverts images itself (per the post).

text: Semantic HTML gets High Contrast Mode support automatically; tweak with the `forced-colors` media query (the post names the old `-ms-high-contrast` for IE and notes Chromium Edge uses `forced-colors`).
why: Custom backgrounds and icons vanish under forced colours.
check: `forced-colors: active` emulation: controls keep borders (use `border: 1px solid transparent` or `outline` so something paints), SVG icons use `currentColor`.
source: /posts/operating-system-and-browser-accessibility-display-modes/ > High Contrast Mode. The post dates from 2020; `forced-colors` is now the standard path [unverified current status].

text: Several modes may be active at once (reduced motion, increased contrast, dark); test combinations.
why: Users configure devices to suit them.
check: run the audit with dark + reduced-motion + forced-colors toggled together.

text: Choose the element by outcome: navigation to a URL (including an in-page anchor) is `<a href="real-url">`; changing something on the current page is `<button type="button">`; sending form data is `<button type="submit">` or `<input type="submit">` inside a `form`. A link with `href="#"` or no `href` is almost always a button in disguise.
why: Each element has different keyboard activation, context menu (open in new tab) and AT semantics; mixing breaks expectations (a quick test: would it make sense to open it in a new tab?).
check: `a:not([href])`, `a[href="#"]`, `a[href^="javascript:"]`, `a[role=button]`, `div[role=button]`, `span[onclick]` count 0 (`H5`); `button` used to navigate (`location=` in click handler) flagged for review.

text: Do not build a button from `div`/`span`/`a` plus `role="button"`. If you must, reproduce the native contract: focusable (`tabindex=0`), Enter fires on key down and repeats, Space fires on key up and cancels if focus leaves, Space must not scroll the page. Mixed native and custom controls on one page will feel inconsistent and may also look different in forced-colors.
why: Native buttons carry all those behaviours and platform styling for free; screen readers vary in how they synthesise Enter/Space.
check: `[role=button]:not(button,input)` count 0; if > 0 a keyboard test (Enter, Space press/release, hold) passes for each.

text: Treat ARIA as technical debt unless needed. Static roles (a `div role=heading aria-level`) are equivalent to HTML and low-risk; replacing interactive HTML (button, select, date input) with ARIA widgets requires knowing every interaction, platform gesture and high-contrast behaviour. Native `<select>` is easier and safer than an ARIA listbox; native date inputs have problems but most ARIA date pickers are worse.
why: E.g. dismissing a native select on mobile with a gesture, forced-colors styling, and keyboard repeat rules are all free in HTML.
check: `[role=listbox],[role=combobox],[role=slider]` presence is justified in the spec; `A1`.

text: Specs use precise pattern names. "Menu" may mean an ARIA application menu, `select`, listbox, combobox, datalist, disclosure widget, accordion, fly-out navigation, tree, popover or custom selector. Deprecated `<menu>`/`<menuitem>` should not be used. Ask what is meant and map it to one pattern.
why: Wrong vocabulary leads to the wrong element and keyboard model.
check: process: component spec names one of the patterns in `component-accessible-anatomy.md`; no `menuitem` element in markup.

text: For clickable cards/block links, do not wrap all content in one link. Link a concise element (the heading or the "Read more"), and extend the hit area with a positioned `::after` covering the card; leave a gap where extra controls (a second link or button) sit and give that control its own stacking. Accept that text selection is blocked in the card, or add a click-duration guard. For voice users the link name must be what they can see.
why: A whole-card link is announced as a long string (about 25 s in the demo), is announced as a link only after its name finishes, and when arrowing every fragment sounds like a separate link.
check: `a:has(h2,h3,p,img)` count 0; `::after` on card link covers the card; extra control hit-test returns itself.

text: Reordering a visual image above the heading with `order: -1` while keeping heading first in the DOM is one of the few justified uses of CSS reordering, because the image belongs to the heading's section. Always check with a reading-order tool.
why: Keeps heading structure meaningful.
check: `visual` + DOM order check (heading precedes image) for informative images.

text: Do not put headings, lists or other structured content inside a `<button>`; the structure is flattened. Dashboard cards that are buttons should contain short text only.
why: Button content is presented as a single string; the heading stops being a heading.
check: `button :is(h1,h2,h3,h4,h5,h6,ul,ol,table,p)` count 0.

text: Make table rows selectable or clickable through real controls in the row (a checkbox with `label`, a link, a button) and stretch its hit area with a `::after` positioned on the `tr`, not with a `click` handler on `tr` and not by converting the table to ARIA `grid`. As of 2026-10-07 the working form is `tr { position: relative }` with `th > label::after { position:absolute; inset:0 }` and no width hack in Chrome, Firefox and Safari 27.
why: Row click handlers make everything in the row announce as clickable and exclude keyboard users.
applies: admin tables, lists with row actions.
check: `tr[onclick],tr[role=button]` count 0; a checkbox/link exists per clickable row; hit-test centre of row cell returns the label/link.

text: There is no native toast. Map messages to ARIA live roles: `status` (polite, atomic) for FYI, `log` for ordered additions, `alert` (assertive, interrupts) for urgent, time-sensitive messages. The region must exist at page render. None of these roles supports rich content or interactive children; if a toast needs a button or structure, it is a (non-modal) dialog/alertdialog and needs focus management. Never move focus to a passive toast.
why: Live regions announce raw text; interrupting alerts strand the user mid-sentence.
check: `[role=status],[role=alert],[role=log]` present at load; `.toast :is(a,button,input)` implies `role=dialog|alertdialog` with focus handling; focus unchanged after a status toast appears.

text: Assume toasts will be missed (magnifier users, distraction, JS errors). Prefer static messages in a persistent region at the top of the page that users can dismiss; if you do use timed toasts, add a message holder (notification centre) or let users adjust or extend the duration, and do not place the container in the middle of the DOM. Reconsider whether the message is needed at all; error and status messages still have to meet 3.3.1, 3.3.3, 4.1.3.
why: Timed messages violate WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable unless adjustable, and non-persistent messages cannot be reviewed.
check: each auto-dismiss toast has either `duration` control, hover/focus pause, or a retrievable log (`[role=log]` or inbox); toast container is last in DOM or a landmark; close control, if present, >= 44 px.

text: Do not disable submit buttons or form fields in forms. Instead, leave the control enabled, and if input is invalid prevent default and show a polite message that names the problem; still protect against double submission on the server. Other buttons (outside gathering input) may be disabled when you explain why, but test with users. Disabled controls are exempt from contrast and invisible to keyboard and often to AT, so reasons stay hidden.
why: Disabled controls hide the reason, cannot be focused, and styles rarely distinguish them; read-only buttons are not a fix.
check: after page load and after typing invalid data: `form :is(button[type=submit],input[type=submit],input:not([type=hidden]),select,textarea)[disabled]` count 0; `button[disabled]` outside forms each have adjacent explanatory text (soft).
source: https://adrianroselli.com/2024/02/dont-disable-form-controls.html. [engine note] Conflicts with `S1`'s requirement that disabled states exist; see section 5.

text: Do not use ARIA `menu`, `menubar`, `menuitem`, `menuitemcheckbox`, `menuitemradio` or `aria-haspopup` for site navigation. Use `<nav>` with lists of links; add disclosure buttons for sub-lists. ARIA menus are for desktop-application-style command menus and restrict children (no links, headings, images), take over arrow keys and require Esc, Home/End, Shift+F10 support. The ARIA Authoring Practices guide is a note, not a standard, and its navigation menu pattern is disputed.
why: Screen readers switch interaction mode and tell users to expect keys that your page may not support; the top-level link stops being a link.
check: `A15` item 8: `nav [role=menu],nav [role=menubar],nav [role=menuitem]` count 0; `nav [aria-haspopup]` count 0.

text: Fly-out navigation pattern: top-level items are real links; an adjacent `<button type="button" aria-expanded aria-controls>` toggles the nested list; name the button from the link's visible text (`aria-labelledby` pointing at the link, not a compound name); mark the current page with `aria-current="page"` (and style from the attribute); Esc closes open sub-lists; clicking outside closes them; no `aria-haspopup`; never put `aria-expanded` on a link; show sub-items on child pages too so script failure does not strand users. For touch, use 44 px buttons.
why: Users tested the link-as-trigger variant as confusing for everyone; sub-pages must remain reachable without script.
check: `nav a[aria-expanded]` count 0; each `nav button[aria-expanded]` precedes or follows an `a` and has `aria-labelledby` referencing its text; Esc closes lists; `a[aria-current=page]` exactly one per nav level.
source: https://adrianroselli.com/2019/06/link-disclosure-widget-navigation.html. A 2026-07 update recommends reading "Link + Popover Navigation" (native `popover` + CSS anchor positioning); not read here.

text: A disclosure widget is a button with `aria-expanded` (true/false), optional `aria-controls`, and the content immediately after it in the DOM. Enter and Space toggle; do not move focus on open for simple disclosures. Hide with `display:none` only when `aria-expanded="false"` (`button[aria-expanded="false"] + div{display:none}`) so visual and programmatic state cannot disagree. Use native `<details>/<summary>` for simple summary-plus-detail cases. Esc and click-outside are extras for overlay-style disclosures (menu-like, popups), not for inline content.
why: Enforcing the visual off the state attribute keeps them in sync; moving focus on a simple toggle loses the user's place if they hit it by accident.
check: `A15` disclosure part; controlled element hidden iff `aria-expanded=false`; `aria-expanded` never on `a`.

text: Call something an accordion only if it is a group of disclosures with a group label (`role=group`/labelled `section`) in which one panel is open at a time (an "exclusive" accordion); keep one open on load. Use `<details name="group">` (supported in Chrome 120+) with a labelled wrapper. Optional: constrain panel height and scroll inside panels (then ensure keyboard access). A set of independent disclosures is just that, not an accordion. (opinion) The author considers accordions mostly slow for users.
why: Predictable semantics; fewer open panels, less page length.
check: `details[name]` groups share the same name; wrapper has accessible name; when one opens, siblings close.

text: Check focus visibility fully, not by a sliver: a focused control partly covered by a sticky footer technically passes 2.4.11 if a pixel row shows, but the control must be legible. Aim for the whole control visible, using `scroll-padding` and avoiding fixed overlays near focusable rows. Also apply text-spacing overrides to catch hidden buttons.
why: "Not entirely hidden" is a weak bar; adversarial layouts satisfy it uselessly.
check: `A5`: for each focusable, after `focus()` the bounding rect is entirely within the viewport minus fixed elements (not merely > 0 px).

text: Choose a toggle's element by behaviour: `<button aria-pressed>` when JavaScript is guaranteed, the effect is immediate, and there is no indeterminate state; `<input type="checkbox">` when it should progressively enhance, takes effect on submit, or can be indeterminate. A switch role affects the application immediately and must be explained in plain text; mis-modelling it can be a Level A failure.
why: Checkbox and switch semantics differ (submit vs immediate).
check: `[role=switch]` controls change app state on activation (not on submit); checkbox toggles inside forms.

text: Styling a checkbox as a toggle: hide the input visually (not `display:none`), draw track and thumb with `::before/::after`, size in `em` so it scales with text, keep colours at 3:1 or better for non-text (grey #767676 on white is 4.5:1, green #36a829 on white is 3:1), show focus and hover with more than colour (outline/shadow plus a dot on the thumb), style disabled and indeterminate states, add `prefers-reduced-motion`, `forced-colors`, dark scheme and RTL variants.
why: Custom toggles routinely lose state cues in high contrast and under zoom.
check: `A2` for track vs background (3:1); `A3`; forced-colors screenshot still shows on/off (`A18`).

text: Make interactive targets at least 44x44 CSS px (WCAG 2.5.5 AAA, Apple 44 pt, Android 48 dp with 8 px gaps, BBC 44 px recommended with 32 px minimum, Microsoft Fluent 40 epx, NN/g 1 cm) and leave dead space between neighbours; links inside text are exempt. WCAG 2.2 AA (2.5.8) requires only 24x24 or enough spacing. Test with a 44 px reference square on real devices (physical size varies with density).
why: Fitts's Law, motor and age-related tremors, one-handed use.
check: `L7` (24 px hard) and `L7b` (44 px on coarse pointer) with hit-test per control.

text: Do not use WCAG minimums as a licence to degrade usability: tiny dismiss buttons in a corner of a modal, 24 px close targets or controls hidden under fixed bars are "adversarial conformance". A close button that meets 24 px only by exception (spacing) should still be 44 px for modals and interstitials.
why: Conformance claims can hide user-hostile patterns.
applies: modals, banners, cookie notices, newsletter overlays.
check: `L7b` for modal close buttons >= 44 px; the close control sits within the first screenful and in DOM order near the start of the dialog.

text: A responsive table is a normal `table` inside a scrolling wrapper: `overflow: auto` on the wrapper, `tabindex="0"` so keyboard users can scroll it, a visible focus outline of at least 3:1, and (traditionally) `role="region"` plus `aria-labelledby` pointing at the caption. In October 2026 Roselli reported that the WCAG working group (AGWG) ruled that a focusable non-interactive element does not need a role or accessible name to pass 2.4.3/4.1.2, so `tabindex="0"` alone can be conformant; whether the role/name help your users is a testing question. Keep the wrapper selector tied to the required markup (`[tabindex]`) so unmarked wrappers do not clip content. Do not use scroll-snap on tables. Avoid nested scrollbars (table scrolling inside a scrolling dialog inside a scrolling page).
why: Prevents two-axis page scroll (1.4.10), keeps semantics, and keeps keyboard access. Snap caused straddling and clipped captions in testing. Android TalkBack once skipped tables inside `tabindex` parents (fixed in Chrome 91).
check: wrapper: `overflow-x:auto`, `tabindex=0` only when overflowing, focus outline contrast >= 3:1; `scroll-snap-type` on table wrapper = none; no ancestor scroll container also scrolling.

text: Do not change `display` on `table`, `tr`, `th`, `td` (block, flex, grid) to reflow tables; older browsers drop table semantics and adding `role="table"` back does not restore header relationships. Safari 17 stopped breaking tables and description lists, but `display: contents` on buttons still breaks keyboard and VoiceOver. If you reflow (stacked cells with generated column labels), add ARIA roles back (`table`, `row`, `cell`, `columnheader`) and accept lost features such as `headers` for spanning cells; prefer scrolling.
why: Screen readers lose the table; the sorting, headers and navigation commands vanish.
check: computed `display` of `table`, `thead`, `tbody`, `tr`, `th`, `td` at 320, 768, 1280 equals `table`, `table-header-group`, `table-row-group`, `table-row`, `table-cell`; if different then `role` attributes present.

text: Sortable table headers: `button` inside `th`; `aria-sort="ascending|descending"` only on the one sorted `th` (remove it from others rather than using `none`); communicate sort affordance with arrows that do not rely on colour alone (outline vs filled shapes), and highlight the sorted column (via `col` styling or `:has`); announce the change (a live region reading "sorted up/down" and clearing after about 1 s) because NVDA, TalkBack and macOS VoiceOver say nothing; use caption, visually hidden description or `aria-describedby` text to say the headers sort; avoid `aria-label` and `aria-roledescription` (translation, support). Build announcement strings from translatable content.
why: Announcement behaviour differs per screen reader; hints must survive translation.
check: after click: exactly one `th[aria-sort]`, others have no attribute; a live region receives text; arrows have non-colour difference (`A18`).

text: Do not use ARIA `grid` for ordinary tables, clickable rows, or lists of links. Grid is an interactive composite widget with one tab stop and arrow-key navigation, and layout-grid pattern examples were judged failing in testing; use `table` + buttons/links, lists with skip links, headings and landmarks for navigation shortcuts. Exception: Excel-like data editors.
why: Hidden keyboard model, brittle responsive behaviour, higher WCAG risk.
check: `[role=grid],[role=treegrid]` count 0 unless spec documents spreadsheet-style editing.

text: Prefer native `<dialog>` with `showModal()` (focus return, inert background, Esc, `aria-modal` equivalent come free). For custom `div role=dialog` you need an `inert` approach and manual focus return. Where initial focus goes is contextual: brief informational message without complexity - the close button is fine; long/complex/unexpected content or legal text - the dialog container or its heading (`tabindex="-1"`), never an "I agree" button; action required - the least destructive control (often Cancel/Close); brief form for a user who just chose to log in - the first field; long or unexpected forms, or on touch devices where a soft keyboard would cover the form - the dialog or heading. Always return focus to the invoker (or a sensible target if it is gone).
why: Focus placement decides what is announced and whether users can accidentally accept something; soft keyboards cover content.
check: `A15` plus per-type scripted assertion: initial `document.activeElement` is not a destructive action button; dialog has accessible name; `[role=dialog]:not(dialog)` count 0 in new code.

text: `dialog.showModal()` already gives modal semantics; do not add `aria-modal`. Do not combine the `popover` attribute with `div[role=dialog]` modals; a popover opens above and blocks a non-native modal, and Esc may close the wrong layer. If you use popovers, convert dialogs to `<dialog>` and test overlapping behaviour (top layer and inertness rules were still unsettled in late 2025).
why: Top-layer stacking can bury a time-out dialog behind a tooltip.
check: pages using `[popover]` have zero `[role=dialog]:not(dialog)`; opening a popover then a modal leaves the modal on top and focusable.

text: Decide dismissal by consequence. Action-required dialogs (legal agreement, safety acknowledgement, login within a protected page) do not close on outside click or Esc and may have no close button (consider a separate page). Informational and marketing dialogs (newsletter, offers, exit intent, sign-in prompts) must close on outside click, Esc and a large close button. Sheets, drawers and lightboxes: ask whether the user needs the occluded page, loses state on close, and how hard it is to restore. Prefer the least destructive outcome for dismissal.
why: Accidental or forced dismissal either loses work or traps the user.
check: classify each dialog in spec (required / informational); informational: Esc closes and focus returns; click outside closes; required: `dialog` has no close affordance but has primary action.

text: When a focused element is deleted or dismissed, move focus on purpose: to the preceding analogous control (previous delete button) when deleting from a group; to the group container (table wrapper, list, heading with `tabindex="-1"`) if the first item was deleted; to the control that had focus before a dismissed message appeared. Give destructive buttons item-specific names, avoid landing on a Delete button the user might double-activate unless confirmation exists, and do not rely on `:focus-visible` alone for the indicator.
why: Otherwise focus resets to the document and keyboard, magnifier and screen reader users lose position.
applies: delete, remove, dismiss, pagination edge cases.
check: Playwright: delete mid-list item - `document.activeElement` is the previous item's action button; delete first - container or heading; never `body`.

text: Avoid the browser's built-in validation bubbles. They show different text per browser, may not be announced, disappear (Chromium bubbles self-dismissed in about 5 s, fixed in 2024), do not scale with zoom, and `required`/`pattern` alone do not tell users the rule in text. Use `novalidate` and your own validation with visible messages, and state the required marker and format in the label or instructions. The author also states a rule against placing error messages under fields (see section 7).
why: WCAG 3.3.1/3.3.2/3.3.3 depend on persistent, accessible text.
check: `form:not([novalidate])` with `[required],[pattern]` flagged; `A10`; each required field's label text or description says it is required.

text: Expose field errors with `aria-invalid="true"` (set only after the user interacted or submitted, remove when valid) and associate the message with `aria-describedby`; a polite live region may announce on blur, an assertive one clips the next field's name. `aria-errormessage` is poorly supported (not announced when focusing or on blur); `aria-describedby` is announced consistently when navigating by field, with Chromium treating it as live (JAWS may read it twice). Expect VoiceOver on macOS and iPadOS to differ. Test with the pairings that matter.
why: Real support tests show `aria-describedby` is the dependable association.
check: `[aria-invalid=true]` has `aria-describedby` resolving to visible text; no field is `aria-invalid=true` on first load; no `aria-errormessage` without `aria-describedby`.

text: A required group of radio buttons: `required` is not valid on `fieldset`; use `role="radiogroup"` with `aria-required="true"` (and `aria-invalid` for errors); also say "required" in the group legend text. Support varies widely (TalkBack conveys nothing), so visible text is the baseline.
why: No native attribute for group required; AT support is inconsistent.
check: `fieldset[required]` count 0; `[role=radiogroup][aria-required]` present for required radio groups and the legend says "required".

text: Name controls in this order: native HTML (`<label for>` with a separate `id`, not an implicit wrapping label, because Dragon and Voice Control do not recognise wrapped labels), then `aria-labelledby` pointing at visible text (can join several ids to make unique names, e.g. in table cells), then visibly-hidden text (use the modern `.visually-hidden` clip pattern, not off-screen positioning), and `aria-label` last. `aria-label` is invisible to voice control, does not enlarge the hit area, is poorly auto-translated and overrides visible text in about a third of real-world uses; `aria-labelledby` overrides a `<label>`. Context may justify exceptions.
why: Internationalisation, voice access and consistency.
check: `[aria-label]` count tracked (soft cap); `[aria-label]` whose text does not contain the visible text fails `label-in-name` (axe); `label` wrapping an input without `for` flagged soft.

text: Do not put `aria-label` on links, do not wrap link text in `aria-hidden`, and do not split a word into one element per letter. Browser reader modes and text-to-speech tools ignore `aria-label` and drop `aria-hidden` content, and letter spans break translation and speech.
why: Non-screen-reader assistive tools (read aloud, reader mode, translation) consume visible text and the DOM, not ARIA names.
check: `a[aria-label]` count 0 (or each equals its visible text); `a [aria-hidden=true]` containing text count 0; letter-split animations (`span` per char) provide a whole-text alternative that remains in the DOM and are not inside links.

text: Do not rely on `<abbr title>` (or `title` in general) to explain abbreviations; exposure differs by browser, screen reader, touch, keyboard and voice access. Expand the term in text on first use, then use the short form.
why: Some users always miss the information.
check: `abbr[title]` flagged; first use of acronyms is expanded (`visual`/lint).

text: Never rely on the browser default focus ring; it vanishes against same-hue backgrounds (measured 1.02:1 to 1.8:1 in real sites) and textured backgrounds. Supply your own focus style with at least 3:1 contrast against the adjacent colours, test it on every surface colour (dark sections, brand blue buttons) and keep it visible in Windows High Contrast.
why: Default rings are tuned for white pages.
applies: all backgrounds, especially coloured CTAs and dark sections.
check: `A3`: for each focusable compute contrast of the indicator against both the element and its background >= 3:1, per section background; forced-colors check (`A18`).
source: https://adrianroselli.com/2017/02/avoid-default-browser-focus-styles.html. [engine note] A 2023 post by the same author warns against relying on `:focus-visible` alone (voice, touch and sighted screen reader users also need position cues); see section 5.

text: Let users enlarge text at least 200% without loss of content or function (use `rem`, flexible containers; do not lock zoom).
why: Apple's stated minimum (140% on watch).
check: Playwright at 200% zoom and at root font-size 32 px: no horizontal scroll at 1280 px, no clipped text.
origin: web:https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility (also inclusion, right-to-left, voiceover, keyboards, charting-data, charts; fetched 2026-10-08)

text: Meet contrast minimums: text up to 17 px 4.5:1; 18 px and larger 3:1; bold text 3:1 (WCAG AA mapping); if the default misses it, supply a higher-contrast scheme under `prefers-contrast: more`; check both light and dark.
why: Apple's audit thresholds.
applies: web: use WCAG's actual large-text definition (24 px regular, ~18.7 px bold) for the 3:1 case; see section 5.
check: per-text-node contrast >= 4.5:1 unless large per WCAG; re-run in dark and `prefers-contrast: more`.
origin: web:https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility (also inclusion, right-to-left, voiceover, keyboards, charting-data, charts; fetched 2026-10-08)

text: Use design-system colours that already carry accessible variants; do not invent unrelated one-off colours for text and controls.
why: variants adapt automatically to Increase Contrast and appearance.
check: every text/control colour is a token.
origin: web:https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility (also inclusion, right-to-left, voiceover, keyboards, charting-data, charts; fetched 2026-10-08)

text: Convey information with more than colour: shapes, icons, labels, patterns, position; allow customising colour schemes for charts where possible.
why: red-green and blue-orange pairs fail for colour-blind users.
applies: web: status chips, charts, form validation.
check: grayscale screenshot test; every state remains distinguishable.
origin: web:https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility (also inclusion, right-to-left, voiceover, keyboards, charting-data, charts; fetched 2026-10-08)

text: Give every key interface element an accessible name (alternative text label) that conveys function, including custom controls and icon-only buttons; keep labels in sync when UI changes.
why: screen readers have only the label.
check: axe `button-name`, `link-name`, `image-alt`, `label` pass; icon-only buttons have `aria-label` or visually hidden text.

text: Describe meaningful images by what they convey (not by repeating nearby captions); mark decorative images as hidden (`alt=""` or `aria-hidden="true"`).
why: reduces noise and cognitive load.
check: `` has `alt` attribute always; decorative ones `alt=""`; no alt text starting with "image of".

text: Every chart or infographic needs a concise overview (type, what each axis shows, bounds, main message), accessible labels for important marks (value plus context such as date), and any interaction must be available to assistive technology; hide visible axis/tick labels from assistive tech when mark labels already carry the values.
why: a chart is not one image; labels need structure.
check: each chart has `figcaption`/summary and a data table or per-mark `aria-label`; axis text `aria-hidden`.

text: Write chart accessibility labels with objective values and unambiguous formats: "June 6" not "6/6", "60 minutes" not "60m", no subjective words (rapidly, gradually), describe what the series represents not what colour it is, and refer to axes consistently.
why: avoids ambiguity and editorialising.
check: regex for `\d+/\d+` and subjective adverbs in aria-labels.

text: Give each page/screen a unique, specific title, and use accurate section headings to build a heading outline.
why: title is the first thing a screen reader announces.
check: unique `<title>` per route; no skipped heading levels.

text: Express visual relationships (grouping, order, linkage) programmatically: DOM order equals reading order; group image with its caption (`<figure>`); landmarks and headings for navigation.
why: sighted proximity cues disappear for screen readers.
check: tab/reading order equals visual order; `<figure>/<figcaption>` for captioned images; landmark roles present.

text: Announce visible content and layout changes (toasts, inline validation, loaded results) to assistive technology.
why: unexpected changes break the user's mental map.
applies: web: `aria-live="polite"`/`role="status"`, `role="alert"` for errors, focus management on route changes.
