why: Smoothness and legibility under streaming data.
check: no `setState` per tick for value overlay; loading state exists; palette generated from a single input.

text: Make defaults the shipped version: opinionated, feel right with zero tuning; options exist only to switch things off or move them.
why: The ideal component needs two lines and no configuration to look finished.
check: component renders acceptably with default props only.

text: A toolbar changes shape rather than swapping panels: colour pick turns the pen row into a palette, size controls become two sliders, minimise rolls into a disc that keeps the current tool; on screens under 680px stand the bar vertically on the left edge and trim tools. Tools behave like what they are named after (pens thin with speed, fountain pen by direction); Shift locks strokes to 8 directions.
why: Shape-morphing keeps spatial orientation; skeuomorphic objects beat icon rows.
check: `visual`; narrow breakpoint 680px for toolbar reflow.

text: Give agents visual feedback by pointing, not describing: attach selector/class/text, bounding box and optionally computed styles; offer four detail levels (compact: selector + note; standard: + position and selected text; detailed: + bounding boxes and nearby context; forensic: everything including computed styles) and let the agent design the format; support pausing CSS animations to annotate a transient state.
why: "Make the avatar smaller" is ambiguous; `img.sid-avatar` is not. Precision decays from observation to description.
check: every critique item names a selector and a measured value, not an adjective.

text: For morphing icons constrain to a shared structure (every icon = exactly three lines; unused lines collapse to an invisible point at the centre, e.g. `{x1:7,y1:7,x2:7,y2:7}` with opacity 0); icons that are the same shape at different angles live in a rotation group and rotate (arrows and chevrons 90 degrees apart, plus and cross 45 degrees apart) instead of interpolating coordinates.
why: Coordinate morphing bends rotated shapes; rotation looks natural.
applies: icon buttons that change state (menu to close, play to pause).
check: icon swaps use shape morph or rotation, not a crossfade (`AnimatePresence` of two SVGs flagged); `visual`.

text: Never rely on the agent's own sense of "looks right": have it expose a sequencer or test harness, review the transitions yourself, and describe each wrong one with the reason.
why: The model "optimised for working rather than feeling right"; after the reason is given it improves.
check: ledger contains human or measured verdict per animation.

text: Check quality along two axes: attention (contrast in varied light, 60fps, colour semantics consistent, objects consistent, accessible labels, appropriate haptics) and intention (motion/icons/colour serve orientation, communication or a goal; shadow exists to show depth or affordance; know when to stop adding features).
why: Quality is noticed by its absence; intent distinguishes polish from decoration.
check: review checklist: each effect (shadow, animation, colour) has a stated function.

text: Be fast and honest about speed: cache data, first paint feels instant, interactions respond in milliseconds, make optimistic guesses to prefetch/pre-render, and show status when slowness is unavoidable.
why: Respecting attention.
check: LCP/INP budgets; loading states present on every async view.

text: Be forgiving: destructive actions are presented clearly and are undoable; errors are never dead ends and use plain language; invalid inputs are highlighted; failed requests are retried; changes queue locally on network loss; avoid indistinguishable colour pairs or offer an override; minimise personal data.
why: Humans are messy and distractible.
check: every delete has undo or confirm; error text contains a next step; invalid field has visible state.

text: Protect drafts: warn on losing unsaved changes, autosave in the background (docked composer, restored comment box after refresh), or make drafts a first-class object.
why: Losing typed content is a horrible feeling.
check: reload during typing restores the field; leaving with dirty state prompts.

text: Destructive actions: red, require confirmation, and put the destructive confirm away from the thumb (iOS action sheets list it at the top); for the highest stakes require typing the name of the thing (GitHub repo deletion). Prefer Undo for reversible changes (archive, swipe) and a delayed send ("magic undo", Gmail) over a confirm dialog.
why: Confirmation fatigue vs real protection; undo is cheaper than asking.
check: destructive buttons use destructive colour token; high-stakes flows require typed confirmation.

text: Minimum tap targets 44pt (Apple) / 48 (Google); "minimum" means going bigger is fine and good when no competing element is adjacent.
why: Touch accuracy.
check: `getBoundingClientRect` of interactive elements >= 44x44 on touch layouts.

text: Prefer sensible defaults over decisions; repeat an entry point in context when users need it there (notification preferences link on the Notifications screen), accepting the DRY violation in the UI; scan content for omissions (missing attachment) and warn before sending.
why: Convention over configuration reduces mistakes; discoverability beats purity.
check: `visual`/flow review.

text: Give coding agents a measurement tool before asking for improvement: phases of instrument (benchmark harness, baseline numbers), diagnose (top 3-5 bottlenecks with hypotheses), iterate (one change at a time, re-measure, commit each success), report (before/after HTML).
why: A "run faster" request with no stopwatch has no feedback; the human becomes the slow, unreliable loop.
check: every optimisation task starts with a recorded baseline in `reports/`.

text: Design-to-code refinement loop: pull the design source, build a first pass (expect it to be wrong), screenshot via browser tooling and inspect properties, list every difference (spacing, colour, typography, radius, shadows, borders, alignment, responsive behaviour), fix one by one verifying in the browser, and stop only when no differences are found; ask rather than guess on ambiguity.
why: The gap between "close enough" and "correct" is where polish lives.
check: the loop produces an enumerated diff list per iteration.

text: Screen candidates for design-engineering by a small task (a multi-select dropdown): strong candidates think about reordering selected items, keyboard navigation and shortcuts without being asked; build a team culture of naming why something is wrong (janky animation, dropped frame, misaligned element, wrong colour).
why: Intuition for "good" and "correct" is built by repeatedly describing defects.
check: critique prompts require a reason per defect.

text: Ask for blunt feedback from people with relevant expertise and good taste, after you have exhausted your own ability, and praise with the same candour.
why: Early feedback is co-design; flattery blocks growth.
check: n/a.

text: Use tinted shadows rather than pure black (Stripe uses semi-transparent blue on a blue theme); 1px depth lines separate stacked cards.
why: Brand-coloured depth reads more refined than default black.
check: `box-shadow` colour has hue matching theme; alpha <= 0.25 [engine note].

text: Navigate with layers that stack and swipe off (cards as views) when you want a sense of "never leaving the dashboard"; give sign-out its own graceful transition (settings card slides left, login appears).
why: Hierarchy shown by stack; rare screens get the same care.
check: `visual`.

text: Tie choreography to input where possible (Carousel's photos fall into alignment according to scroll speed, not a timer); lead the user with motion toward the intended action (Foursquare logging in).
why: Tracking input proves the system is responsive.
check: scroll-linked progress rather than time-based for onboarding sequences.

text: Undoing should feel instant rather than a reversed animation: Inbox lets removed rows slide away on done, but undo snaps the restored items back so the user sees the mistake corrected at once (author's reading, hedged).
why: Speed to remedy matters more than symmetry; reversal can make users wonder if undo completed.
check: `visual` (undo transition <= 100ms).

text: Apply the same micro-interaction to every control of the same kind (Instagram's follow/like buttons bounce and scale identically everywhere); rare screens (about page, settings, empty groups) get a detail too; pairing meaning with colour keeps location legible (Inbox: green done, yellow snoozed, blue inbox).
why: Consistency teaches the pattern; colour as navigation.
check: all `button` of a variant share the same `:active` transform and transition; colour semantics map documented.

text: Open to the content the user came for (NeuBible launches into the text), remember position, and let reading settings return the user to where they were; teach by doing (Quartz has users perform the gestures); prime permission prompts with an explainer before the OS dialog (Carousel/Dropbox).
why: Time-to-value and trust.
check: time from launch to primary content; permission explainer precedes OS prompt.

text: Contextual copy: change search placeholder with the active filter; unliking can use a distinct icon (broken heart) so the reverse action has its own personality.
why: Small contextual cues are free polish.
check: `placeholder` varies with filter state.

text: Disable all transitions for the frame in which the theme changes: inject `* { transition: none !important }`, toggle the theme, force style recalc by reading `getComputedStyle(styleEl).opacity`, then remove the style. `requestAnimationFrame` is not reliable here.
why: Transitioning every element to new theme values hurts performance and cannot animate images/icons anyway.
check: toggle code path contains the injected style and a forced reflow; or `next-themes` with `disableTransitionOnChange`.
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Custom link underline: `background-image: linear-gradient(c,c); background-size: 100% 1px; background-position: left bottom; background-repeat: no-repeat`; offset with `left 1.05em`; weight via height (e.g. `0.25em`); hide the line behind descenders with `text-shadow: 0.1em 0 var(--background), -0.1em 0 var(--background)` and reset `text-shadow: none` in `::selection`; dashed via `repeating-linear-gradient` with `background-size: 1ch 1px`.
why: `text-decoration` offers insufficient control; works across wrapped lines.
check: `visual`.
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Inputs with a prefix that should react to input focus: place the prefix after the input in the DOM and visually reorder with flex `order`, then use `input:focus + .prefix` (or `:focus-within` now).
why: CSS has no previous-sibling selector.
check: n/a (implementation hint).
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Segmented tabs with a moving, colour-inverting highlight use two stacked lists and animate `clip-path` with the Web Animations API; mark the duplicate `aria-hidden`.
why: No `mix-blend-mode` hacks, any colours work.
check: duplicate list `aria-hidden="true"`.
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Nested menu items that expand in place (iOS 16 style) reveal with `clip-path`, counter-scale the child with `transform: calc(1 / var(--transform))`, and tint the backdrop gray so text and background dim at different rates.
why: In-place expansion is ergonomic and keeps context.
check: `visual`; known bugs: border flicker, Safari subpixel jitter animating `font-variation-settings`, Firefox needs `:has`.
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Be aware that `filter: blur()` bleeds light at element edges, `backdrop-filter` on a pseudo-element breaks `border-radius`, and an SVG filter fix (`feGaussianBlur` + `feComponentTransfer` + `feFuncA`) introduces banding; animating `stdDeviation` with SMIL `<animate>` works while Chrome has issues animating `backdrop-filter`.
why: Blur entrances/exits are trending; each approach has a trade-off.
check: test on Chrome and Safari before shipping blur transitions; prefer small blur radii.
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Reveal sidebars with `transform: translateX` plus negative `margin-right` so inner content is not skewed; accept it is not purely GPU-accelerated (Linear uses it).
why: Content shifting layout cannot be done with compositor-only properties.
check: `visual`; INP test on mid-range device.
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Drag affordances on dense timelines appear only when hovering the edges after a short delay (pseudo-elements with `animation-delay`).
why: Keeps the dense view clean.
check: `visual`.
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Safari dark mode shows a white favicon background when the favicon lacks contrast; brighten the primary colour (Linear: `#6E79D6` -> `#8299FF` fixed it), reduce white space or add a border; flush the Favicon Cache to test.
why: Safari aggressively adjusts low-contrast icons.
check: favicon primary colour luminance high enough against `#000` and `#282828`.
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Use `rem` for type so the user's browser font-size setting is honoured; note browser scaling and zooming are different; a hard-coded `html { font-size }` or `px` opts out; measure the user's default with `font-size: medium` (16px typical, 24px at "Very Large").
why: Almost no sites respect browser font scaling; scaling only main content (as cnn.com did) is a compromise.
check: `html` has no `px` font-size; body text sizes in `rem`/`em`.
source: https://paco.me/writing/px-vs-rem ; https://paco.me/writing/browser-default-font-size (verified; "no reason to use rem when scaling is ignored" is his note)
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Command palette quality bar: render hundreds of items at reasonable performance (original test set 249 items, goal 2,000); keyboard-first with compound components.
why: The component is used constantly; jank is felt every time.
check: open with 2,000 items < 100ms [engine note: threshold].
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Custom video controls need YouTube-style shortcuts: Space/K play-pause, 1-9 seek to 10-90%, Left/Right/J/L jump, `.` and `,` frame step, plus fullscreen.
why: Power-user parity with native players.
check: key handlers present.
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Keep personal/product sites simple: prefer performance, simplicity and craft over adding animations and features; static documents can ship with JavaScript disabled.
why: Maintainability; "my previous site felt disingenuous and abandoned".
check: page renders with JS disabled.
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Re-render only for state keys a component actually reads (hook-getter via Proxy, SWR style).
why: Fewer renders in shared state.
check: profiler: components reading only `name` do not render when `username` changes.
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: In Electron mac windows position the traffic lights at `{ x: 19, y: 18 }` for a native feel.
why: Native alignment.
check: `trafficLightPosition` set.
section: 2.5 Paco Coursey: CSS and craft tricks

text: Seed `examples/` and teardown candidates from Lovin's /sites list (about 290 links) and the 22 App Dissection posts; treat them as inspiration targets, not rules, and record why each is good before copying anything.
why: Taste calibrates against respected work and needs the reason (Emil).
check: each example entry has a "why" line.

text: State one purpose for every animation (explain, feedback, spatial continuity, soften appearance, or rare-moment delight). If you cannot state one, remove it.
why: Motion without purpose is noise that costs attention each time it repeats; unpurposeful motion also makes interfaces feel slow and can reduce trust.
check: review: each `transition`/`animation`/Motion usage maps to a one-line purpose in the PR or ledger; unlabelled ones are flagged.

text: Run the frequency test before animating: used 100+ times/day or fired by keyboard = no animation; tens of times/day (hover on list rows, menu rows) = no animation or near zero; occasional (modal, drawer, toast) = standard; rare (onboarding, feedback form, celebration) = may delight.
why: Initial delight fades and the animation then slows users down and feels disconnected from the key they pressed.
check: handlers bound to `keydown`/shortcut libs/`cmdk`-style lists produce no `transition`/`animation` on the changed element; list-row hover has `transition-duration: 0ms` or none.

text: Command palettes and keyboard-navigated lists: the highlight moves instantly (0ms). Judgement exercise "frequency of use": a 150ms hover-colour transition on menu rows is the worse choice, the 0ms version is the right one.
why: The highlight lags the key press and the user's flow breaks.
applies: command palette, menus, selects navigated with arrows.
check: computed `transition-duration` of `[role=option]`/`[role=menuitem]` backgrounds is `0s` under keyboard modality; `visual` otherwise.

text: Keep UI animations under 300ms. Recommended bands: micro-interactions 100-150ms; standard UI such as tooltips and dropdowns 150-250ms; modals and drawers 200-300ms.
why: Shorter animation makes the UI feel like it is listening; 180ms select beats 400ms.
check: parse computed `transition-duration`/`animation-duration`; flag >300ms on non-hero interactive elements; `visual` for JS springs.

text: Scale duration with the distance and size of the moving object: larger elements slower, longer travel longer. Exit animations can be about 20% faster than the entrance.
why: Perceived velocity should stay constant; a short duration on a full-screen panel feels jarring.
applies: drawers, full-screen menus, side panels, modals.
check: `exit duration <= 0.85 * enter duration` on paired overlays; for panels covering >50% of viewport width, duration >= 300ms is acceptable (demo: full-screen menu 400ms vs 200ms; the longer is the intended answer).
source: https://emilkowal.ski/ui/agents-with-taste ; https://emilkowal.ski/ui/train-your-judgement (verified; the A/B labels of ex.1 were not mapped with certainty, the explanation text is unambiguous)

text: Bounce is a brand-personality dial: default to zero; add only a small value (demo compared bounce 0.4 vs 0) when the brand is explicitly playful (learning app yes, finance app no).
why: Bounce reads as playful; zero reads as professional and safe.
check: spring `bounce > 0` or overshoot `cubic-bezier` y>1 requires a recorded personality choice; `bounce >= 0.4` flagged.

text: Pick easing with this flowchart: entering or leaving the viewport -> ease-out; moving or morphing while staying on screen -> ease-in-out; hover/colour change -> ease; constant motion (marquee, progress, time) -> linear; default -> ease-out.
why: Deceleration at the end is gentle, and the sharp start makes it feel faster.
check: classify each transition by role; `linear` only on loops/progress/hold timers; bare `ease-in` on any enter animation is an error.

text: Do not use `ease-in` for UI entering or exiting (the toast exercise: `cubic-bezier(.42,0,1,1)` loses to `cubic-bezier(.25,.1,.25,1)` at identical 400ms).
why: It speeds up at the end, the opposite of what the eye wants; same duration, feels slower.
check: computed `transition-timing-function` equals `ease-in` or `cubic-bezier(0.42, 0, 1, 1)` on enter/exit -> fail.

text: Prefer stronger custom curves over the CSS keywords `ease-in-out`/`ease-out` for impact; source: easings.co, or the author's set. Curves he uses in the essays: drawer/sheet `cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)`; reveal/theme-wipe `cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)`; Sonner toast `ease` at 400ms; demo ease-out-cubic `[0.215, 0.61, 0.355, 1]` for staggered list items.
why: Built-in curves are too gentle; "custom easing feels more energetic".
check: grep tokens file for named curves; flag raw keyword `ease-in-out` on large moves.

text: Use `linear` only for a deliberately mechanical duration: hold-to-confirm fill is `clip-path` 2s `linear` on press, then release returns in 200ms `ease-out`.
why: Slow where the user is deciding, fast where the system is responding; the linear 2s fill shows exact progress of a held press.
check: `:active` transition 2s linear + release <=200ms ease-out for hold-to-delete; any other `linear` >200ms is suspect.

text: Pressable elements shrink on `:active`: `transform: scale(0.97)` with `transition: transform 160ms ease-out`. Do not go to 0.9 (the judgement exercise labels a clearly visible shrink too aggressive).
why: Immediate acknowledgement that the interface heard you.
check: `:active` rule exists with scale in [0.95, 0.98]; transition 100-160ms.

text: Never animate in from `scale(0)`. Start from a visible shape: default 0.95 + opacity 0; allowed 0.9+ for larger surfaces; tooltips/very small popovers 0.97.
why: Real objects do not appear from a point; a deflated balloon keeps a shape.
check: grep `scale(0)`, `scale: 0`, `initial={{ scale: 0 }}`, `scale-0` on enter states; compute `initial scale >= 0.9` (see section 5 for the 0.8 conflict).

text: Anchored popovers, dropdowns and menus set `transform-origin` to the trigger. Base UI: `transform-origin: var(--transform-origin)`; Radix: `transform-origin: var(--radix-dropdown-menu-content-transform-origin)` (use the matching variable per primitive). Center origin is wrong for anchored overlays. Modals stay center-origin.
why: Growth out of the trigger shows causality. The difference shows most when both axes mismatch (top-right).
check: computed `transform-origin` of anchored popups is not `50% 50%` unless the popup is centered on its trigger.

text: Tooltip: delay before the first one opens; once one is open, siblings open instantly with no animation. With Base UI: `[data-instant]{transition-duration:0ms}`. Tooltip enter transition: `transform 0.125s ease-out, opacity 0.125s ease-out`, from `scale(0.97)` and opacity 0, origin = trigger.
why: The delay prevents accidental activation; skipping it for neighbours makes the whole toolbar feel fast.
check: CSS contains a `[data-instant]` (or equivalent) zero-duration rule; tooltip transition is 125ms.

text: Use `will-change: transform` when an animation looks shaky; animate a child instead of the parent when hover causes flicker; give small tap targets a 44px minimum hit area using a pseudo-element.
why: Promotes the layer to the compositor; moving the hovered element changes the hover hit area and re-triggers hover; small hit areas fail touch.
check: icon-only buttons: pseudo-element or padding yields >= 44x44 hit box; `will-change` only toggled on elements that actually animate.
source: https://emilkowal.ski/ui/agents-with-taste (skill table) (verified, from the author's skill file)

text: Add a small blur (about 2px) to a crossfade when the two states read as two separate objects and tuning easing/duration did not fix it. Keep blur under 20px.
why: Blur bridges old and new state so the eye reads one morphing object. It is a last resort, not a default.
check: `filter: blur()` in a transition is <= 4px (his demo: 2px); no blur transition on large areas.

text: Sequence the layered pieces of an entrance by importance, not uniformly: the least important element (a pill badge) only fades, the headline moves most. Stagger delays must differ per tier; uniform delays flatten hierarchy.
why: Motion encodes importance; uniform stagger looks artificial.
check: `visual`: delays differ per hierarchy tier; not all siblings share one step.

text: Do not layer entrance animations on a panel and its children (panel slides in with a 0.28s delay, children then stagger at 0.05s steps after a 0.3s delayed start). Prefer the single-step version.
why: Layering adds time before the content is usable; the exercise's right answer is the one without layers.
check: child `delayChildren`/delay <= the parent's duration; total entrance <= 300ms for panels.

text: Toggleable UI (menus, modals, accordions, drawers, toasts) uses CSS transitions or springs, not keyframe animations, so rapid toggling retargets smoothly instead of jumping.
why: A keyframe cannot change its end value while running; a transition can.
check: `animation:`/`@keyframes` on elements that toggle on user input -> flag; `transition:` expected.

text: With Motion's `AnimatePresence`, use `mode="popLayout"` when removing items from a flowing list so the exiting item leaves document flow on frame one and siblings reflow in parallel with the exit.
why: Default mode keeps the exiting element in flow until it finishes, so the gap closes after a pause.
check: grep `AnimatePresence` around list item removal: `mode="popLayout"` present, children have `layout`.

text: Toast enters from translateY(100%) via a mounted-state flip and a CSS transition (`transform 400ms ease`), not a keyframe; the exit leaves in the same direction as the entrance.
why: Spatial consistency makes swipe-down-to-dismiss feel natural; transitions survive rapid additions.
check: `data-mounted` (or `@starting-style`) pattern; entry and exit axis identical.
source: https://emilkowal.ski/ui/building-a-toast-component (verified; `@starting-style` mentioned as a simpler modern option)

text: Stacked toasts: position absolute; y offset = 14px * index (the `lift` gap), scale = 1 - 0.05 * index (0.95, 0.9 ...); in stacked mode all toasts take the height of the front toast so edges line up; hovering the area expands to real heights (offset = sum of preceding heights + gap * index).
why: Scale and offset create depth; uniform height keeps the stack tidy.
check: computed transforms of toast N: `translateY(-14px*N) scale(1-0.05N)` (14px, 0.05 are Sonner defaults, tune with brand).

text: Toast lifetime is 4 seconds by default; pause the timer while hovered and while `document.hidden` is true (visibilitychange).
why: A toast fired in a background tab expires unseen.
check: timer logic reads `document.hidden`; `duration` default 4000ms.

text: Swipe-to-dismiss is momentum-based: remove if `abs(distance) >= SWIPE_THRESHOLD` OR `velocity = abs(distance) / elapsedMs > 0.11`. Update a CSS variable (`--swipe-amount`) during the move; capture the pointer at drag start so dragging continues outside the element; allow upward drag with friction (slows and stops) instead of a hard block.
why: A fast short flick expresses intent; hard walls feel broken; pointer capture prevents dropped gestures.
check: velocity branch exists; `setPointerCapture` on pointerdown; reverse-direction drag is damped.
source: https://emilkowal.ski/ui/building-a-toast-component (verified; 0.11 found by trial and error per the author)

text: Fill the gaps between stacked toasts with an `:after` pseudo-element so the hover state does not drop when the pointer crosses a gap.
why: Gaps belong to no toast, so the expanded state would collapse.
applies: stacked or gapped hover groups (toasts, toolbars, nested menus).
check: hover container has no dead gaps; pseudo-element bridges them.

text: API for imperative UI: expose a function you can call anywhere (`toast("text")`), one mount point (`<Toaster />`), and a promise form with three states (loading, success, error). No hooks or context required of the caller.
why: Developer experience decided adoption; the other half of Sonner's success was beautiful defaults and animation.
check: `visual`/API review: one import, one mount.

text: Sheet/drawer motion: `transition: transform 0.5s cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)` (matches the iOS sheet curve from Ionic). 500ms is correct here even though general UI stays under 300ms, because it mimics the native sheet and follows a finger.
why: Matching the native curve and duration makes it feel native.
check: computed curve equals `cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)`; duration 500ms for finger-driven sheet only.

text: During a drag write `transform: translateY(npx)` directly on the dragged element; do not update an inherited CSS custom property.
why: Changing an inherited variable recalculates style for every descendant; with a ~20+ item list the drag dropped frames, direct style fixed it.
applies: any drag or scroll-linked update at 60fps.
check: pointermove handler writes `element.style.transform`, not `style.setProperty('--x')` on a parent of a large subtree.

text: Drag vs scroll: only start dragging the drawer when its inner content is scrolled to the top; after a fast scroll reaches the top, block drag for 100ms so momentum does not close it by accident. Dragging up past the top is damped (the farther you drag the less it moves).
why: Mirrors native sheets; real objects slow before they stop.
check: `shouldDrag` guard; 100ms lockout; damping function.

text: Ignore touches after the first one until release (multi-touch guard); keyboard avoidance uses `visualViewport` resize: set drawer height to `visualViewport.height - OFFSET` and `bottom = max(innerHeight - visualViewport.height, 0)`.
why: A second finger makes the drawer jump; the browser's default scroll-to-input hides content.
check: test on a physical device: open drawer, focus input, content stays visible; second finger does nothing.

text: Snap points: on release, snap to the nearest point (fractions of viewport or fixed px; px for inputs that must stick out evenly); flick velocity may skip points or dismiss.
why: Matches iOS Maps-style sheets, momentum-aware.
check: nearest-point logic + velocity.

text: Background-scale effect: while a drawer opens, scale the page wrapper and animate its border radius from the drag progress (dragging 40% down gives 60% of the max radius).
why: Makes the page read as a lower sheet.
check: `visual`.

text: Test touch components on a real phone (USB plus Safari devtools) or the Xcode simulator, not by shrinking a desktop window.
why: Keyboard, momentum, safe areas and multi-touch only exist on device.
check: ledger entry names the device.

text: Prefer animating `clip-path: inset(...)` over width/height for reveals, comparison sliders, tab indicators and scroll-progress lines: no layout shift, compositor-friendly, no extra overflow wrapper.
why: The element already occupies its space; only visibility changes.
applies: image reveal, before/after slider, tabs, progress line, theme wipe.
check: reveal animations animate `clip-path`/`transform`/`opacity`, not `height`/`width`.

text: Image reveal: start `clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0)` -> `inset(0 0 0 0)`, 1s, `cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)`, trigger once when at least 100px of the image is in view (`useInView({ once: true, margin: "-100px" })`, or IntersectionObserver).
why: Triggered at viewport entry or the user never sees it.
check: observer or `useInView` present, `once`; duration 1000ms is a hero value, not UI (see section 5).

text: Tabs with a colour-inverting indicator: duplicate the tab list with active styling (blue background, white text), `aria-hidden` and `tabIndex=-1`, and clip it to the active tab with `inset(0px R% 0px L% round 17px)`; animate that value on change. Do not rely on a text-colour transition.
why: The text and background change in one stroke; colour transitions never match the sliding indicator.
check: overlay copy is `aria-hidden`; clip uses offsetLeft/offsetWidth percentages.

text: Scroll-progress line: map `scrollYProgress` (offset `["start end", "end end"]`) to clip `inset(0 0 X% 0)` with X from 100% to 0%.
why: Looks drawn like SVG but is a clipped div; the offset prevents reversal after the section passes.
check: `visual`.

text: Turn each taste decision into a written rule with the reason, numbers, and a decision table or flowchart; keep it strict so an agent does not invent its own rules. Package per aspect (animation, typography, layout, icons, colour) as skill files.
why: "That's the why. There's no magic." Strict rules transfer taste to agents.
check: every taste rule in `knowledge/` has Why and a Check or `visual`.

text: Calibrate taste by studying, not liking: do not label things good or bad; explain why a specific interaction feels good; keep a curated list of respected makers; practise building; ask critique from the right person.
why: "Taste is a trained instinct", not personal preference.
check: ledger notes contain a reason for each approval or rejection.

text: Train judgement with paired comparisons: view A and B, pick, write the reason in words, then compare to a reference breakdown. Cover size, easing, entry, intent, frequency, scale, removal, interruption, popover origin, stagger, layering.
why: Writing why builds the skill of articulating judgement; AI-generated motion "works but feels mediocre".
check: each A/B decision in review logs includes a one-line reason tied to a rule id.

text: Keep deliberate friction in the build process: for each AI-generated section or effect write what it is for and drop it if it has no reason.
why: Cheap generation removed the cost that filtered weak ideas; unthought output "exists but is not designed".
check: brief-to-render ledger lists a purpose per section.
source: https://emilkowal.ski/ui/friction-as-a-feature (verified; the application to the pipeline is [engine note])

text: Ship documentation that lets people touch the component: interactive examples with copy-ready code, built before launch.
why: Lowers the barrier; part of why Sonner won.
check: every component doc has a live demo.

text: Typography rules from his skill file: cap body text near 65ch; `tabular-nums` on price/number columns; use the ellipsis character `…` not `...`; loosen letter-spacing on uppercase labels; declare a fallback stack with matching x-height and weight to avoid layout shift; underline only links; prefer bold over italic for interface emphasis.
why: Each one protects reading rhythm, alignment, or an affordance.
check: `max-width` of text blocks <= 70ch; `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on numeric columns; uppercase labels have `letter-spacing > 0`; non-link elements have no `text-decoration: underline`.

text: Fire lightweight, reversible actions (showing an overlay, search reveal, unlock) during the gesture when the moving elements reach their logical resting place; fire destructive or committing actions only on release, regardless of distance.
why: Waiting for finger-up on a light action feels broken; triggering a destructive action mid-swipe removes the chance to change your mind.
check: `visual`/test: delete/dismiss handlers run in `pointerup`/`touchend`, not `pointermove`.

text: During a gesture apply the input delta to the element immediately (1:1), then animate to the committed state after a threshold or on release.
why: Immediate tracking tells the user the object is manipulable; a threshold-then-animate response gives no affordance.
check: `visual`; pointermove handler writes transform before any easing.

text: Gestures and transitions must be interruptible: tapping or swiping back mid-animation reverses or retargets immediately (iOS Settings push is the counterexample). Use transitions/springs rather than fixed keyframe timelines.
why: Real objects are interruptible; waiting for an animation to finish feels unresponsive.
check: toggle the control twice quickly: state follows the latest input without jump.

text: Motion origin follows the semantic source: launch from the object that triggered it (icon, button), or from the side that matches its place in the stack; reserve the generic entrance for cases with only one possible source.
why: Origin shows where the thing lives and how it relates.
check: `visual`: `transform-origin` and enter direction match trigger location.

text: Show feedback near the trigger: inline checkmark on a successful copy (not a notification), highlight the relevant input(s) on form error, start transitions at the trigger location.
why: The system must say "I understood you" where the user is looking.
check: copy button swaps its own icon/label for >=1s; error styles are on the invalid field.

text: When a finger covers the content being manipulated, show a magnified or enlarged echo (loupe above the caret, enlarged key on press), and keep a drag alive even when the finger leaves a thin control (sliders).
why: Interacting with something you cannot see is uncomfortable.
applies: touch sliders, text selection, keyboards, scrubbers.
check: slider track uses pointer capture; `visual` for echo.

text: Use infinite targets (screen corners/edges) or pointer-centred radial menus for frequently used actions when it fits; place commonly used menus in corners.
why: Fitts's law: time depends on distance and size; targets at the screen edge cannot be overshot.
check: primary navigation anchored to an edge or corner; target size >= 44px (touch) or >= 24px (pointer).

text: Predict intent from context where possible (do not ask): adjust brightness for scanning, blur app content in the app switcher when it holds sensitive data, auto-show relevant state.
why: The most natural input is no input.
check: `visual`/review.

text: Inside nested menus use a prediction cone so the pointer can travel diagonally to a submenu without the menu closing.
why: Sloppy pointer paths close menus accidentally.
check: submenu close delay or safe-triangle logic present.

text: Remove motion from high-frequency, low-novelty actions: opening a command menu or right-click menu, adding/deleting list rows, hovering trivial buttons, keyboard-driven focus changes. Menus may fade out gently but not animate in; a quick Cmd+Tab-style trigger can skip the UI entirely.
why: After a few days the animation feels like waiting; removing it makes the whole app feel faster than tuning it.
check: `transition-duration` is 0 on menu rows and on open of command menu; enter animations absent on keyboard-initiated opens.
source: https://rauno.me/craft/interaction-design ; https://interfaces.rauno.me/ ; https://rauno.me/craft/novelty (verified; his own bookmarks app anecdote)

text: Spend novelty at about 10%: onboarding, first login, rare destinations get the expressive treatment once; return visits show the page instantly. Implement "first time only" with a cookie flag (set on login, read by middleware, flag cleared after the animated variant is served).
why: A welcome flourish on every visit loses its meaning; contrast creates the effect.
check: animated intro variant gated by a flag; reload shows no animation.

text: Keep rhythm in novelty: do not place two high-novelty animations back-to-back; separate them with quiet interludes. Do not make every element signal itself as novel; reserve the accent colour similarly.
why: When everything announces itself, nothing stands out.
check: scroll map of high-novelty sections: no two adjacent.

text: Animation values stay proportional to the trigger size, and interaction animations stay at or under 200ms to feel immediate.
why: A small control cannot justify a large swoop; long durations feel laggy.
check: computed durations of `:hover`, `:active`, toggle, menu <= 200ms; displacement relative to trigger.
source: https://interfaces.rauno.me/ (verified; see section 5 for the 300ms comparison)

text: Do not animate a dialog in from scale 0 -> 1; fade opacity and scale from about 0.8. Do not scale buttons on press from 1 -> 0.8; use about 0.96, or about 0.9 for stronger.
why: Large jumps in scale look cheap; small controlled values feel physical.
check: `scale(0)` grep; press scale in [0.9, 0.98].
source: https://interfaces.rauno.me/ (verified; conflicts with Emil, see section 5)

text: Looping animations pause when off-screen (IntersectionObserver) to offload CPU/GPU; auto-playing videos beyond what the device can take are paused or unmounted off-screen.
why: Many simultaneous loops/videos choke devices, especially iOS.
check: each infinite `animation` or video has a visibility observer; `playsinline muted` set on iOS autoplay videos.

text: Disable all transitions and animations while the theme switches; no animated theme toggle.
why: Hover/focus transitions fire on every element when theme variables change, causing a visible mess.
check: theme toggle injects a `* {transition: none !important}` style (or uses `next-themes`' disableTransitionOnChange) for one frame.

text: Reduced motion: pause looping complementary animations with `animation-play-state: paused` rather than `animation: none`; keep a blinking caret visible while paused (`opacity: 1 !important`); explicit user inputs are not intentionally reduced when they have no large amplified effect.
why: Abruptly cancelling looks broken; a caret that pauses in its invisible phase vanishes.
check: `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` rule sets `animation-play-state: paused` on loop classes; caret opacity 1.

text: Create depth by layering: blur the inner or back layer to lower it on the Z axis, fade the bottom edge of the container into the page, add offset frames and out-of-focus objects, and make decorative layers use the primary subject to communicate the product idea (Preview Deployments = many offset browser frames).
why: A flat, centred specimen with overlays added as an afterthought reads as sloppy; depth of field is what eyes expect.
check: hero has >=2 depth layers (blur/scale/opacity differences); `visual`.

text: When a modal/menu launches, dim and/or blur the backdrop to de-emphasise it and signal that only the overlay is interactive; tapping the backdrop closes.
why: Depth of field plus honest affordance.
check: backdrop has blur or dim; backdrop click closes.

text: Choreograph by splitting a transition into discrete states and delaying competing elements: blur the underlying layer first, then reveal items that share its space; reverse the order when the trigger differs (tap -> immediate input, suggestions slightly later). Always prioritise the area near the trigger.
why: Parallel revealing causes odd layering and splits attention; sequencing sets a reading order.
applies: search overlays, command menus (first open only), onboarding.
check: each element in an overlay entrance has a defined state/timing; the trigger-adjacent element animates first.

text: Stagger similar siblings by a small amount for loading grids, unlock/reveal, and hover text effects; the interface should not feel slower as a result.
why: Elements do not jarringly appear all at once; users can track what arrived.
applies: grids/lists on first load, hero text.
check: per-item delay present; total cascade capped (see hub).

text: Elements that stay interactive while the rest recedes should slide away without blurring; elements that become inactive blur with the background.
why: Blur communicates "inactive layer"; sliding with full opacity says "still reachable".
applies: docks, bottom bars, toolbars during overlays.
check: `visual`.

text: Clicking an input's label focuses the input (`<label for>` or wrapping).
why: Larger target and standard behaviour.
check: every `input` has an associated label (`input.labels.length > 0`).

text: Wrap inputs in a `<form>` so Enter submits; use semantic `type` (`password`, `email`, ...); use the `required` attribute and HTML validation where it fits; turn off `spellcheck` and `autocomplete` on inputs where they get in the way (most of the time per the source).
why: Native behaviours, mobile keyboards, less custom code.
check: `input` has `form` ancestor; `type` not default text for email/password fields.
source: https://interfaces.rauno.me/ (verified; autocomplete-off is the source's stance, tension with a11y/autofill, see section 5)

text: Prefix/suffix decorations (icons) sit absolutely positioned on top of the input with padding and forward clicks to focus the input.
why: One visual field, one focus target.
check: decoration `pointer-events` forwards to input.

text: Toggles take effect immediately (no confirm); buttons disable after submission to avoid duplicate requests; interactive elements disable `user-select` on inner content; decorative glows/gradients set `pointer-events: none`; list items have no dead zones between them (grow padding rather than add gaps).
why: Standard polish: no duplicate network calls, no accidental text selection, no hijacked events, continuous hit areas.
check: `[role=switch]` change handler commits state; submit button disabled during pending; decorative layers computed `pointer-events: none`.

text: Use optimistic updates: change local state immediately and roll back with feedback on server error. Do authentication redirects on the server before the client loads.
why: Perceived instant response; no janky URL flicker.
check: `visual`/code review.

text: Empty states prompt the next action (create an item), optionally with templates.
why: A blank list is a dead end.
check: empty-state view contains a primary button.

text: Style `::selection`; gradient text must unset the gradient on `::selection`.
why: Default selection on gradient clipped text becomes unreadable.
check: `::selection` rule exists; gradient-text selectors have `::selection { background-clip: ...; -webkit-text-fill-color: ...}` override.

text: Apply `-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased` and `text-rendering: optimizeLegibility`; subset fonts to the needed alphabets; `-webkit-text-size-adjust: 100%` to stop iOS landscape resize.
why: Cleaner rendering on macOS, smaller payload, stable sizes on rotate.
check: computed values on `body`.

text: Font weight must not change on hover or selected state (layout shift); do not use weights below 400; medium-size headings look best at 500-600.
why: Weight changes reflow neighbouring text; thin weights hurt legibility (opinion).
check: `font-weight` equal across `:hover/[aria-selected]` states; computed weight >= 400 on text.

text: Use `clamp()` for fluid headings, e.g. `clamp(48px, 5vw, 72px)` (his Next.js hero used `clamp(48px, 5vw, 76px)`); use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for tables, timers, and anything that shifts layout.
why: Smooth scaling without breakpoints; stable numerals.
check: `font-size` of `h1` uses `clamp(`; numeric columns have `tabular-nums`.

text: Render pull-quote marks in a serif (Georgia) for finesse and offset the quote with `text-indent: -0.4em` so lines align vertically.
why: A sans quote mark looks default; the hang keeps the text edge straight.
check: quote glyph font-family differs from body; `text-indent` negative.

text: Hover states are only visible on hover-capable devices: wrap in `@media (hover: hover)`.
why: Touch devices flash hover on press.
check: every `:hover` that changes visuals is inside the media query.

text: Input font size >= 16px (iOS zooms on focus otherwise); do not autofocus on touch devices; `muted` + `playsinline` on autoplay videos; set `touch-action` on custom pan/zoom components; if removing the tap highlight (`-webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent`) replace it with an equivalent.
why: iOS behaviours that break layout or gestures.
check: computed `font-size >= 16px` on inputs; no `autofocus` attribute on touch UIs.

text: Large `blur()` for `filter` and `backdrop-filter` is slow; scaling and blurring filled rectangles produces banding, so use radial gradients instead; `translateZ(0)` sparingly; toggle `will-change` only for the duration of a janky scroll animation; bypass React re-renders for real-time values (wheel delta in a ref, write DOM directly); adapt to hardware and network.
why: Paint cost and banding.
check: blur radii <= 20px on animated nodes; no permanent `will-change` on many elements.

text: Animate glows by toggling opacity (and transform) of pseudo-elements that carry the `box-shadow`; never animate `box-shadow` itself.
why: Animating box-shadow repaints every frame; weak phones drop frames.
check: transitions list contains no `box-shadow`.

text: Build hero visuals as layered CSS/SVG that paints without client JS, then progressively enhance with a code-split shader that fades in after load; detect low-power devices and skip the shader.
why: Fast first paint on the hero; the enhancement is optional.
check: hero visible with JS disabled; shader loaded via dynamic import.
source: https://rauno.me/craft/vercel (verified; layer order top to bottom: heading, SVG triangle, CSS grid lines, SVG rays, CSS rainbow gradient, GLSL shader)

text: Draw focus rings with `box-shadow`: `0 0 0 2px var(--app-background), 0 0 0 4px var(--focus-color)` and `transition: none` on `:focus-visible`; keep one colour/shape app-wide, match the trigger radius, and do not clip on overflow. (Modern Safari honours radius with `outline`, see section 5.)
why: Consistent, radius-following focus is rare; Discord is cited as the model.
check: every focusable has `:focus-visible` style with visible 2px ring and contrast >= 3:1 against both surfaces; ring not clipped by `overflow:hidden`.

text: Give focusable text links a small radius with matching padding/negative margin (`border-radius:2px; padding-left:2px; margin-left:-2px`) so the focus ring looks right without moving the text.
why: Rounded corners only show on focus but make the ring nicer.
check: `visual`.

text: Disabled buttons have no tooltips (they leave the tab order, so keyboard users never hear why); icon-only controls have an explicit `aria-label`; tooltips triggered by hover contain no interactive content; use real `` for images; illustrations built from HTML get one `aria-label` on a `role="img"` wrapper with the inner tree `aria-hidden`.
why: Screen reader output for raw illustration DOM is noise.
check: `button[disabled][title], button[disabled][data-tooltip]` absent; icon buttons have accessible name; decorative trees `aria-hidden`.

text: List-like focusables are navigable with up/down arrows and deletable with Cmd+Backspace; dropdown menus open on `mousedown` for immediate response (keyboard open still works).
why: Power-user speed.
check: keyboard handler tests; `onMouseDown` on menu trigger.

text: Accessible code blocks: hide decorative file icon, label the copy button, announce copy success in a visually hidden `role="log"` `aria-live="polite"` region, hide CSS-counter line numbers from screen readers with `content: counter(line) / ""`, wrap complementary code in `<aside aria-label="...">`.
why: Line numbers and unlabeled icons are noise; success must be audible.
check: axe + VoiceOver pass; live region exists.

text: Use an SVG favicon with an embedded `prefers-color-scheme` style.
why: Visible on dark browser chrome.
check: `link[rel=icon][type="image/svg+xml"]`.

text: Draw dotted container grid lines with a repeating `linear-gradient` background (1px high, 5px period, colour at 50% then transparent) plus a mask to fade the ends (`--fade-stop: 90%`, `--offset: -100px` to bleed out) instead of `border: dotted`.
why: Precise dot control and edge fade on one element.
check: `visual`.
section: 2.9 Layout and visual craft (Next.js and Vercel pages)

text: Build modular grids from guides drawn by `display: contents` wrappers and absolutely positioned guide cells (rows * columns cells), so empty cells still show guides and `auto` placement keeps working. 1080px content with 3 x 360px columns keeps 14-16px text at a comfortable line length. Crosshair marks sit at cell intersections.
why: The "show the frame" aesthetic stays stable across pages, so navigation reads as only content changing.
check: column width 320-400px for 14-16px copy; guides server-rendered.
section: 2.9 Layout and visual craft (Next.js and Vercel pages)

text: Use container queries (`container-type: inline-size`, `@container (max-width: 560px)`) for widgets instead of window width, and label code-driven visuals as `role="img"`.
why: Components know their own space; drop-in reuse.
check: component-level `@container` rules instead of `@media` in reusable parts.
section: 2.9 Layout and visual craft (Next.js and Vercel pages)

text: Style variants via data attributes (`data-variant="callout"`) instead of toggling many class names.
why: Less duplication; easy CSS.
check: `[data-variant]` selectors.
section: 2.9 Layout and visual craft (Next.js and Vercel pages)

text: Contrast aesthetics deliberately: introduce one element that differs in form (rotation, hand-drawn, bitmap vs serif, ASCII vs soft 3D) so curiosity asks "why is this different?", but avoid it in productivity software; use for first impressions and tone.
why: Equal-weight elements say nothing; the right amount of contrast invites attention (opinion).
check: `visual`: exactly one contrast motif per section.
section: 2.9 Layout and visual craft (Next.js and Vercel pages)

text: Ship the static version when it is an improvement; follow with animation and adjustments in later PRs.
why: Big PRs stall.
check: n/a.
section: 2.9 Layout and visual craft (Next.js and Vercel pages)

text: Build a homepage, persona page or product page in this order: navbar, hero (header, subheader, image), social proof, CTA with a one-line incentive, features and objections, repeat CTA, footer. Deviate only with a stated reason.
why: Familiar order lowers confusion; Julian ties purchase rate to desire minus labor and confusion, and says each departure from the template adds confusion for the average visitor.
check: list the top-level section roles in DOM order; the first five must match navbar, hero, proof, CTA, features; the last two must be CTA and footer.

text: Make the hero header fully descriptive: a stranger who reads only the H1 must be able to say what the product is or does. Reject slogan-style headers of the "Improve your workflow" or "Supercharge your collaboration" kind.
why: If the visitor does not understand what is sold at once, they leave from laziness or skim and form a wrong impression.
check: (1) H1 contains a concrete noun naming the product category or the thing delivered; (2) H1 does not match the banned-verb list `supercharge|empower|revolutioni[sz]e|unleash|elevate|streamline|reimagine|improve your workflow|next[- ]gen`; (3) cold-read test: ask a model with no product context what is sold from the H1 alone.

text: Derive the header from a value proposition: name the bad alternative people use today, state how this product is better, then turn that into an action statement. Then add one hook, either a bold specific claim or a pre-empted objection, never both stuffed in.
why: Specificity is what makes a header descriptive; the hook is what makes people keep reading ("how is that possible?"). Bloating the header with several objections makes it hard to read.
check: header plus subheader contain either a number, time or comparison claim, or an objection phrase ("no coding", "in 5 minutes"); header is at most about 2 sentences.

text: Find the key objection by surveying real customers, with two questions: what almost stopped you from buying, and why do non-customers not buy. Address only the biggest one in the header and leave the rest to the body of the page.
why: Unaddressed doubts make visitors bounce before they scroll; surveying beats guessing.
check: process: brief lists the surveyed objections and marks which one the header answers; `visual` for the page.

text: Keep the subheader to one or two sentences: first say what the product is, then say how the header's claim is possible.
why: The subheader makes the bold claim believable and must stay breezy so momentum holds.
check: sentence count of the paragraph under the H1 is 1-2; second sentence references a mechanism or feature.

text: When the product serves several major personas, offer a persona chooser near the top that routes to persona-specific sections or pages.
why: One generic message cannot be both specific and relevant; routing keeps each visitor's page specific ("choose your own adventure").
check: hero contains 2-3 persona links/cards each with distinct destination; `visual` otherwise.

text: Put social proof directly under the hero as a logo collage (press and best-known customers) or a customer count if impressive. If there are no notable customers yet, give the product free to people at well-known companies and show their logos once they use it.
why: The aim is to look like everybody already knows the product and to make the visitor feel left out.
check: a logo/stat strip is the next sibling section after the hero; logos count at least 5 for B2B (Evil Martians gives no hard count; this threshold is an [engine note]).

text: Give the features section 3 to 6 features. Each is one block: a short header stating the value proposition, a paragraph that describes it and handles the objection it raises, and an image that reinforces it.
why: Header-paragraph-image gives skimmers and readers two speeds and avoids a wall of text.
check: count feature blocks (3-6); each contains heading + paragraph + media element.

text: Write feature headers as blunt value propositions (portable-grill example: "Cooks and sears", "No clean up", "Cooks more than just meat"). Avoid "Empower your sales" and "Revolutionize your workflow".
why: Visitors decide from the header whether the feature is relevant to them and whether to read the paragraph.
check: feature H3 text is at most about 6 words and fails the banned-verb regex from LW-02.

text: Make the features read as one running narrative: each feature paragraph should echo the hero value proposition (for example finishing with a clause that ties back to the hero promise).
why: Repetition of the core promise in new contexts converts a list of features into one argument.
check: key noun/verb from the H1 appears in at least half of the feature paragraphs.

text: For a complex feature, put extra detail behind an in-place reveal button instead of a separate page; if the detail is long, link out as a fallback.
why: An in-place reveal keeps the visitor in the flow of the page.
check: feature blocks with long copy (over about 60 words) use `<details>` or a disclosure button.

text: Feature images must demonstrate the product doing its job. For software show the product in action (a GIF or UI shot) and avoid abstract decorative imagery; blur tiny text that distracts, so the eye lands on how it works. For physical goods show use cases and build-quality close-ups.
why: Showing the product de-risks the visitor's time investment; abstract art says nothing about value.
check: each feature media element is a product screenshot, video or UI render (alt text names a product action); count of purely decorative images in feature blocks is 0.

text: Write the CTA as the next step of the hero's promise ("Find food", "Start learning"), not a context-free ask such as "Request a meeting".
why: A CTA that continues the narrative feels natural to click; a vague one raises the "why would I?" question.
check: CTA label contains a verb plus object that appears in the H1/subheader; label is not in `get started|submit|click here|learn more|request a demo` unless the product is sales-led.

text: Before shipping, get the draft reviewed by two audiences, people outside the market and people inside it, and have both score six criteria: conversion (would you hand over a card now), interest (1-10), clarity (what is unclear), expansion (what you want more of), brevity (what would you delete if half had to go), disbelief (what felt like scammy sales speak).
why: Outsiders reveal over-assumed knowledge; insiders test uniqueness against competitors.
check: process; record the six scores per reviewer in the verdict.

text: For an early-stage developer product use the skeleton hero, trust block, feature block, social-proof block, optional supporting blocks (comparison, pricing, FAQ, changelog preview), final CTA. Lead with clean type, layout and breathing room; defer flashy interaction.
why: Early teams need to validate quickly; across the sample the winning rules were no salesy copy and clever, simple execution.
check: section order and count; at most 1 marquee/animated hero decoration (matches the repo's anti-slop limits).

text: Default the hero to a centered composition: large headline, supporting graphic directly below, max-width container. Use side-by-side text-left/visual-right only as a deliberate exception.
why: In the sample the vast majority were centered; it reads stable and trustworthy. Left-right splits read as classic SaaS and were rare in dev tools.
check: computed `text-align:center` on H1 and the main visual is below the H1 within the same container; `visual` for exceptions.

text: Choose the hero visual by product maturity and shape: animated product UI (most effort, best for demos), static product UI (fast and valid), switchable multi-UI (many use cases, messaging not yet narrowed), live embed (narrow utility tools only), code snippet (SDKs, libraries, infra), abstract illustration or text-only (no UI yet or product lives under the hood).
why: The visual must match what exists; faking UI that does not exist erodes trust.
check: hero visual type is declared in the brief; code-heavy products without UI use a snippet.

text: Use two hero CTAs: a bold primary with a specific verb ("Start building", "Download now") and a visually lighter or outlined secondary (docs, GitHub, waitlist) that does not compete.
why: One converts paying users; the other gives developers immediate value through docs or open source.
check: exactly 2 CTAs in the hero; the secondary has lower fill emphasis (outline/ghost) than the primary; primary label is not "Get started".

text: Place the trust block immediately after the hero. B2B: customer logos (about half the sample used an auto-scrolling belt to save height; with few logos use one testimonial with a photo and name). Individual-user tools: big numbers (GitHub stars, usage, awards).
why: It is the fastest credibility builder; the right proof type depends on whether buyers are companies or individuals.
check: next section after hero is logos or stats; a belt, if used, pauses on hover/reduced motion.

text: Tell the feature story from the user's problem, not from a function list. Ranking in the sample, weakest to strongest for early products: list of functions, then task-oriented slogans ("Build faster"), then problem-oriented stories; bold standalone statements suit established brands; mission-statement openings work only when the problem is real and under-appreciated.
why: Problem framing creates resonance; function lists do not connect to need.
check: each feature section opens by naming a pain or situation (contains "without", "stop", "no more", or a problem noun) rather than only a capability name; `visual` otherwise.

text: Pick a feature layout to fit content: full screenshots with short captions (UI-heavy), alternating chess rows (more text per feature), icon plus headline plus line (SDKs, many small features), belts (many small items), bento (needs deliberate composition to avoid clutter), tabs (feature categories or personas).
why: Layout is a rhythm tool; bento and belts break vertical rhythm, chess rows add it.
check: max 2 consecutive chess rows (repo rule) and at least 2 distinct layout families in the feature area.

text: Use curated testimonials styled to fit the page (avatar, name, company logo for B2B), not live tweet embeds. One quote is enough at the start; when scaling, moderate any auto-pulled feed. Where possible put a short quote directly beneath the feature it praises.
why: Curation guarantees relevant, positive, well-formatted proof; contextual quotes reinforce a specific value claim.
check: testimonial blocks have 1-4 quotes each with attribution; no third-party embed iframes.

text: Early on, supporting blocks beyond an FAQ are optional. Add a comparison table only when the product is not revolutionary but wins on execution, speed or DX; keep pricing on its own page unless it is simple; add a changelog or blog strip only as an "we are shipping" signal for mature teams.
why: Extra blocks dilute a young page; each has one narrow job.
check: presence list vs. maturity declared in the brief; FAQ is an accordion near the end with practical questions.

text: Set an interaction latency budget: treat 100 ms as the maximum and aim for under 50 ms; for rendering a new thread aim for one or two frames (under 32 ms). Measure everything you want to make fast; cache locally, preload and prerender what is likely next; keep animation minimal; offer keyboard shortcuts with in-UI hints and a command palette (⌘K).
why: Superhuman builds speed as a product feature; the vendor cites older third-party figures for latency cost.
check: measure input-to-visual-response time on core actions (INP below 100 ms; 50 ms target); `performance.measure` marks on key interactions.
