why: Full engagement needs a task that is neither too hard nor too easy, with immediate feedback.
check: `visual`; every primary action has a visible success or failure state.

text: In multi-step flows show how far the user has come and what remains (step indicator, progress bar, checklist); start the indicator ahead of zero when real progress has been made.
why: Effort accelerates as the goal gets closer, so visible progress sustains motivation.
check: flows with 3 or more steps expose a `role="progressbar"` or a "step n of N" label that updates per step.

text: Signal unfinished content or tasks (progress, a partly visible next section, a to-do state) so people are invited to continue.
why: Interrupted or incomplete items stay in mind longer than finished ones.
check: the next section peeks above the fold at 1440 x 900 and 390 x 844; incomplete setup shows an explicit state.

text: Design the emotional peaks and the final moment on purpose (first success, confirmation, completion) and eliminate negative peaks (stressful waits, error dead-ends).
why: People judge an experience mainly by its most intense point and its ending, and recall negative moments more strongly.
check: every flow ends in a designed confirmation state with a next step; wait states over 1 s have progress or reassurance copy.

text: Invest in visual quality because users read it as usability, but verify usability separately by testing, since polish can hide real problems.
why: Attractive design raises perceived ease and tolerance for minor faults, which also masks them in studies.
check: `visual`; run a task-based usability pass that is independent of the visual rating.

text: Spend effort and screen space on the features that serve most users, using analytics to find the few causes behind most of the outcomes.
why: Inputs and outputs are lopsided; a minority of causes drives most results.
check: top 20% of used features are reachable in the first level of navigation (needs analytics); `visual` otherwise.

text: Treat every design judgement as vulnerable to bias (confirmation, anchoring, familiarity); validate with evidence from users instead of conviction.
why: Mental shortcuts speed decisions but produce systematic errors, in designers as well as in users.
check: `visual` (process): decisions logged with evidence and a falsifier.

text: Snap every transition and animation duration to the M3 ladder: 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500, 550, 600, 700, 800, 900, 1000 ms. Do not use values between rungs (e.g. 180, 220, 320, 375).
why: A closed ladder makes motion feel like one system and makes review mechanical.
check: collect computed `transition-duration` and `animation-duration` (and JS-driven durations) and flag any value not in the set.

text: Pick the duration bucket by how much of the screen changes: small utility changes (state, icon, toggle) 50-200 ms; component enter/exit and expansion 250-400 ms; large panels and full-screen transitions 450-600 ms; extra-long 700-1000 ms only for page-level or choreographed moments. [engine note] This size-to-bucket mapping is M3 guideline prose recalled from memory, not part of the token files; the engine's own ceiling for ordinary UI is lower (see section 5).
why: Perceived speed depends on distance and area; the same duration feels slow on a small element and abrupt on a big one.
check: computed duration against the element's bounding-box area: icon or control under 100 px wide should be at or below 200 ms; full-viewport panel at or above 300 ms.
source: https://m3.material.io/styles/motion/overview (not readable; prose recalled) plus the token ladder above.

text: Use `cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1)` (standard) for movement that stays on screen, `cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0, 1)` (standard-decelerate) for entering, `cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 1, 1)` (standard-accelerate) for leaving.
why: Entering elements should arrive fast and settle; leaving ones should start slow and clear out; the curve encodes direction.
check: computed `transition-timing-function` on entering elements equals the decelerate curve and on exiting elements equals the accelerate curve; no bare `ease` or `ease-in-out` on UI transitions.

text: For expressive or hero motion use `cubic-bezier(0.05, 0.7, 0.1, 1)` (emphasized-decelerate) to enter and `cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 0.8, 0.15)` (emphasized-accelerate) to exit, with durations from the medium-long range (see MDX-02). Do not treat the token `easing-emphasized` as a separate curve: in the web tokens it equals standard.
why: The emphasized pair has a longer settle tail, which reads as intentional rather than utilitarian.
check: stylesheet contains the exact emphasized pair when the page uses expressive entrances; `easing-emphasized` is not mapped to a third curve.

text: Use `cubic-bezier(0, 0, 1, 1)` (linear) only for motion with no spatial meaning: progress bars, spinners, scrubbing, colour or opacity cross-fades driven by time.
why: Linear speed looks mechanical for objects that move through space, and natural for things that fill or rotate at constant rate.
check: `linear` appears only on `progress`, spinner, or opacity/colour transitions.

text: Do not mix easing families. The "legacy" family (0.4, 0, 0.2, 1 / decelerate 0, 0, 0.2, 1 / accelerate 0.4, 0, 1, 1) is the Material 2 set; a product uses either legacy or standard/emphasized, not both.
why: Two families on one screen make equivalent interactions feel different.
check: count distinct easing families in the stylesheet: no page uses both the legacy and standard bezier sets.

text: When a spring is used, spatial properties (transform, size, border-radius) take damping 0.9 with stiffness 1400 (fast), 700 (default) or 300 (slow); effect properties (opacity, colour, blur) take damping 1.0 with stiffness 3800 (fast), 1600 (default) or 800 (slow).
why: Overshoot on position reads as life; overshoot on opacity or colour is invisible or wrong (opacity cannot exceed 1), so effects must be critically damped.
check: spring config for opacity/colour has damping ratio 1 (bounce 0); spatial springs have damping between 0.8 and 1.

text: Interactive state is a translucent overlay of the content colour on the container: hover 8%, focus 10%, pressed 10%, dragged 16% (latest tokens). The older v0.192 set used focus 12% and pressed 12%; pick one set and use it everywhere.
why: An overlay keeps contrast relationships intact in light and dark and works on any container colour without defining extra colours per state.
check: `:hover` styling uses an overlay (`color-mix`, `::before` with opacity, or an alpha-composited background) whose alpha is 0.08 plus or minus 0.01; focus and pressed alphas equal 0.10 (or 0.12 if the product pinned v0.192).

text: Draw the keyboard focus indicator as a 3 px ring offset 2 px outside the component (inner variant: 3 px inset, offset -3 px).
why: A thick offset ring stays visible against both the component and the surface; it exceeds the WCAG 2.2 minimum focus appearance of 2 px.
check: computed `outline-width` on `:focus-visible` is at least 3px (2px is the WCAG floor) and `outline-offset` is 2px; outline colour contrast against adjacent colours is at least 3:1.

text: Disabled controls: content (label, icon) at 38% opacity of `on-surface`; container fill at 12% of `on-surface`. Do not remove the control's shape.
why: Two distinct opacities keep a disabled button recognisable as a button while clearly inactive.
check: disabled button computed label opacity or alpha is 0.38 and fill alpha 0.12 (filled variants).

text: Use only these corner radii: 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 28, 32, 48 px and full (9999px). The 20, 32 and 48 steps exist only in the latest set. Directional variants: extra-small-top 4/4/0/0, large-top 16/16/0/0, large-start 16/0/0/16, large-end 0/16/16/0, extra-large-top 28/28/0/0.
why: A closed radius scale prevents arbitrary 6, 10, 14 px drift.
check: all computed `border-radius` values (excluding 50% and 9999px pills) are in the set.

text: Map component classes to corners: buttons, chips-as-pills, switch track, slider track and handle, nav indicator = full; assist chip = 8; cards (elevated, filled, outlined) = 12; outlined text field and menu = 4; filled text field = 4 top only; dialog = 28; checkbox box = 2.
why: Corner size scales with component size and prominence: small controls get small or full radii, big floating surfaces get large radii.
check: computed `border-radius` of `button`, `.card`, `dialog`, `input` against this map.
source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/material-components/material-web/main/tokens/versions/v0_192/_md-comp-dialog.scss (and the sibling component files for card, button, text field, chip, checkbox)

text: Elevation levels are 0, 1, 3, 6, 8, 12 dp. Resting buttons and cards sit at level 0; filled button rises to level 1 on hover; reserve levels 3 and above for menus, dialogs, FABs and floating UI.
why: Shadows signal "this floats above the content"; using them on everything removes the signal.
check: `box-shadow` blur radius of non-floating cards and buttons is at most 1-3 px or none; floating layers (menu, dialog, popover) have a stronger shadow than the page content.

text: Build surfaces from the container ladder, not from arbitrary greys. Light: lowest #ffffff, low #f7f2fa, container #f3edf7, high #ece6f0, highest #e6e0e9, dim #ded8e1, base surface #fef7ff. Dark: lowest #0f0d13, low #1d1b20, container #211f26, high #2b2930, highest #36343b, bright #3b383e, base surface #141218. (Baseline purple scheme; the tone numbers are neutral 100/96/94/92/90/87/98 light and 4/10/12/17/22/24/6 dark.)
why: Equal-step tonal surfaces create reliable layering and keep nested cards distinguishable in both themes.
check: nested surfaces (page, card, popover) differ by at least one container step; adjacent same-tone surfaces need a border.

text: Always pair a fill role with its `on-` role (on-primary on primary, on-primary-container on primary-container, on-surface on surface, and so on); do not put `on-surface` text on a primary fill. Baseline measured contrast: on-surface on surface 16.2:1 light / 14.4:1 dark; on-primary on primary 6.44 / 7.71; on-primary-container on primary-container 13.3 / 7.2; on-error on error 6.54 / 7.66.
why: Pairs are generated with a fixed tone gap (e.g. 40 against 100, 90 against 10), which guarantees contrast; ad-hoc pairs lose that guarantee.
check: compute contrast of every text/background pair: at least 4.5:1 for text under 24 px (or 18.66 px bold), 3:1 for large text and UI components.
source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/material-components/material-web/main/tokens/versions/v0_192/_md-sys-color.scss (ratios computed by the engine from the resolved hex)

text: Control boundaries (outlined field, outlined button, checkbox, switch outline) use the `outline` role: tone 50 light (#79747e, 4.33:1 on surface) / tone 60 dark (#938f99, 5.87:1). Use `outline-variant` (tone 80 light #cac4d0, 1.62:1; tone 30 dark #49454f, 1.99:1) only for dividers and decoration.
why: WCAG 1.4.11 needs 3:1 for the boundary of an interactive control; `outline-variant` deliberately fails that.
check: `border-color` on input, select, outlined button contrasts at least 3:1 with its surface; `hr`, card dividers may be lower.

text: Dark theme is a separate tone assignment: primary tone 80 (#d0bcff) on surface tone 6 (#141218), containers tone 30, on-colours tone 20 or 90; dark primary is lighter and less saturated than light primary (tone 40 #6750a4). Do not simply invert or reuse the light hex values.
why: Perceived brightness and halation differ on dark; tone-based assignment keeps contrast and saturation balanced.
check: dark `--primary` has higher luminance than the dark surface by at least 4.5:1 and lower chroma than the light primary.

text: Use the 15-style type scale as-is: display 57/64, 45/52, 36/44; headline 32/40, 28/36, 24/32; title 22/28, 16/24, 14/20; body 16/24, 14/20, 12/16; label 14/20, 12/16, 11/16 (size/line-height in px). Pick a role, do not pick a size.
why: A fixed set of size-and-leading pairs keeps hierarchy discrete; one role equals one look.
check: distinct computed `font-size` values on a page are a subset of {57, 45, 36, 32, 28, 24, 22, 16, 14, 12, 11} (apps) and each `line-height` equals the paired value.

text: Body copy is 16/24 (ratio 1.5) or 14/20 (ratio 1.43); small body 12/16 (1.33). Never set running text below 12 px; the 11 px label-small is for single-line labels only.
why: Leading ratio 1.33-1.5 holds for sizes up to 16 px; below 12 px legibility drops sharply on non-retina or low vision.
check: computed `font-size` of `p`, `li`, `td` is at least 14px (12px allowed for captions); `line-height / font-size` at least 1.33.

text: Apply the scale's tracking: display-large -0.25 px, headline and display-medium/small and title-large 0, title-medium +0.15, title-small and label-large +0.1, body-large +0.5, body-medium +0.25, body-small +0.4, label-medium and label-small +0.5 px. Small text gets positive tracking; only the largest display size gets negative.
why: Small sizes need extra air for letterform separation; large sizes look gappy and are tightened.
check: computed `letter-spacing` at font-size 11-16 px is greater than or equal to 0; below 0 only when font-size is at least 48 px.

text: Weights: display, headline, title-large and body are 400; title-medium/small and all labels are 500. For emphasised text step up one rung (400 to 500, 500 to 600) rather than jumping to 700; 700 appears only as the static-font bold reference (the emphasized label-large maps to it).
why: One-step weight changes preserve texture; strong jumps create banding on screens at small sizes.
check: computed `font-weight` on body text is 400; heading weights are within {400, 500, 600}; no more than three distinct weights on a page.

text: When the font is variable, set the optical size axis to roughly the pixel size (opsz 57 for 57 px down to 11 for 11 px) and keep wdth 100.
why: Optical sizing gives small text sturdier forms and large text finer ones without changing family.
check: `font-variation-settings` or `font-optical-sizing: auto` present on a variable font that exposes opsz.

text: Choose layout by window width class, not by device: compact 0-599, medium 600-839, expanded 840-1199, large 1200-1599, extra-large 1600 and up (dp or CSS px). Height classes: compact below 480, medium 480-899, expanded 900 and up. Treat width as the primary axis and consult height only for landscape phones.
why: Foldables, split screen and browser windows make device type meaningless; the available window is what constrains the layout.
check: media queries or container queries use breakpoints at 600 / 840 / 1200 / 1600 px (or document why Tailwind's 640 / 768 / 1024 / 1280 / 1536 is used instead).

text: Component sizes: button 40 px high, label 14/20 weight 500, 18 px icon; text field icons 24 px, outline 1 px resting and 2 px focused; navigation bar 80 px high with a 64 by 32 pill indicator and 24 px icons; switch track 52 by 32 with handle 16 (off) / 24 (on) / 28 (pressed); checkbox box 18 with a 2 px outline and 2 px corner; slider handle 20, track 4; assist chip 32 high with 1 px outline; icon button icon 24.
why: These are the fixed visual sizes; touch hit areas are enlarged separately without changing the visual size (M3 web components use an invisible larger target; the exact figure is not in the token files).
check: computed heights of `button` at 40px visual with hit area at least 44px through padding or a pseudo-element; switch width 52.

text: Review every screen against the 10 heuristics: visibility of system status; match to the real world; user control and freedom (undo, visible exit); consistency and standards; error prevention; recognition over recall; flexibility and efficiency (accelerators); aesthetic and minimalist design; help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors; help and documentation.
why: They are broad predictors of usability problems derived from a factor analysis of 249 problems and stable since 1994.
check: `visual` checklist pass; mechanical sub-checks: every async action has a pending/success state, destructive actions have undo or confirm, a cancel/back exit exists in every modal and flow.

text: Respond to input within 0.1 s so it feels direct (selection highlight, button press); keep results under 1 s so flow of thought is unbroken (show a busy indication past about 0.1 s of actual wait); for waits near or beyond 10 s show a percent-done indicator and a way to cancel; use an indeterminate spinner or running log only when progress is unknowable.
why: These three limits come from human perception: instantaneous, flow-preserving, attention-retaining.
check: measure input-to-first-paint: at most 100 ms for press/hover/selection feedback; at most 1000 ms for navigation results; operations over 10 s expose `<progress>` or `role="progressbar"` with a cancel control.

text: For waits of 2-10 s use a small, unobtrusive progress cue rather than a loud modal bar; time UI animations by the clock, not by how fast the machine happens to run.
why: A heavy indicator on a short wait causes display inertia (flashing changes the user cannot follow).
check: `visual`; animation durations use CSS time, not frame-count loops.

text: Define usability as five measurable components (learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors, satisfaction) plus utility; test early with about five users per round, individually, observing behaviour, and iterate rather than running one large study; retest after implementation.
why: Most major problems surface with five users, and structural problems are cheap to fix only early.
check: `visual` (process): each design brief names tasks and a pass criterion per component.

text: Run a heuristic evaluation with 3-5 independent evaluators, each timeboxed to 1-2 hours, with two passes (learn the flow, then look for violations), narrow scope (one task, one section, one user group, one device), and consolidate by clustering. Treat a violation as a flag, not a verdict, and confirm with users before deciding.
why: A single evaluator misses issues; independence prevents bias; context decides whether a violation matters.
check: `visual` (process): the critique step records issue, heuristic number, severity, and recommendation per evaluator.

text: Build hierarchy from contrast, scale and grouping. Use no more than about three sizes (small/medium/large: body 14-16 px, subheads 18-22 px, headline up to 32 px in the article's web example), no more than two large elements per view, at most three contrast levels, and about two primary plus two secondary colours.
why: If everything is emphasised nothing is, and too many similar colours or sizes flatten perceived hierarchy.
check: count distinct computed font-size tiers in a section (target 3); count elements with font-size at or above the headline tier per viewport (at most 2); count distinct hues in UI chrome (at most about 4 plus neutrals). Note: marketing heroes often exceed 32 px, so apply the ratio between tiers rather than the cap.

text: Do not rely on colour alone to carry hierarchy or meaning; reserve warm bright colours (red) for warnings and errors.
why: Colour-blind users lose colour-only differences, and a warning colour used decoratively dilutes alerts.
check: each status or hierarchy colour is paired with weight, size, icon or text; red/danger tokens appear only in error/destructive contexts.

text: Group with space first, containers second: related items sit closer to each other than to other groups (heading closer to its content than to the preceding section), and add borders or backgrounds only where spacing alone fails.
why: Proximity and common region create structure; extra boxes add clutter.
check: heading margin-bottom smaller than section margin-top above it; fewer than two nested bordered containers per section.

text: Squint-test every layout: blur the render with a 5-10 px radius and confirm the intended order of attention survives; also test with real content, because a strongly coloured image can hijack the hierarchy (it did at a 20 px blur in the article's example).
why: Blur strips text and reveals the true visual weight order.
check: render a blurred screenshot (gaussian 5-10 px) and compute that the CTA or headline region has the highest local contrast or saliency score; `visual` fallback.

text: Put the most important points in the first two paragraphs; start headings, subheadings, bullets and links with the information-carrying words (the first two words should give the gist); use bullets, numbers, bold key phrases and visible subheads; cut filler.
why: Unformatted text is scanned in an F shape: the first lines and the first words of each line get most fixations, so late or right-hand content is skipped.
check: first two words of each H2/H3/list item/link are not stopwords or the brand name; no paragraph block over about 5 lines without a break `[engine note]`; no link text that is just "click here", "more", "go".

text: Expect several scan patterns: F, layer cake (headings only), spotted (looking for a number or word), marking (eyes fixed while scrolling), bypassing (repeated line starts are skipped), commitment (rare full reading), and lawn mower for card or zigzag grids (left to right, then back right to left on the next row). Do not repeat the same leading words across list items.
why: Layouts shape the pattern, and repeated openings are skipped.
check: sibling list items/cards do not share the same first two words; grid cards put the key label at the start of each card.

text: Pull quotes, inline promotions and in-article ads interrupt reading; readers who were reading closely often drop into light scanning after hitting one. Place them at section ends or outside the reading column.
why: Eye-tracking showed attention falling after such inserts.
check: no pull quote or promo block interrupts a text run shorter than about 600 words `[engine note]`.

text: Keep the highest-priority content and the primary CTA above the fold and in the top half of the first viewport; secondary and related material goes lower.
why: About 57% of viewing time is above the fold, 65% of that in the top half of the viewport, and the 100 px just above the fold gets about twice the views of the 100 px below.
check: at 1440x900 and 390x844 the H1 and primary CTA bottoms are within the first viewport, ideally within the top 60%.

text: Avoid false floors: make sure something visibly continues below the viewport (cut-off text, next card peeking, a cropped image); a lone arrow is a weak substitute for real content continuity.
why: A fully self-contained first screen looks finished, so people do not scroll.
check: at common viewports an element straddles the fold line (starts above, ends below) or a next-section heading is visible within 120 px of the bottom edge.

text: Give long pages signposts at the top (anchor links, a short overview) and a reason to scroll (a glimpse of interesting content, a clear story), because people scroll only if the top promises value; most attention ends by the third screenful.
why: Scrolling is an extra action; 81% of viewing time falls in the first three screenfuls.
check: pages over 3 screens have in-page navigation or a section index and the most important proof appears before 2160 px of scroll depth.

text: Do not style real content like advertising or place it in ad zones (top banner, right rail) or next to ads; avoid small bordered promotional rectangles, text-in-image, animated or coloured promo boxes for important messages.
why: People learn to skip ad-like content and the skip spreads to neighbouring items (banner blindness).
check: key messages are not in a right rail card styled with a coloured rectangle plus text-in-image; headline/CTA text is live HTML, not baked into an image.

text: State plainly who you are and what you do in a short tagline or headline visible at first glance (no vague welcome message, no jargon, no feature slogan), and let the page's value proposition answer why choose you over others.
why: If purpose is not obvious at a glance, visitors leave.
check: H1 or the text directly beneath it names the product category and benefit; H1 does not start with "Welcome"; the tagline is visible without scrolling or animation.

text: Logo top-left, linking to the homepage on every page, plus an explicit Home or equivalent path; do not hide the home link inside a funnel in a way that traps users.
why: Users orient from the homepage and expect the logo there.
check: header `a` containing the logo has `href="/"` and sits in the leftmost 25% of the header at desktop widths.

text: Surface the top 1-4 user tasks as clear starting points; include a search box that looks like a box and is about 27 characters wide on sites large enough to need search; start link labels with the keyword; show real examples of content rather than only category names.
why: Visitors look for a starting task, the "little box" to type in, and concrete evidence of what is inside.
check: count of primary task links in the first viewport is between 1 and 4; search input width is at least 27ch (or about 25-27 characters) when present; hero area contains specific content examples or screenshots.

text: Do not decorate with generic stock imagery; use pictures that show real products, places, or people tied to the topic, and do not over-format critical areas such as navigation with heavy boxes and graphics.
why: Decorative or frivolous images are skipped and heavy formatting makes important areas look like ads.
check: `visual`; hero image has an alt describing product or subject, not "people smiling at laptop" `[engine note]`.

text: Keep homepages simple and conventional; minimise motion (do not animate just to draw attention; moving items read as ads), avoid autoplaying video, give a pause control for anything moving over 5 seconds, and let users reduce scroll effects; do not animate the logo, tagline or headline; load content immediately.
why: Unconventional layouts raise cognitive load; motion harms accessibility and delays reading; bounce probability rises 32% when load time goes from 1 s to 3 s (Google figure cited by NN/g).
check: headline and tagline have no scroll-triggered or entrance animation delaying visibility beyond 300 ms; any autoplay media over 5 s has a visible pause button; `prefers-reduced-motion` disables scroll effects.

text: Do not show popups or splash screens before the user has seen content, or right after login, or while a critical task is in progress; the only acceptable early overlays are legally required ones (consent, age check). Ask for feedback or an email after a meaningful action, preferably with a nonmodal overlay in a corner, and offer a static feedback link instead. Never stack overlays.
why: Overlays interrupt goals and are among the most disliked patterns; value should come before a request (reciprocity).
check: no `dialog`, modal or overlay opens within the first 5 s of page load or before a scroll or click event (except cookie/age); at most one overlay visible at a time.

text: Show prices, or representative prices, ranges or typical scenarios, for B2B and B2C offers; prefer a few worked scenarios over a complex calculator; do not make "contact sales" the only way to learn cost.
why: Price is the top information need: it fixes product category, enables comparison and budget planning, and hiding it reads as evasive.
check: pricing page or section contains at least one numeric price or range for each public tier; a "Contact us" only card is accompanied by a starting-from figure or sample scenario.

text: Product pages need at least: descriptive name, recognisable images with enlarged view, price including extra charges, options with selection, availability, clear add-to-cart with visible confirmation, concise description; reviews, extra images, video and related items are expected extras; show negative reviews too.
why: Missing information makes shoppers abandon or buy the wrong thing.
check: DOM contains product name, price element, images, option controls, availability text, and a cart button; confirmation state after add exists.

text: Show primary navigation on desktop; do not hide it behind a hamburger. On mobile, a hamburger is an acceptable trade-off, but a combination (some key links visible plus a menu) is better than fully hidden.
why: In a study of 179 participants on 6 sites, hidden navigation was used in 27% of desktop tasks versus 48% (visible) and 50% (combo); on mobile 57% hidden versus 86% combo; discoverability roughly halves, tasks take longer and feel harder.
check: at 1280 px wide the top-level navigation links are present as visible `a` elements in the header (not only inside a menu button); on 390 px at least the primary CTA or one key link is visible next to the menu button.

text: Put menus where people expect them: primary navigation in the header (websites) or left side (applications); utility navigation above primary and search at the top; local navigation on the left on desktop; footer menu at the bottom. Indicate the current location in the menu and with breadcrumbs on deep pages.
why: Users expect these locations; missing current-location indication is the most common menu mistake.
check: current page link has `aria-current="page"` and a visible style; pages deeper than two levels have breadcrumbs.

text: Make menu links high-contrast over any background (including carousels and images), large enough to tap or click, left-justified in vertical lists with key terms first, with a caret or arrow on items that open submenus.
why: Low contrast and tiny spaced links are a major source of failure; a caret tells people an item opens a submenu rather than navigates.
check: menu text contrast at least 4.5:1 against the rendered background; items with a submenu contain an icon or caret; menu link hit height at least 44 px on touch.

text: Use click- or tap-activated submenus, not hover-only ones; avoid cascading menus deeper than two tiers (use a mega menu of 2-3 tiers or routing pages); do not cover the whole screen with an open menu on large screens; consider sticky or partially sticky menus on long pages; put the most common dropdown items closest to the trigger.
why: Hover is unavailable on touch and keyboard, deep cascades cause drop-out errors, full-screen menus feel like page changes, and distance affects acquisition time (Fitts).
check: menu opens on `click` or `focus`+`Enter`, not only `:hover`; nesting depth of dropdowns at most 2.

text: Sticky headers: keep them as short as the readable text and tap targets allow (maximise content-to-chrome ratio), opaque with strong contrast to content (no translucent bars over text), with no animation except a shrinking logo or a partially persistent header that slides in over roughly 300-400 ms after a few pixels of upward scroll; no delayed "stalker" movement; first ask whether a sticky header is needed at all.
why: A sticky bar takes space on every screen; translucent ones make content hard to read; motion distracts.
check: computed header height at most about 64-72 px on desktop and 56 px on mobile `[engine note]`; header background alpha is 1; header transition-duration at most 400 ms.

text: Link labels carry information scent: describe the destination in the user's words; avoid "Click here", "Learn more", "Explore" as the only text; do not make the user guess what a button does.
why: People decide where to click from the label plus nearby context; vague labels hide good pages and cannot be told apart by a scanner.
check: no `a` or `button` text matches /^(click here|learn more|more|explore|read more|here)$/i unless an accessible name or adjacent heading disambiguates it (and prefer visible text).

text: Use progressive disclosure: show the few most-needed options first, reveal advanced ones on request with an obvious, clearly labelled control; keep to two levels (three at most); use a staged (wizard) flow only for steps with little interdependence.
why: It improves learnability, efficiency and error rate; the initial display signals importance.
check: advanced section sits behind a disclosure control with `aria-expanded` and a descriptive label; no more than 3 disclosure levels.

text: Keep forms short: drop any field that can be derived, collected later, or omitted; every cut field raises conversion. Show 1-2 optional fields at most, marked as optional.
why: Less effort per form means fewer abandonments; forms that follow guidelines had 78% first-try error-free submission versus 42% for violating forms in one CHI study.
check: count visible inputs per form step (flag more than about 7 `[engine note]`); optional fields are labelled "optional".

text: Use a single column, one field per row; short related fields (city/state/zip) may share a row; sequence fields in the conventional order; list the most common option values first; make Tab order follow visual order.
why: Multiple columns break vertical momentum.
check: form inputs share the same left edge except for allowed short pairs; DOM order equals visual order (no positive `tabindex`).

text: Put the visible label above its field (below is wrong, inside is wrong), close to its field and farther from other fields; section unrelated groups with headings or fieldsets; use real `label` elements.
why: Labels above fields scan fastest on mobile and short forms, and ambiguous spacing causes misreading.
check: each `input` has an associated visible `label` positioned above it; label-to-field gap smaller than field-to-next-label gap.

text: Do not use placeholder text as a label, and avoid it for essential hints; keep instructions and examples persistent outside the field. Floating labels are an improvement but still inferior to a label and hint outside the field when space allows.
why: Disappearing text strains memory, prevents checking work, hides the hint during errors, makes filled fields less noticeable and look pre-filled, has poor default contrast and inconsistent screen reader support.
check: every `input` with a `placeholder` also has a persistent visible `label`; placeholder text is not the only description of the format.

text: Size fields to the expected input (a city field of about 19 characters covered 99.9% of names), use radio buttons rather than a dropdown for 2-3 options, state any format or password rules up front, accept any reasonable format, and use the right mobile keyboard, autocomplete/autofill, defaults, history and computed values; do not autocorrect names, addresses or emails; allow paste.
why: Hidden rules and format policing create avoidable errors; filling fields for the user saves effort.
check: `autocomplete`, `type` or `inputmode` attributes present on email, tel, address, card fields; no `autocorrect` on name/email; password requirements text exists before the first error; no `onpaste` blocking.

text: Do not add Reset or Clear buttons; if a cancel is needed for sensitive data, make it much less prominent than Submit and keep it away from the fields; the primary action should be placed near the fields it submits.
why: Accidental deletion outweighs the rare wish to start over.
check: no `type="reset"` inputs/buttons; Cancel control has lower visual weight (ghost/link) than Submit.

text: Validate inline once the user finishes a field (on blur or at a natural completion), not while they are still typing and not on an untouched field; confirm success only where it helps (username available, password strength); give live guidance for error-prone fields such as new passwords.
why: Early errors feel hostile; immediate feedback reduces correction cost; success marks on trivial fields distract.
check: an error element does not appear until blur/submit; an empty untouched field never shows an error on focus loss unless the user has typed.

text: Show the error message adjacent to the field in error, in plain language, with redundant cues (red text, outline or tinted background, and an icon); a summary at the top may supplement but never replace the inline message; do not report errors only in tooltips; use modals sparingly (only for simple or optional-to-proceed cases); give extra help (support link, examples) after 3 or more repeated errors on the same form.
why: Proximity cuts working-memory load; colour alone fails colour-blind users; tooltips and summaries force extra steps and memory.
check: `aria-describedby` links the input to an error element placed within about one line of the field; error state has non-colour cue (icon or text); `aria-invalid="true"` set; error text contrast at least 4.5:1.

text: Write error messages that are human-readable (no codes), precise about the problem, constructive about the fix, polite, and never blame the user (avoid "invalid", "illegal", "incorrect"); preserve the user's input so they can edit it; offer likely fixes as one-tap options when you can; use severity-appropriate presentation (inline or toast for minor issues, modal for blockers); avoid humour in frequent errors.
why: Heuristic 9 and the efficiency principle: protect effort and recover quickly.
check: error strings do not match /invalid|illegal|incorrect|error code|\b[A-Z]{2,}-?\d{3,}\b/i; form fields retain their value after a failed submit.

text: Make touch targets at least 1 cm by 1 cm physical (about 38 CSS px at 96 dpi; use 44 px as the working minimum), leave about 2 mm between neighbouring targets and make the target big enough before adding space, enlarge primary or in-motion actions, avoid tiny map pins, dot indicators and swatches as the only tap target, and expand hit areas beyond the visible glyph.
why: Small and crowded targets slow taps and cause slips; tapping a small item that is easy to see is the view-tap asymmetry trap.
check: `getBoundingClientRect()` width and height of every interactive element on a 390 px viewport at least 44 CSS px (use 38 as the hard floor); gap between adjacent targets at least 8 CSS px.

text: Build trust with the four levers: design quality (clear organisation, appropriate colour and imagery, no typos or broken links), up-front disclosure (contact info, what the base price includes, extra fees, delivery windows), comprehensive correct current content (including photos of the process, not only the end result), and connection to the wider web (third-party reviews carry more weight than on-site testimonials).
why: Users judge credibility fast from these signals; spelling errors and hidden costs lower it sharply.
check: contact method or utility link visible in header or footer; fees and inclusions stated near the price; spell-check passes; no 4xx links in a crawl; reviews link to an external source where available.

text: Do not gate content or demand personal details (address, email, login) before the user has seen value; avoid long quote forms as the way to learn cost.
why: Asking too much too soon breaches trust and drives people away.
check: primary informational content is reachable without a form; first-step required fields number two or fewer.

text: Write microcopy in the order clarity, concision, character: signpost location, give information scent, say why it matters to the user, use terms the audience knows; front-load the key word ("Out of stock - notify me"); keep titles under about 60 characters and descriptions under about 160 so search results do not truncate them; add personality last and tailor it to the audience.
why: Busy users read only the first words; truncated meta text loses meaning.
check: `<title>` length at most 60 chars, meta description at most 160 chars; button labels start with the action or key noun; `visual` for tone.

text: Do not use deceptive patterns: obstruction (hard to cancel or decline), visual or wording tricks (double negatives, moved close buttons), nagging after a decline, emotionally manipulative decline text, sneaking or preselected extras. Persuasion (social proof, anchoring, scarcity) is acceptable only when the facts are true and the user can easily choose otherwise.
why: They harm users, are common (over 10% of sampled shops in a 2019 study) and are increasingly illegal; they hit vulnerable users hardest.
check: decline/cancel/close controls are present, same prominence tier as accept, and not moved off the dialog; no pre-checked paid add-ons (`input[type=checkbox][checked]` near price); decline labels are neutral; cancel flow takes no more clicks than signup.

text: Decide how the body text looks before anything else: pick base size, line height, measure and typeface for `p` first, then derive headings, captions and components from them.
why: Body text is the largest share of any page, so those four values set legibility and the first impression.
applies: all (strongest for content, docs, long-form, marketing body copy).
check: the four computed values (`font-size`, `line-height`, characters per line, `font-family`) exist as tokens on `p` before heading tokens do; `visual` for process.

text: Judge each typographic choice by whether it makes the message easier to receive, not by how it looks in isolation; make the most important element of a text (a number, a warning, the product name) the visually dominant one.

text: Use the three marks for different jobs: hyphen (-) for line-end hyphenation and compound words/phrasal adjectives (five-dollar bills, high-school grades; not after -ly adverbs; usually not after prefixes such as nonprofit); en dash (–, `–`) for ranges (1880–1912, pages 330–39) and for connections or contrasts between pairs (conservative–liberal); em dash (—, `—`) for a break in the sentence stronger than a comma and weaker than a colon or parentheses.

check: whatever unit is used for `max-width`, confirm the actual characters per line by measurement (PT-SZ-08), not by the nominal `ch` number.

text: Be careful tying a mobile layout to pixel-width media queries: as phones have grown, thresholds drift upward, and a mobile layout can then appear in large desktop windows. A CSS pixel on a phone and on a desktop display are not the same visual size because reading distance differs.
why: Media queries cannot tell desktop from mobile; the author even suggests JavaScript device detection, which [engine note] is not recommended here (use container queries and input/pointer media features).
check: media query min/max-width thresholds ≤ ~1024 px for "mobile" layouts; `visual` at 768 and 1024.

text: Mark paragraph starts with either a first-line indent of 1-4 times the font size (`text-indent: 1em` to `4em`) or space between paragraphs, never both. Skip the indent on the first paragraph of a text and on paragraphs right after a heading. Use the low end in narrow blocks (3 in or less), the high end in wide ones.
why: One signal suffices; an indent smaller than the type size is invisible, bigger than four times detaches the first line from the left edge.
check: for `p + p`: either `text-indent` > 0 or `margin-top`/`margin-bottom` > 0 but not both; `text-indent` between 1em and 4em when used.

text: Default to left-aligned text. Centre only short phrases and titles (a name on letterhead, a major section heading), and use hard line breaks to choose where centred lines break; never centre a whole text block.
why: Both edges of a centred block are uneven, so reading is harder and the block aligns poorly with other elements. Books, newspapers and magazines rarely centre text.
check: `text-align: center` on `p` or blocks with > 3 lines is a fail (T20 uses > 200 characters).

text: Justified text is a taste choice, but if used it must be hyphenated; on the web, where the browser's justification engine is rudimentary, prefer left alignment. Never distribute justification space between letters.
why: Word spacing in each line is stretched; without hyphenation gaps become huge. Letter-spacing variation line to line wrecks the font's designed spacing.
check: `text-align: justify` requires computed `hyphens: auto` and `lang` set; `letter-spacing` is constant across lines.

text: Hyphenation: mandatory with justified text; optional on a left-aligned rag (turn it off if it does not help; it improves evenness but not legibility); essential as lines get shorter; always off in headings (`hyphens: none`). Use a soft hyphen to fix a word that hyphenates badly.
why: With few words per line, breaking only at spaces leaves ragged or gappy lines; headings are short and hyphens there cause more harm than good.
check: computed `hyphens` on headings is `none`/`manual`; on narrow columns (< 40 characters) prose has `hyphens: auto` or text is not justified.

text: Add 5-12 percent letterspacing (`letter-spacing: 0.05em` to `0.12em`) to all-caps and small-caps text, especially at small sizes; do not exceed the point where extra letters would fit in the gaps.
why: Capitals are drawn to sit next to lowercase, so they look too tight in a row. Include the spacing in the style definition so it is never forgotten.
check: for `text-transform: uppercase` or `font-variant-caps: small-caps`: computed `letter-spacing / font-size` in 0.05-0.12.

text: Leave lowercase body text at default spacing. Body-text fonts are spaced for about 9-13 pt; letterspace lowercase only below about 9 pt (12 px) to keep letters distinct, and remove letterspacing from lowercase at headline sizes.
why: Fonts tuned for the text-size band need the opposite correction at the extremes.
check: body `letter-spacing` 0 at 13-17 px; display sizes may be negative (see T-LS-01); text < 12 px may be slightly positive.

text: Keep kerning on at all sizes and use the font's built-in metrics for spacing; do not replace font spacing with algorithmic "optical" spacing except to rescue a font with bad spacing or one pushed beyond its design range.
why: Kerning pairs and spacing are the designer's most consequential work; synthetic spacing guesses wrong on asymmetric letters (a, r, t) and creates jitter in body text.
check: computed `font-kerning` is not `none`; no CSS that zeroes `letter-spacing` overrides within words; `visual`.

text: Make headings only slightly bigger than body: use the smallest increment that is visibly different (for 12 pt body, go to 12.5 or 13 pt, about +4 to +8 percent); do not follow the browser habit of doubling.
why: Emphasis does not need a doubling; small size changes plus space and bold already separate a heading. In-document headings differ in job from display type (hero/headline).
applies: docs | articles | long-form prose. Not a rule for marketing display type (see section 5).
check: for in-article `h2`/`h3`: `font-size` ratio to body ≤ about 1.25 when body is ≥ 16 px (soft; the book states +4-8 percent in print). For product pages see T-SC-03.

text: Limit heading levels to three, two if possible; cure over-deep outlines structurally rather than inventing more styles (bold, italic, underline, caps, indent) to tell levels apart.
why: Readers cannot hold more than three levels; stacking tricks creates train-wreck headings.
check: count of distinct heading levels used in one article ≤ 3 (`h1` title plus two or three).

text: Style headings in sentence case, bold (or just regular), left-aligned, not underlined, not all caps, not italic, and not centred; heading text should be a phrase, not a full sentence if caps would be needed.
why: Bold is easier to read and stands out better than italic; all-caps and Title Case read as shouting or as titles; headings that are sentences are too long for caps.
applies: docs | articles | long-form; landing hero headings may be centred (exception in section 5).
check: `h2-h4`: computed `text-transform: none`, `text-decoration: none`, `font-style: normal`; `text-align` not centre in running prose.

text: Emphasise headings with space above and below first (more above than below so a heading belongs to the text it introduces), then with small size or weight changes. If paragraphs are separated by space, the space around headings must be larger still.
why: White space adds emphasis without adding a mark; headings relate to what follows, not what precedes.
check: `margin-top` of `h2/h3` > `margin-bottom`, ratio ≥ 1.2 (the book gives no figure; T-SC-08 suggests ≥ 1.4); heading gap > paragraph gap; top margin not so large that a heading falls off the first screen.

text: If a bold heading looks heavy, reduce its size by 0.5-1 pt instead of raising it; use two indent levels at most even if there are more heading levels; put a rule above a heading rather than below it so it separates sections instead of tying the heading to its own text.
why: Darker colour compensates size; random indents look messy; a rule above divides the previous section from the new one.
check: `visual`; `border-top` rather than `border-bottom` on section headings (soft).

text: Keep headings with the text they introduce: prevent hyphenation, and prevent a break between a heading and its first line (`break-after: avoid`, `break-inside: avoid`, `text-wrap: balance` as [engine note] aids).
why: A heading stranded at the bottom of a page or column looks like an error.
check: `h1-h6` have `break-after: avoid` in print stylesheets; none at the bottom of a page in a print preview.

text: For hierarchical numbering use tiered numbers (1, 1.1, 1.1.1), not Roman numerals, letters or romanettes; produce them with CSS counters (`counter-increment`, `counter()` with nested counters).
why: Numbers alone avoid ambiguity (is lowercase `i` first or ninth?), and a tiered number is unique so position in the hierarchy is clear.
check: numbered headings use digits with dots only.

text: Format block quotations in a slightly smaller size and tighter line spacing, indented 2-5 em on the left (0.5 to 1 in in print) and optionally the same on the right; no quotation marks around them; keep them rare and edited, not a dump of source text.
why: The indent must be noticeable but not shrink the measure below range; long block quotes signal "skip this" to readers.
applies: docs | articles. (Pull quotes in marketing pages are a separate display style.)
check: `blockquote`: `margin-left`/`padding-inline-start` between 2em and 5em; no leading/trailing quote glyphs; line-height ≤ body.

text: Use real list markup (`ul`/`ol`) for bullets and numbers. The marker may be a different font or a smaller size than the item; markers should be only as large as needed (hollow bullets read as subtler than solid), never an asterisk, and simple geometric dingbats beat pictorial ones.
why: Manual lists are error-prone; an oversized marker competes with the text.
check: no lines starting with `•`, `-`, `*` or `1.` typed inside `p`; marker size ≤ 1.1em (soft).
